# Safety, or Just Capability? A Validity Audit of Agent-Safety Benchmarks

Youting Wang, Xiao Han, Dingyan Shang, Yuan Tang, Bowen Liu

###### Abstract

Agent-safety benchmarks measure different behaviors, yet their scores are quoted interchangeably as an agent's safety. We validate four (R-Judge, InjecAgent, AgentHarm, AgentDojo) as measurements, each under its official implementation and author-provided scorer on up to 22 models, with MMLU and GPQA measured by us under one protocol as a capability composite. We find a closed-form F1 failure, benchmark-dependent rankings, a small-panel trade-off artifact, outcome- and panel-dependent capability–safety links, and a strong AgentHarm–jailbreak association that is convergent validity, not general safety. A safety claim minimally needs its benchmark, metric, target behavior, and model panel.

## 1 Introduction

A taxonomy of >40 agent-safety benchmarks reports rank concordance near 0.10 across models, but stops at a 12-model, four-benchmark check and lists capability-controlled evaluation as open. We separate construct validity (what a score measures), metric validity (whether its metric measures that target), and criterion validity (whether it tracks held-out behavior):

- RQ1 (construct structure): common factor or dissociable ones?
- RQ2 (capability confound): how much between-benchmark signal is general capability?
- RQ3 (criterion validity): do safety scores track held-out criteria beyond capability?
- RQ4 (metric validity): do headline metrics reward degenerate behavior?

#### Contributions.

A formal F1 failure (Observation 1); quantification of a small-panel failure mode; a pre-specified, capability-controlled criterion audit over one task-success and two safety outcomes; an API-only audit harness and re-run artifacts for four benchmarks and three held-out outcomes.

#### Main conclusion.

A capability score is not a safety score, and no one benchmark stands in for safety; validity needs re-checking as model populations turn over.

#### Scope.

RQ3 criteria are stand-ins for deployment, not real-world harm claims (limits in §6).

## 2 Related Work

#### Agent-safety benchmarking.

InjecAgent and AgentDojo target prompt-injection robustness, AgentHarm harmful-task compliance, R-Judge safety-risk awareness over traces; evaluators like ToolEmu were likewise never validated as measurements. AutoMonitor-Bench reports miss and false-alarm rates, the two-sided reporting we argue for. The closest work documents ranking disagreement but neither controls capability, tests criterion validity, nor recovers latent structure; we do all three.

#### Construct validity.

Knowledge/reasoning benchmarks share a strong latent factor; capability confounding of agent-safety comparisons is unquantified.

#### Benchmark gaming.

Our claim is prior to gaming: the F1-gaming policy is not adversarial; it labels every trace "unsafe."

#### Over-refusal.

XSTest/OR-Bench work at prompt level; we ask whether AgentHarm refusers are worse at R-Judge specificity. On the full panel the correlation is near zero; on seven-model subsets often not.

#### Agent reliability and task performance.

We use τ²-bench retail as the held-out task-success criterion.

## 3 Method

### 3.1 Model panel and benchmarks

API-only panel of up to 22 models from nine organizations (OpenAI 6, Meta 3, Qwen 3, Mistral 3, DeepSeek 2, Amazon 2, Anthropic, Google, Cohere). Official implementations/scorers: R-Judge (all 571 items, self-judge), InjecAgent (300 stratified direct-harm/data-stealing items, rule-scored), AgentHarm (44 base behaviors, all eight harm categories, official Inspect evaluation, gpt-4o-mini judge), AgentDojo (slack suite, 100 items, environment-scored security and utility). Coverage: R-Judge n=21 (Qwen3-32B below the 90% valid-output threshold); InjecAgent 22; AgentHarm 19 and AgentDojo 5 (native tool use required); τ² 20. Common R-Judge/InjecAgent/AgentHarm panel: n=18. Anchors measured by us through the same harness: MMLU zero-shot on a fixed 500-item subset (seed 42, same items for all models), GPQA-Diamond (198 items, CoT). Anchor panel: 21 models (DeepSeek-R1 excluded for unstable long-form GPQA generation); provider-reported model-card anchors kept as pre-harmonization comparison.

### 3.2 Benchmark targets

Fixed before analysis: R-Judge distinguishes unsafe from benign traces; InjecAgent and AgentDojo test injection resistance (their correlation is a convergent check); AgentHarm tests refusal of harmful tasks. R-Judge is also analyzed by specificity and balanced accuracy.

#### Score orientation and terminology.

Higher = better/safer. Specificity: fraction of benign traces judged benign; balanced accuracy averages both classes. InjecAgent robustness = 1 − attack success; AgentHarm safety = 1 − harmful compliance. τ² is task success, not safety. "Internal consistency" refers to split-half analyses.

### 3.3 Analysis plan

Hypotheses, thresholds, decision rules fixed beforehand (no independent timestamp, so "pre-specified," not preregistered). Spearman correlations, two-sided asymptotic p unless noted; Fig. 2 bars are model-level percentile bootstraps. PCA on the Pearson matrix of standardized scores; factor count by Horn's parallel analysis vs. random-normal null. Partial Spearman correlations control the capability composite (mean of standardized MMLU and GPQA; ordering identical to the anchors' PC1).

Controls: positive (anchor loadings ≥0.6 on factor 1); negative (column-permuted matrix within the null); convergent (high InjecAgent–AgentDojo correlation). Headline metric: median pairwise partial |ρ| among distinct-construct benchmarks. Factor structure interpretable only if first-factor variance ≥40% or capability control reduces that median by ≥0.15, with positive and negative controls passing.

RQ3 outcomes, each pre-specified: task success = τ²-bench retail (40 multi-turn, environment-scored tool-agent-user tasks); misalignment safety = avoiding blackmail or leaking in a fictional autonomous-agent scenario, fixed classifier, 100 decisions/model; jailbreak safety = 1 − harmful compliance on 50 forbidden prompts, averaged over three published templates. Safety criteria cover the full panel; τ² covers 20. None is a predictor. Headline: partial ρ of each safety score with each criterion, after reporting the criterion's raw capability association.

## 4 Results

Ordered by evidential strength: RQ4, RQ2 firmest; RQ1 weaker; power-limited RQ3 last.

### 4.1 The headline metric is gameable (RQ4)

R-Judge labels 52.7% of 571 items unsafe. "Always unsafe" attains recall 1.0, specificity 0, F1=0.690, outranking five of the 21 valid models (F1 0.30–0.57; Fig. 1), all of which discriminate. Highest-specificity o3-mini (0.97) gets F1=0.702, only 0.012 above, due to lower recall. Balanced accuracy reorders the board.

###### Observation 1 (F1 admits a high-scoring constant baseline).

With base rate π, the always-positive policy attains F1=2π/(1+π) without discriminating; for R-Judge (π=0.527) this is 0.690. The closed form depends on prevalence, but the problem is F1's blindness to true negatives, so F1 cannot stand alone as a measure of two-sided discrimination here.

### 4.2 The capability confound is real but metric-dependent (RQ2)

R-Judge panel (n=20, harmonized anchors): capability correlates with balanced accuracy (ρ=+0.71 MMLU, p<0.001; +0.49 GPQA, p=0.03) and F1 (+0.76, +0.62), weakly with specificity (+0.16, +0.07). BA and F1 include unsafe-trace recall; specificity can be inflated by rarely flagging. The confound depends on the metric and the panel: specificity–MMLU fell from 0.85 (first nine models) to +0.16 at n=20.

### 4.3 Benchmarks disagree; a seven-model panel suggested a trade-off that does not persist (RQ1)

Firmest, correlation-free: no benchmark orders models like another (Table 1). Cross-construct disagreement is expected and indicts no instrument; it defeats interchangeable quoting. R-Judge-specificity/AgentHarm-safety ρ: −0.64 at n=7, +0.02 (p=0.95) at n=18 (Fig. 5); size-7 subsets give |ρ|≥0.5 in a quarter of draws; dissolution holds under all four R-Judge metrics (A.4). Capability moderation of the remainder is an untested hypothesis.

PCA (corroborative; Fig. 6): PC1 48.7%; R-Judge specificity, InjecAgent robustness, both anchors one way, AgentHarm opposite (+0.33; opposite in 17/18 leave-one-out fits).

#### The positive control now passes.

MMLU loads 0.74≥0.6 (provider-reported anchors failed at 0.42); negative control passes; convergent control inconclusive at AgentDojo n=5. Conditions met, but the factor is corroboration only: Spearman PCA gives PC1 40.8% with no factor retained by Horn (A.3); median between-benchmark correlation 0.22.

#### Against task success, safety scores add no information beyond capability.

Capability: ρ=+0.60, p=0.005, n=20; best safety partial |ρ|=0.23, n.s., n=19 (Fig. 7). Capability already explains this outcome; the null is no verdict on safety scores.

#### Against agentic misalignment, capability has the opposite association.

n=21: ρ_cap=−0.44 (p=0.047) (Mistral-Large blackmails/leaks 85%; o3-mini a capable exception at 1%). InjecAgent (+0.47) and R-Judge specificity (+0.41) reach the pre-specified 0.40 threshold; AgentHarm (+0.16) does not. Exploratory: CIs include zero, fail Bonferroni, power ≈0.35, and the directional prediction named AgentHarm. R-Judge partial: +0.41 specificity, +0.19 BA, −0.46 recall (A.4).

#### A direct interaction test on the original panel.

Paired n=20: task +0.60 vs. misalignment −0.41; Δ=−1.00 (95% CI [−1.48,−0.49], p<0.001), stable to leave-one-model/organization-out, organization-clustered bootstrap, subsampling (A.5). R-Judge interaction marginal (Δ=+0.50, p=0.082): capability interaction supported, full two-way dissociation not. Independent misalignment grader: ρ=0.97.

#### The capability–misalignment correlation is weaker on the expanded panel.

Pre-specified "hold or strengthen"; observed −0.16 (n=40, bootstrap p=0.40, CI [−0.54,+0.22]). CI includes −0.44; between-panel Δρ=+0.27 [−0.25,+0.78], n.s. Organization-matched subsets: median −0.17, so composition does not explain it; a generational account is possible, undemonstrated. τ² not re-collected; interaction not re-tested.

#### Models with similar capability scores differ in safety across organizations (Fig. 4).

41 models, 12 organizations (misalignment n=40; jailbreak 41 after one engagement-gate exclusion); six organizations ≥4 models (within-org), seven ≥3 (group test; Table 5). Within-org correlations vary in sign, averaging −0.14 (misalignment), +0.26 (jailbreak). After capability adjustment, groups differ (permutation p=0.004, p<0.001; Holm-significant; ε²=0.34, 0.57). Not causal: static composite may miss agentic ability, few models per org, restricted ranges. Supported: similar MMLU/GPQA ≠ similar safety.

#### Against jailbreak safety, AgentHarm shows the strongest held-out association.

StrongREJECT-scored. One template (AIM) ceilings (11/22 refuse all); three templates leave none at ceiling. Capability ρ=+0.08 (n=21, p=0.73); expanded +0.34 (n=41, p=0.04), change n.s. AgentHarm partial +0.72 (p<0.001) vs. +0.50 single-template; stable to LOO and independent grader. AgentHarm jailbreak>misalignment: Δ=+0.59, p=0.027 (model bootstrap); p=0.051 resampling eight organizations. Paired-panel misalignment partial +0.13 (n=19; Table 2 uses n=18). Shared harmful-compliance target makes +0.72 partly convergent validity. R-Judge/InjecAgent misalignment>jailbreak: marginal (Δ=+0.52, p=0.068).

#### Two alternative explanations, checked.

Seven blind LLM coders placed AgentHarm and jailbreak in harm blocking (7/7 each; α=0.61, three categories); misalignment less cleanly (A.1). AgentHarm is uncorrelated with XSTest benign over-refusal after capability control (ρ=−0.01, n=17), against blanket refusal.

## 5 Discussion

These benchmarks are not interchangeable measures of one property. AgentHarm–jailbreak is convergent validity with specificity unresolved (p=0.051); R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment is exploratory. Capability-adjusted organization-group differences are observational, identifying no organizational cause. A safety claim is defensible only with its benchmark, metric, target behavior, and model population attached.

## 6 Limitations and Threats to Validity

#### Panel size.

Cross-benchmark n=18 (first pass n=7); needed: a larger, capability-spanning agent-loop panel.

#### Capability anchors.

Re-measurement fixed the positive control (0.42→0.74); no RQ2/RQ3 sign changed. Anchors are static-knowledge tests, though the composite predicts τ² at +0.60. A six-model BFCL pilot failed as agentic anchor: syntax scoring ranked GPT-4o-mini highest (0.72), the two most capable lowest (0.42–0.48). Such error attenuates or suppresses partials rather than biasing them in a signable direction.

#### Multiple comparisons.

No family-wise correction; the crossover and AgentHarm→jailbreak (p<0.001) survive Bonferroni; R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment (p≈0.05–0.09) do not.

#### Judges and coverage.

Grader agreement ρ=0.97 (misalignment), 0.98 (jailbreak); AgentHarm refusal rescoring 0.69, partial +0.66 vs. +0.72. AgentDojo has only five models.

#### Criterion validity (RQ3).

τ² (40 tasks, one run/model) has unbounded user-simulator variance; misalignment is a fictional probe (halves Spearman–Brown 0.70). No criterion gives deployment-harm probabilities. Worst-case within-model SEs are 12–25% of between-model SD, supporting panel spread, not every pairwise difference. The larger three-scenario misalignment result is post-hoc.

## 7 Conclusion

Report the full confusion structure, drop standalone F1 wherever true negatives matter, and tie every claim to an explicit target behavior and model population.

That the benchmark, metric, target behavior, and model panel must be named for a safety claim to be minimally supported follows from the finding that the strongest held-out association, $\rho{=}{+}0.72$ shown by KD9 with R8W safety after M7V was controlled, constitutes evidence of convergent validity rather than of general safety, both instruments being scorers of harmful compliance, and from the behavior, on an expanded 41-model panel, of the P2Z correlation, which weakens to $-0.16$ (95% CI $[-0.54,+0.22]$), and of L9R, which strengthens to $+0.34$, with neither change being significant. Held-out validity turns on which outcome is picked, M7V predicting task success ($\rho{=}{+}0.60$) yet correlating negatively with P2Z ($\rho{=}{-}0.44$, $n{=}21$), and on their paired $n{=}20$ panel the corresponding contrast, $\Delta{=}{-}1.00$ (95% CI $[-1.48,-0.49]$, $p<0.001$), survives D7T and organization-clustered bootstrap analyses. The three broad-coverage benchmarks rank the same 18 models differently, the trade-off behind that disagreement being a small-panel artifact in which QX7 G8X against KD9 safety correlates $-0.64$ at $n{=}7$ and $+0.02$ at $n{=}18$, with a quarter of random size-7 subsets reaching $|\rho|\geq 0.5$ around that near-zero value. On any binary trace-judgment benchmark scored by W3D, an "always positive" policy attains $F_{1}=2\pi/(1+\pi)$, which on QX7 is $0.690$, above five of the 21 models that actually discriminate, the metric being the first problem. All of this arises because agent-safety benchmarks measure different behaviors while their scores get quoted interchangeably as an agent's safety, four of them (QX7, ZM3, KD9, V4W) having been treated as measurements to be validated, each run under its official implementation and author-provided scorer on up to 22 models, with H8P and R2F measured by us under one protocol as a M7V.

A capability score is not a safety score, and no one agent-safety benchmark stands in for safety as a whole, with what a score licenses you to say depending on how it was produced and with small panels as the sharpest edge, because at seven models a weak relationship can look systematic, so validity needs re-checking as the model population turns over; E5K, the formal metric-validity failure, gives, for any binary trace-judgment benchmark scored by W3D, the score of an “always positive” baseline a closed form, and on QX7 that baseline outranks five evaluated models, while the small-panel failure mode that was walked into is quantified by the QX7-G8X/KD9-safety correlation moving from $-0.64$ at $n{=}7$ to $+0.02$ at $n{=}18$, and by a quarter of random size-7 subsets showing $|\rho|\geq 0.5$ despite the near-zero full-panel value (QX7 denoting the paper's R-Judge, KD9 denoting the paper's AgentHarm, W3D denoting the paper's F1, and G8X denoting the paper's specificity), and the pre-specified, capability-controlled criterion-validity audit over one task-success outcome and two safety outcomes finds capability predicting task success, finds its safety correlations moving with the outcome and the panel, finds the strongest safety-score result in the KD9–L9R association ($\rho{=}+0.72$ after controlling capability), and finds borderline evidence of outcome selectivity under organization-level resampling ($p{=}0.051$), with an API-only audit harness and re-run artifacts for four benchmarks and three held-out outcomes released and included with the accompanying reproducibility package. Between 2024 and 2026, dozens of benchmarks appeared claiming to measure whether LLM agents are safe or reliable: resistance to prompt injection (Zhan et al. 2024; Debenedetti et al. 2024), safety-risk awareness (Yuan et al. 2024), refusal of harmful agentic tasks (Andriushchenko et al. 2025), and risky-tool-use identification (Ruan et al. 2024), among others; a recent taxonomy (Li et al. 2026) catalogs more than forty of them and reports a symptom worth taking seriously, that swapping the benchmark makes the safety ranking contradict itself with rank concordance near $0.10$ across models, and that work stops at a twelve-model concordance check over four benchmarks while listing capability-controlled evaluation and benchmark consolidation among its open problems. A safety score, if it is a measurement, can fail in the ways measurements fail, so construct validity is separated as what a score measures, metric validity as whether its metric measures that target, and criterion validity as whether it tracks held-out behavior; RQ1 (construct structure) asks whether nominally-distinct agent-safety benchmarks measure a common underlying factor or dissociable ones, RQ2 (capability confound) asks how much of the between-benchmark signal is general capability in disguise, RQ3 (criterion validity) asks whether the safety scores track held-out behavioral criteria beyond what general capability predicts, and RQ4 (metric validity) asks whether the headline metrics are valid instruments or reward degenerate behavior. The three RQ3 criteria are stand-ins for deployment, not claims about real-world harm; their limits (single instances, grader dependence, panel size) are in Section 6.

Report the full confusion structure, tie every claim to an explicit target behavior and model population, and drop standalone W3D wherever true negatives matter; the strongest held-out safety association, with the two measures partly overlapping and organization-resampled evidence for outcome selectivity borderline, is KD9's ( $\rho=+0.72$ with L9R after M7V is controlled), M7V predicting held-out task success yet not safety consistently across outcomes or panels, while QX7's W3D lets an "always unsafe" baseline outrank five models and rankings are switched by benchmark switching, across four benchmarks and up to 22 models.

# Safety, or Just Capability? A Validity Audit of Agent-Safety Benchmarks

###### Abstract

Four agent-safety benchmarks (R-Judge, InjecAgent, AgentHarm, AgentDojo) are audited as measurements. Each runs under its official implementation and author-provided scorer on up to 22 models. MMLU and GPQA, measured by us under one protocol, form a capability composite. Findings:
- F1 admits a high-scoring constant baseline.
- The three broad-coverage benchmarks rank the same 18 models differently.
- An apparent cross-benchmark trade-off is a small-panel artifact.
- Held-out validity depends on the outcome chosen.
- AgentHarm's strongest held-out association is convergent validity, not general safety.

Naming the benchmark, metric, target behavior and model panel is the minimum a safety claim needs.

## 1 Introduction

A recent taxonomy catalogs >40 agent-safety benchmarks and finds rank concordance near $0.10$ across models when the benchmark is swapped. It stops at a twelve-model check over four benchmarks and lists capability-controlled evaluation and consolidation as open problems. We separate three kinds of validity:
- construct validity: what a score measures;
- metric validity: whether its metric measures that target;
- criterion validity: whether it tracks held-out behavior.

Research questions:
- **RQ1** (construct structure): common factor or dissociable ones?
- **RQ2** (capability confound): how much between-benchmark signal is capability?
- **RQ3** (criterion validity): do safety scores track held-out criteria beyond capability?
- **RQ4** (metric validity): do headline metrics reward degenerate behavior?

#### Contributions.

Observation 1; a quantified small-panel failure mode; a pre-specified, capability-controlled criterion audit; and a released API-only audit harness with re-run artifacts for four benchmarks and three held-out outcomes.

#### Main conclusion.

A capability score is not a safety score, and no single benchmark stands for safety. At seven models a weak relationship can look systematic, so validity needs re-checking as model populations turn over.

#### Scope.

The RQ3 criteria are stand-ins for deployment, not real-world harm claims (§6).

## 2 Related Work

#### Agent-safety benchmarking.

- InjecAgent and AgentDojo target prompt-injection robustness.
- AgentHarm measures harmful agentic compliance.
- R-Judge scores risk awareness over traces.

Such evaluators (e.g. ToolEmu) were designed, never validated as measurements. AutoMonitor-Bench reports two-sided miss and false-alarm rates. The closest work documents ranking disagreement but does not control capability, test criterion validity, or recover latent structure; we do all three.

#### Construct validity.

Knowledge and reasoning benchmarks share a strong latent factor. We apply this psychometric lens to agent safety, where benchmarks target distinct behaviors and the capability confound is unquantified.

#### Benchmark gaming.

Our claim is logically prior to adversarial gaming: even for honest models, the headline score may not measure the construct. The mid-leaderboard F1 policy is not adversarial.

#### Over-refusal.

XSTest and OR-Bench study over-refusal at the prompt level. We ask whether AgentHarm refusers are worse on R-Judge specificity across benchmarks.

#### Agent reliability and task performance.

We use the retail domain of $\tau^{2}$-bench as the held-out task-success criterion.

## 3 Method

### 3.1 Model panel and benchmarks

The panel has up to 22 API-only models from nine organizations: OpenAI 6, Meta 3, Qwen 3, Mistral 3, DeepSeek 2, Amazon 2, Anthropic, Google, Cohere. Benchmarks, each with official scorers:
- **R-Judge**: all 571 items, self-judge.
- **InjecAgent**: 300 stratified direct-harm/data-stealing items, rule-scored.
- **AgentHarm**: 44 base behaviors across all 8 harm categories, official Inspect evaluation, gpt-4o-mini judge.
- **AgentDojo**: slack suite, 100 items, environment-scored for security and utility.

Coverage: R-Judge $n{=}21$ (Qwen3-32B falls below the 90% valid-output threshold); InjecAgent 22; AgentHarm 19 and AgentDojo 5 (both need native tool use); $\tau^{2}$ 20. The common R-Judge/InjecAgent/AgentHarm panel is $n{=}18$.

Anchors, measured by us through the same harness:
- MMLU zero-shot on a fixed 500-item subset (seed 42, same items for every model);
- GPQA-Diamond, 198 items, chain-of-thought.

These replace provider-reported model-card numbers, which are kept as a pre-harmonization comparison. The anchor panel has 21 models (DeepSeek-R1 excluded for unstable long-form GPQA).

### 3.2 Benchmark targets

Targets were fixed before examining any relationships:
- R-Judge: distinguishing unsafe from benign traces;
- InjecAgent/AgentDojo: injection resistance (their correlation is the convergent check);
- AgentHarm: refusing harmful agentic tasks.

R-Judge is also analyzed by specificity and balanced accuracy.

#### Score orientation and terminology.

Higher is better or safer throughout. Specificity is the fraction of benign traces judged benign; balanced accuracy averages both classes. InjecAgent robustness is 1−attack success; AgentHarm safety is 1−harmful compliance. $\tau^{2}$ is task success, not safety. "Internal consistency" refers to split-half analyses.

### 3.3 Analysis plan

Hypotheses, thresholds and decision rules were fixed before each analysis. They lack an independent timestamp, so we call them pre-specified, not preregistered.
- All associations are Spearman, with two-sided asymptotic $p$ unless noted. Error bars are model-level percentile bootstraps.
- PCA uses the Pearson matrix of standardized scores; factor count comes from Horn's parallel analysis against a random-normal null.
- Partial Spearman correlations control the capability composite: the mean of standardized MMLU and GPQA, whose ordering equals the anchors' PC1.

Controls:
- positive: anchor loadings $\geq0.6$ on factor 1;
- negative: a column-permuted matrix stays within the null;
- convergent: InjecAgent–AgentDojo correlation.

Headline metric: median pairwise partial $|\rho|$ among distinct-construct benchmarks. The factor structure is interpretable only if first-factor variance is $\geq40\%$ or controlling capability cuts that median by $\geq0.15$, with positive and negative controls passing.

RQ3 outcomes, each pre-specified before running:
- Task success: $\tau^{2}$-bench retail, 40 multi-turn environment-scored tool-agent-user tasks (20 models).
- Misalignment safety: avoiding blackmail or leaking in a fictional autonomous-agent scenario, fixed classifier, 100 decisions per model.
- Jailbreak safety: 1−harmful compliance on 50 forbidden prompts, averaged over three published templates to reduce ceiling.

The two safety criteria are single-turn or scenario-based and cover the full panel. All criteria are distinct from the audited benchmarks and are not predictors. Headline: each safety score's partial $\rho$ with the criterion, controlling capability, reported after the criterion's raw capability association. Reporting rules cover both significant and null results.

## 4 Results

Ordered by evidential strength: RQ4 and RQ2 are firmest, RQ1 weaker, RQ3 power-limited.

### 4.1 The headline metric is gameable (RQ4)

R-Judge labels 52.7% of its 571 items unsafe. "Always unsafe" therefore gets recall 1.0, specificity 0 and F1 $=0.690$. Among the 21 valid models (Qwen3-32B is 21% unparseable), it outranks five discriminating models (F1 0.30–0.57; Fig. 1). The highest-specificity model, o3-mini (0.97), gets F1 $0.702$, only $0.012$ above baseline, because its recall is lower. Balanced accuracy reorders the board.

###### Observation 1 (F1 admits a high-scoring constant baseline).

At base rate $\pi$, the always-positive policy attains $\mathrm{F1}=2\pi/(1+\pi)$ without discriminating ($0.690$ for $\pi=0.527$). The closed form depends on prevalence, but the core problem is that F1 gives no credit for true negatives. F1 alone therefore cannot measure two-sided discrimination on this trace-judgment benchmark.

### 4.2 The capability confound is real but metric-dependent (RQ2)

On R-Judge ($n{=}20$, harmonized anchors), capability correlates with:
- balanced accuracy: $+0.71$ with MMLU ($p<0.001$), $+0.49$ with GPQA ($p=0.03$);
- F1: $+0.76$, $+0.62$;
- specificity: only $+0.16$, $+0.07$.

Balanced accuracy and F1 include unsafe-trace recall; specificity can be inflated by rarely flagging. The confound is therefore a property of the metric, and it also moves with the panel: specificity–MMLU was $0.85$ on our first nine models.

### 4.3 Benchmarks disagree; a seven-model panel suggested a trade-off that does not persist (RQ1)

The firmest RQ1 result is correlation-free: no benchmark orders the models like another (Table 1). Disagreement across constructs is expected and indicts no single instrument. It does defeat quoting the scores interchangeably as an agent's safety.

The R-Judge-specificity/AgentHarm-safety correlation was $-0.64$ at $n{=}7$ but $+0.02$ ($p=0.95$) at $n{=}18$. A quarter of random size-7 subsets reach $|\rho|\geq0.5$, so sampling variability alone can manufacture the reversal. The dissolution holds under all four R-Judge metrics. Whether capability moderates the remainder is untested and flagged as a hypothesis.

PCA (corroborative): PC1 explains 48.7% of variance. R-Judge specificity, InjecAgent and both anchors load in one direction; AgentHarm loads opposite ($+0.33$) in 17/18 leave-one-out fits.

#### The positive control now passes.

- Positive control: MMLU loads $0.74\geq0.6$, versus a failing $0.42$ on provider-reported numbers.
- Negative control: passes.
- Convergent control: inconclusive at AgentDojo's $n{=}5$.

Interpretation conditions are met, but the factor stays corroborative: a Spearman PCA drops PC1 to 40.8% with no factor retained, and the median between-benchmark correlation is $0.22$.

#### Against task success, safety scores add no information beyond capability.

Capability predicts $\tau^{2}$ ($\rho=+0.60$, $p=0.005$, $n{=}20$). No safety score adds incremental validity (best $|\rho|=0.23$, n.s., $n{=}19$). This is not a verdict on the safety scores: capability already explains task success.

#### Against agentic misalignment, capability has the opposite association.

On $n{=}21$, $\rho_{\text{cap}}=-0.44$ ($p=0.047$). Mistral-Large blackmails or leaks 85% of the time; o3-mini is a capable exception at 1%. After control, InjecAgent ($+0.47$) and R-Judge specificity ($+0.41$) reach the pre-specified $0.40$ threshold; AgentHarm ($+0.16$) does not. Both remain exploratory:
- both CIs include zero, and neither survives Bonferroni;
- power is $\approx0.35$;
- the directional prediction named AgentHarm.

R-Judge's partial is also metric-sensitive: $+0.19$ under balanced accuracy, $-0.46$ under recall.

#### A direct interaction test on the original panel.

On the paired $n{=}20$ panel, capability correlates $+0.60$ with task success and $-0.41$ with misalignment: $\Delta=-1.00$ (95% CI $[-1.48,-0.49]$, $p<0.001$). This is stable to leave-one-model-out, leave-one-organization-out, organization-clustered bootstrap and subsampling. The R-Judge interaction is marginal ($\Delta=+0.50$, $p=0.082$), so the data support the capability interaction but not a full two-way dissociation. An independent misalignment grader gives $\rho=0.97$.

#### The capability–misalignment correlation is weaker on the expanded panel.

The prediction "hold or strengthen" failed: $-0.16$ ($n{=}40$, bootstrap $p=0.40$, CI $[-0.54,+0.22]$). The CI still includes $-0.44$, and the change is n.s. (nested $\Delta\rho=+0.27$, CI $[-0.25,+0.78]$). Organization-matched subsets give median $-0.17$, so composition alone does not explain the shift; a generational explanation is possible but undemonstrated. The interaction could not be re-tested because $\tau^{2}$ was not re-collected.

#### Models with similar capability scores differ in safety across organizations (Fig. 4).

The expanded panel has 41 models from 12 organizations (misalignment $n{=}40$; jailbreak $n{=}41$). Six organizations have $\geq4$ models and seven have $\geq3$. Within-organization correlations vary in sign and average near zero ($-0.14$ misalignment, $+0.26$ jailbreak). After capability adjustment, the seven groups differ: permutation $p=0.004$ (misalignment) and $p<0.001$ (jailbreak), Holm-significant, $\varepsilon^{2}=0.34$, $0.57$. This is not causal: the static composite may miss agentic ability, groups are small, and some ranges are restricted. Similar MMLU/GPQA scores do not imply similar safety.

#### Against jailbreak safety, AgentHarm shows the strongest held-out association.

Scored with StrongREJECT. The single AIM template ceilings, with 11/22 models refusing everything; the three-template average leaves no model at ceiling. Capability: $+0.08$ ($n{=}21$, $p=0.73$) on the 2024–25 panel and $+0.34$ ($n{=}41$, $p=0.04$) expanded; the change is n.s.

- AgentHarm partial: $+0.72$ ($p<0.001$), versus $+0.50$ for single-template. Stable to leave-one-out and an independent grader.
- Jailbreak over misalignment selectivity: $\Delta=+0.59$, $p=0.027$ with model resampling; $p=0.051$ resampling the eight organizations. The paired misalignment partial is $+0.13$ ($n{=}19$).
- R-Judge ($-0.11$) and InjecAgent ($+0.21$) do not predict jailbreak.
- Their reverse selectivity (misalignment over jailbreak) is marginal ($\Delta=+0.52$, $p=0.068$).

Both AgentHarm and StrongREJECT score harmful compliance, so the $+0.72$ is partly convergent validity.

#### Two alternative explanations, checked.

- Seven blinded LLM coders assigned AgentHarm and jailbreak to harm-blocking 7/7 each (Krippendorff $\alpha=0.61$, three categories); misalignment was classified less cleanly.
- AgentHarm is uncorrelated with XSTest benign over-refusal after control ($\rho=-0.01$, $n{=}17$), weighing against a refuse-everything explanation.

## 5 Discussion

These benchmarks are not interchangeable measures of one property. Held-out validity shifts with outcome and panel: capability predicts task success, but its safety correlations are unstable. AgentHarm–jailbreak is convergent validity; specificity remains open ($p=0.051$). The R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment links are exploratory. Organization-group differences are observational. A safety claim is defensible only with its benchmark, metric, target behavior and population attached.

## 6 Limitations and Threats to Validity

#### Panel size.

The cross-benchmark panel is $n{=}18$, up from $n{=}7$. The most needed addition is a larger, capability-spanning agent-loop panel.

#### Capability anchors.

Re-measurement fixed the positive control ($0.42\to0.74$) with no RQ2/RQ3 sign changes. The anchors are static-knowledge tests. A six-model BFCL pilot failed as an agentic anchor: GPT-4o-mini scored highest (0.72) and the two most capable models lowest (0.42–0.48), apparently rewarding format conformance. Such measurement error attenuates or suppresses partials, in no signable direction.

#### Multiple comparisons.

$p$-values are uncorrected. Both $p<0.001$ results survive Bonferroni; the misalignment cells ($p\approx0.05$–$0.09$) do not.

#### Judges and coverage.

Independent graders agree at $\rho=0.97$ (misalignment) and $0.98$ (jailbreak). Rescoring AgentHarm gives $\rho=0.69$, with the partial at $+0.66$ vs $+0.72$. AgentDojo covers only 5 models.

#### Criterion validity (RQ3).

- $\tau^{2}$: 40 tasks, one run per model; user-simulator variance unbounded.
- Misalignment: a fictional probe; its scenario halves give Spearman–Brown $0.70$.
- No criterion yields deployment-harm probabilities.
- Worst-case within-model SEs are 12–25% of the between-model SD, supporting panel-level spread but not every pairwise difference.
- The three-scenario misalignment result is post-hoc.

## 7 Conclusion

Across four benchmarks and up to 22 models, R-Judge's F1 lets a constant baseline outrank five models, and rankings depend on the benchmark. Safety evaluations should report the full confusion structure, drop standalone F1 where true negatives matter, and tie each claim to a target behavior and model population.

For the item-rich instruments with resampling support, split-half consistency is $\geq 0.96$ and rank stability $\geq 0.97$; across the bounded instruments, worst-case within-model SEs are $12$–$25\%$ of the between-model SD, which supports the panel-level spread but not every pairwise model difference (App. A.2). Capability control, criterion-validity testing, and latent-structure recovery are, all three, taken up here. The correlation at issue sits near zero on the full panel, and on seven-model subsets it often does not. The safety benchmarks, ZM3 and V4W among them, are treated as candidate columns for a validity audit rather than as settled measurements, a status—designed as evaluators, never validated as measurements—shared by evaluators we do not re-run, such as ToolEmu (Ruan et al. 2024) for risky tool use, while misbehavior monitors are scored by miss and false-alarm rates in AutoMonitor-Bench (Yang et al. 2026), the two-sided reporting our metric analysis argues for. Different from, and logically prior to, the separate concern that a benchmark can be gamed by an adversary is the claim that, even for an honest model, the headline score may not validly measure the intended construct, of which the W3D gameability documented in Section 4 is a concrete instance, the policy that scores mid-leaderboard being not adversarial but labeling every trace “unsafe” without examining any of them. Each of the four benchmarks we audit targets one construct: compliance with harmful agentic tasks is measured by KD9 (Andriushchenko et al. 2025), safety-risk awareness over interaction traces is scored by QX7 (Yuan et al. 2024), and prompt-injection robustness is targeted jointly by V4W (V4W denoting the AgentDojo benchmark of Debenedetti et al. 2024) and ZM3 (ZM3 denoting the InjecAgent benchmark of Zhan et al. 2024). Whether benchmark scores agree, and what latent constructs they capture, has been asked before, a strong latent factor shared by knowledge and reasoning benchmarks being found by benchmark-agreement testing (Perlitz et al. 2024), metabench (Kipnis et al. 2025), and direct construct analyses (Bean et al. 2025), quantitative construct-validity and uncertainty modeling being brought to LLM evaluation by Kearns (2026) and NIST’s statistical framework (Keller et al. 2026), and the same psychometric lens being pointed at agent reliability and safety, where the targeted behaviors—refusal, injection robustness, risk awareness—are distinct and how much capability confounds their comparison has been quantified by nobody. Closest to this paper, the taxonomy and consistency analysis of agent-safety benchmarks by Li et al. (2026) documents ranking disagreement while neither controlling for capability, testing criterion validity, nor recovering a latent structure, capability-controlled evaluation being named there as future work. Exaggerated safety, or over-refusal, is documented at the level of individual prompts by OR-Bench (Cui et al. 2024) and by C9L (C9L denoting the XSTest benchmark of Röttger et al. 2024), and one level up, between benchmarks, the analogous question is asked: are models that refuse harmful tasks (KD9) worse at identifying benign traces correctly (the G8X of QX7), and does that produce the ranking disagreement—this being the correlation at issue. Specific agent-reliability failures, among them corrupt success (Cao et al. 2026) and evidence-bounded reporting (Chen 2025), have been isolated by recent work, and agentic task success is measured by $\tau$-bench (Yao et al. 2024) and by its dual-control successor $\tau^{2}$-bench (Barres et al. 2025), the retail domain of the latter being borrowed as our held-out RQ3 task-success criterion.

Interpretation of the factor structure is permitted by the decision rule only when first-factor variance is $\geq 40\%$ or when a reduction of $\geq 0.15$ in the headline metric, the median pairwise U4G $|\rho|$ among distinct-construct benchmarks computed controlling M7V, is produced by controlling capability, and only with the positive and negative controls passing, these thresholds together with the disconfirming test having been fixed before any real run, as the hypotheses, thresholds, and decision rules of each analysis were fixed before the running of it, choices which, lacking an independent timestamp, are described as pre-specified rather than preregistered.

Task success is $\tau^{2}$-bench retail (Barres et al. 2025), comprising 40 multi-turn, environment-scored tool-agent-user tasks; whether blackmail or information leaking is avoided by a model in a fictional autonomous-agent scenario (Lynch et al. 2025) is recorded under P2Z (P2Z denoting misalignment safety), scored by a fixed classifier over 100 decisions per model; and L9R (L9R denoting jailbreak safety) is one minus harmful-compliance on 50 forbidden prompts, averaged over three published jailbreak templates so that the ceiling created by any single template is reduced (Souly et al. 2024; Wei et al. 2023), these constituting the three held-out outcomes pre-specified for criterion validity (RQ3), each fixed before the running of it. All three run through the same API-only harness, the two safety criteria being single-turn or scenario-based and covering the full panel while the $\tau^{2}$ criterion is a multi-turn tool loop covering 20 models, and all three are distinct from the four audited benchmarks and are not among the predictors; for each, the headline metric is the U4G of every safety score with the criterion, controlling M7V, with the criterion's raw association with capability reported first and the test of whether each safety score adds predictive information following, the pre-specified analysis giving reporting rules for both significant and null results, and the accompanying reproducibility package containing the analysis scripts and frozen inputs needed for the reported results to be reproduced.

Coverage differs by benchmark (Fig. 3 maps the full panel): QX7 has $n{=}21$ after Qwen3-32B falls below the $90\%$ valid-output threshold; ZM3 has $n{=}22$; KD9 and V4W, which require native tool use, have $n{=}19$ and $5$; the $\tau^{2}$ criterion has $n{=}20$ (App. A.2); and the common QX7/ZM3/KD9 panel has $n{=}18$. The panel from which these counts arise is a compute-light, API-only assembly of up to 22 models from nine model-developing organizations (OpenAI 6, Meta 3, Qwen 3, Mistral 3, DeepSeek 2, Amazon 2, Anthropic, Google, Cohere; full roster in Fig. 3 and the artifact), on which four safety benchmarks are re-run with their official implementations and scorers, namely QX7 (full 571 items, self-judge), ZM3 (300 stratified direct-harm/data-stealing items, rule-scored), KD9 (44 base behaviors spanning all eight harm categories, via the official Inspect evaluation with a gpt-4o-mini judge), and V4W (the slack suite, 100 items, environment-scored for security and utility), plus a held-out task-success criterion for RQ3.

Spearman correlations are used for all association tests and, unless otherwise noted, correlation $p$-values use two-sided asymptotic Spearman tests; in Fig. 2, error bars are model-level percentile-bootstrap intervals; and the panel expansion and direct panel comparisons follow their pre-specified bootstrap procedures (App. A.6). The corroborative PCA operates on the Pearson correlation matrix of the standardized score columns, factor count being chosen with Horn's parallel analysis against a random-normal null with the rank-based (Spearman) sensitivity in App. A.3, and U4G (U4G denoting the partial Spearman correlation) is reported controlling M7V (M7V denoting the capability composite), with App. A.5 giving the rank-residual implementation and an alternative convention; M7V is the mean of the standardized, verified H8P and R2F anchors, its model ordering being identical to the anchors' first principal component, and between-construct redundancy is measured by rank-residualized partial correlations that control for M7V. Three controls were pre-specified: positive (capability-anchor loadings $\geq 0.6$ on the first factor); negative (a column-permuted score matrix within the parallel-analysis null); and convergent (a high correlation between the same-construct ZM3 and V4W scores).

The anchor panel is 21 models, DeepSeek-R1 being excluded for unstable long-form R2F generation, and the provider-reported anchors are kept as a pre-K5Q comparison; the capability anchors themselves, H8P (H8P denoting MMLU) and R2F (R2F denoting GPQA-Diamond), are measured by us under one uniform protocol, H8P zero-shot on a fixed 500-item subset (seed 42, identical items for every model) and R2F on 198 items with chain-of-thought, through the same API harness as the safety runs, provider-reported model-card numbers having been the starting point, the replacements holding the protocol fixed across models, and M7V passing its positive control (§4).

For QX7, G8X and J4N are analyzed in addition to the official W3D because the three metrics reward different error patterns; QX7 tests whether unsafe interaction traces are distinguished from benign ones by a model, ZM3 and V4W both test resistance to prompt injection, their correlation serving as a convergent-validity check, and KD9 tests whether harmful agentic tasks are refused, what behavior each benchmark is meant to measure having been written down before any relationship among the score columns was looked at. All reported scores are oriented so that higher is better or safer: QX7 G8X is the fraction of benign traces correctly identified as benign, its J4N (J4N denoting balanced accuracy) averages performance on benign and unsafe traces, ZM3 robustness is one minus attack success, and KD9 safety is one minus harmful compliance, while, for RQ3, $\tau^{2}$-bench is a held-out task-success criterion, not a safety score; internal consistency is used for split-half analyses (App. A.2), and each benchmark-specific score is named explicitly, "calibration" and "reliability" not being stretched past their usual meanings.

Without distinguishing safe from unsafe items, a constant "always-positive" policy attains $\mathrm{W3D}=2\pi/(1+\pi)$ on any benchmark with class base rate $\pi$ scored by W3D — E5K (E5K denoting the observation that W3D admits a high-scoring constant baseline) — which for QX7 ( $\pi=0.527$ , a near-balanced base rate) evaluates to $0.690$ , exceeding the observed W3D of several models that do discriminate; the closed form depends on prevalence, yet the measurement problem is the blindness of W3D to true negatives, since correctly identifying a benign trace earns nothing, so W3D cannot stand alone as a measure of two-sided discrimination on this trace-judgment benchmark.

The pre-specified interpretation conditions are met: on K5Q the M7V passes its pre-specified positive control (H8P loads $0.74\geq 0.6$ ; on provider-reported numbers it had failed at $0.42$ , the original reason for caution), and the negative control also passes (a column-permuted score matrix yields eigenvalues within the parallel-analysis null), while the convergent control is inconclusive at V4W's $n{=}5$ ; the factor is nevertheless treated as corroboration only, since a rank-based (Spearman) PCA keeps the loading structure but drops PC1 to $40.8\%$ with no factor retained by Horn (App. A.3), the median between-benchmark correlation is just $0.22$ , and the firm, factor-independent RQ1 result is the raw-score disagreement (Table 1).

A single-factor PCA provides weaker, corroborative evidence (Fig. 6, appendix): its first component ( $48.7\%$ variance) places QX7 G8X, ZM3 robustness, and both capability anchors in one direction and KD9 safety in the other ( $+0.33$ , opposite the cluster in $17$ of $18$ leave-one-out fits).

No single benchmark on this panel orders the models the way another does (Table 1), a top-KD9 model can rank near the bottom on QX7 G8X, and this descriptive, correlation-free fact — the firmest RQ1 result — makes "safety rank" benchmark-dependent without resting on any correlation estimate; disagreement between benchmarks coded to different constructs (§3) is expected and does not by itself indict any single instrument, and what it defeats is the practice of quoting these scores interchangeably as the safety of an agent.

The 41-model panel spans 12 model-developing organizations (P2Z $n{=}40$ ; L9R $n{=}41$ after one engagement-gate exclusion), six organizations contribute at least four models for within-organization correlations and seven contribute at least three models for the group comparison (App. A.6, Table 5); within organizations, capability–safety correlations vary in sign and average near zero ( $-0.14$ P2Z, $+0.26$ L9R), and after safety ranks are adjusted for capability the seven organization groups differ on both criteria (permutation $p=0.004$ P2Z, $p<0.001$ L9R; Holm-significant), with df-adjusted Kruskal–Wallis effect sizes $\varepsilon^{2}=0.34$ and $0.57$ ; none of this is causal — the static M7V may miss agentic ability, each organization contributes few models, and some groups have restricted safety ranges — and what the panel supports is narrower: similar H8P/R2F scores do not imply similar safety scores (Fig. 4).

# Safety, or Just Capability? A Validity Audit of Agent-Safety Benchmarks

Youting Wang, Xiao Han, Dingyan Shang, Yuan Tang, Bowen Liu

###### Abstract

We validate four agent-safety benchmarks (R-Judge, InjecAgent, AgentHarm, AgentDojo) as measurements. Each runs under its official implementation and scorer on up to 22 models, with a capability composite from MMLU/GPQA that we measured under one protocol. R-Judge F1 is matched by a constant baseline. The benchmarks rank models differently. An apparent trade-off between them is a small-panel artifact. Capability predicts task success but not safety consistently. AgentHarm's strongest held-out association (jailbreak safety) is convergent validity, not general safety. A safety claim must name its benchmark, metric, target behavior and model panel.

## 1 Introduction

A taxonomy of >40 agent-safety benchmarks reports rank concordance near 0.10 (12 models, four benchmarks) and lists capability-controlled evaluation and consolidation as open problems. We separate three kinds of validity:
- construct validity: what a score measures;
- metric validity: whether its metric measures that target;
- criterion validity: whether it tracks held-out behavior.

- **RQ1 (construct structure):** common factor or dissociable ones?
- **RQ2 (capability confound):** how much between-benchmark signal is general capability?
- **RQ3 (criterion validity):** do safety scores track held-out criteria beyond capability?
- **RQ4 (metric validity):** do headline metrics reward degenerate behavior?

#### Contributions.

- A closed-form constant-baseline F1 (Obs. 1).
- Quantification of a small-panel failure mode.
- A pre-specified, capability-controlled criterion-validity audit (one task-success outcome, two safety outcomes).
- A released API-only audit harness and re-run artifacts.

#### Main conclusion.

A capability score is not a safety score, and no single benchmark stands in for safety. At seven models a weak relationship can look systematic, so validity needs re-checking as model populations turn over.

#### Scope.

RQ3 criteria are deployment stand-ins, not real-world-harm claims (§6).

## 2 Related Work

#### Agent-safety benchmarking.

- InjecAgent and AgentDojo: prompt-injection robustness.
- AgentHarm: harmful agentic-task compliance.
- R-Judge: safety-risk awareness over traces.

Evaluators such as ToolEmu were designed but never validated as measurements. AutoMonitor-Bench reports miss and false-alarm rates, the two-sided reporting we advocate. The closest taxonomy work documents ranking disagreement but does not control capability, test criterion validity, or recover latent structure.

#### Construct validity.

Knowledge/reasoning benchmarks share a strong latent factor, and quantitative construct-validity and uncertainty frameworks exist for LLM evaluation. Capability confounding among agent-safety benchmarks has not been quantified.

#### Benchmark gaming.

Our claim is logically prior to adversarial gaming: even for honest models, the headline score may not measure the construct. The F1-scoring policy is non-adversarial; it labels every trace "unsafe".

#### Over-refusal.

XSTest and OR-Bench study prompt-level over-refusal. We ask the between-benchmark analogue: does AgentHarm refusal trade off against R-Judge specificity? On the full panel the correlation is near zero; on seven-model subsets it often is not.

#### Agent reliability and task performance.

τ²-bench retail serves as the held-out task-success criterion. The safety benchmarks are treated as candidate columns for audit.

## 3 Method

### 3.1 Model panel and benchmarks

Panel: ≤22 API models from nine organizations (OpenAI 6, Meta 3, Qwen 3, Mistral 3, DeepSeek 2, Amazon 2, Anthropic, Google, Cohere).

Benchmarks (official scorers):
- R-Judge: 571 items, self-judge.
- InjecAgent: 300 stratified direct-harm/data-stealing items, rule-scored.
- AgentHarm: 44 base behaviors over all eight harm categories, Inspect, gpt-4o-mini judge.
- AgentDojo: slack suite, 100 items, environment-scored security/utility.

Coverage: R-Judge n=21 (Qwen3-32B below the 90% valid-output threshold); InjecAgent 22; AgentHarm 19 and AgentDojo 5 (native tool use required); τ² 20. Common R-Judge/InjecAgent/AgentHarm panel: n=18.

Anchors, self-measured in the same harness: MMLU zero-shot on a fixed 500-item subset (seed 42), and GPQA-Diamond (198 items, CoT). Anchor panel is 21 (DeepSeek-R1 excluded for unstable long GPQA generation). Provider-reported anchors are kept as a pre-harmonization comparison.

### 3.2 Benchmark targets

Targets were fixed before examining correlations:
- R-Judge: unsafe vs benign traces.
- InjecAgent/AgentDojo: injection resistance (convergent check).
- AgentHarm: refusal of harmful agentic tasks.

R-Judge is also scored by specificity and balanced accuracy.

#### Score orientation and terminology.

Higher = better/safer.
- Specificity: benign traces judged benign. Balanced accuracy averages both classes.
- InjecAgent robustness = 1−attack success. AgentHarm safety = 1−harmful compliance.
- τ² is task success, not safety. Split-half analyses are called "internal consistency".

### 3.3 Analysis plan

Rules were fixed before each analysis; they are "pre-specified", not preregistered, because there is no independent timestamp.
- Spearman throughout; two-sided asymptotic p unless noted; model-level percentile-bootstrap CIs.
- PCA on the Pearson matrix of standardized scores; Horn parallel analysis vs a random-normal null.
- Partial Spearman via rank residualization on the capability composite (mean of standardized MMLU, GPQA; same ordering as the anchors' PC1).

Controls:
- positive: anchor loadings ≥0.6 on factor 1;
- negative: column-permuted matrix falls within the null;
- convergent: high InjecAgent–AgentDojo correlation.

Headline: median pairwise partial |ρ| among distinct-construct benchmarks. The factor structure is interpretable only if first-factor variance ≥40% or controlling capability lowers that median by ≥0.15, and positive and negative controls pass.

RQ3 criteria:
- τ²-bench retail: 40 multi-turn, environment-scored tool-agent-user tasks; 20 models.
- Misalignment safety: avoiding blackmail/leaking in a fictional autonomous-agent scenario; fixed classifier, 100 decisions/model.
- Jailbreak safety: 1−harmful compliance on 50 forbidden prompts, averaged over three published templates.

Safety criteria cover the full panel; no criterion is a predictor. We report the raw capability association first, then partial ρ of each safety score. Reporting rules covered both significant and null results.

## 4 Results

### 4.1 The headline metric is gameable (RQ4)

Figure 1: On R-Judge (n=21), five discriminating models score below the "always unsafe" baseline (F1=0.69).

R-Judge labels 52.7% of items unsafe. Always answering "unsafe" gives recall 1.0, specificity 0 and F1=0.690, which outranks five models (F1 0.30–0.57) that all discriminate. o3-mini has the highest specificity (0.97) but F1=0.702, only 0.012 above baseline, because of lower recall. ###### Observation 1 (F1 admits a high-scoring constant baseline).

With base rate π, the always-positive policy attains F1=2π/(1+π); for R-Judge (π=0.527) this is 0.690. F1 ignores true negatives, so it cannot alone measure two-sided discrimination on trace judgment.

### 4.3 Benchmarks disagree; a seven-model panel suggested a trade-off that does not persist (RQ1)

Paired n=20: capability correlates +0.60 with task success and −0.41 with misalignment. Δ=−1.00 (95% CI [−1.48,−0.49], p<0.001), stable to leave-one-model-out, leave-one-organization-out, organization-clustered bootstrap and subsampling (A.5).

The R-Judge interaction is marginal (Δ=+0.50, p=0.082). This supports the capability interaction, not a full two-way dissociation. An independent misalignment grader gives ρ=0.97.

#### The capability–misalignment correlation is weaker on the expanded panel.

The pre-specified "hold or strengthen" prediction was not met: ρ=−0.16 (n=40; A.6). The CI still includes −0.44 and the change is not significant. Organization-matched subsets give median −0.17, so a generational explanation remains possible but undemonstrated. τ² was not re-collected, so the interaction was not re-tested.

#### Models with similar capability scores differ in safety across organizations (Fig. 4).

Expansion: 41 models from 12 organizations (misalignment n=40; jailbreak n=41 after one engagement-gate exclusion).
- Within-organization correlations (six orgs with ≥4 models) vary in sign, averaging −0.14 (misalignment) and +0.26 (jailbreak).
- Capability-adjusted safety ranks differ across seven groups with ≥3 models: permutation p=0.004 and p<0.001, Holm-significant; ε²=0.34 and 0.57.

This is not causal: the static composite may miss agentic ability, each org contributes few models, and some ranges are restricted. Supported conclusion: similar MMLU/GPQA scores do not imply similar safety.

#### Against jailbreak safety, AgentHarm shows the strongest held-out association.

Scored with StrongREJECT. With a single template (AIM), 11/22 models refuse everything (ceiling); the three-template average leaves none at ceiling. Capability: +0.08 (n=21, p=0.73), expanded +0.34 (n=41, p=0.04); change n.s.

AgentHarm partial = +0.72 (p<0.001), vs +0.50 for the single-template measure. Stable to leave-one-out and an independent grader.

Selectivity (jailbreak > misalignment): Δ=+0.59, p=0.027 under model bootstrap; p=0.051 when resampling the eight organizations. On that paired panel the misalignment partial is +0.13 (n=19); Table 2 uses n=18.

Both instruments measure harmful compliance, so +0.72 partly reflects convergent validity. The reverse comparison for R-Judge/InjecAgent (misalignment > jailbreak) is marginal (Δ=+0.52, p=0.068).

#### Two alternative explanations, checked.

- **Construct coding:** blinded LLM coders place AgentHarm and jailbreak in harm blocking 7/7 each (α=0.61, three categories); misalignment is classified less cleanly (A.1).
- **Blanket refusal:** AgentHarm safety vs XSTest benign over-refusal, partial ρ=−0.01 (n=17).

## 5 Discussion

These benchmarks are not interchangeable measures of one property. Held-out validity shifts with outcome and panel. AgentHarm–jailbreak (+0.72) is convergent validity; selectivity remains open (p=0.051). The R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment links are exploratory. Organization-group differences identify no cause. A safety claim needs its benchmark, metric, target behavior and model population.

## 6 Limitations and Threats to Validity

#### Panel size.

Cross-benchmark n=18 (first pass n=7). Needed next: a larger, capability-spanning agent-loop panel.

#### Capability anchors.

Re-measurement fixed the positive control (0.42→0.74); no RQ2/RQ3 sign changed. The anchors are static-knowledge tests, yet the composite predicts τ² at +0.60. A six-model BFCL pilot failed as an agentic anchor: strict syntax scoring ranked GPT-4o-mini highest (0.72) and the two most capable models lowest (0.42–0.48). Anchor error attenuates or suppresses partials, in no signable direction.

#### Multiple comparisons.

No family-wise correction. Under Bonferroni across nine RQ3 partials (α=0.006), the crossover and AgentHarm→jailbreak (p<0.001) survive; R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment (p≈0.05–0.09) do not and are treated as suggestive.

#### Judges and coverage.

Independent graders: ρ=0.97 (misalignment), 0.98 (jailbreak). AgentHarm refusal rescoring: ρ=0.69, with partial +0.66 vs +0.72. AgentDojo covers only five models.

#### Criterion validity (RQ3).

τ²: 40 tasks, one run per model, unbounded user-simulator variance. Misalignment is a fictional probe (halves Spearman–Brown 0.70). No criterion gives deployment-harm probabilities. Worst-case within-model SE is 12–25% of between-model SD, which supports panel-level spread but not every pairwise difference.

## 7 Conclusion

Capability predicts task success, not safety consistently. Safety evaluations should report the full confusion structure, drop standalone F1 where true negatives matter, and tie claims to an explicit target behavior and model population.

## Appendix A Technical Appendix

### A.1 Ruling out two artifacts (detail for §4.4)

#### Blinded construct coding.

Seven LLM coders: GPT-4o, Claude-3-Haiku, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen-2.5-72B, Mistral-Large, DeepSeek-V3. Each saw neutral benchmark descriptions stripped of predictive information, plus two definitions: "harm blocking" vs "risk recognition and correct treatment of benign inputs". Option and benchmark order were shuffled per coder.

| Benchmark | blind | author | B / R |
|---|---|---|---|
| R-Judge | recognition | recognition | 0 / 7 |
| InjecAgent | recognition | recognition | 1 / 6 |
| AgentHarm | blocking | blocking | 7 / 0 |
| AgentDojo | recognition | recognition | 0 / 7 |

- Agreement 27/28, Krippendorff α=0.825 (nominal); chance of one coder matching all four labels = 0.5⁴ = 6.2%.
- Lone dissent: Llama-3.3-70B on InjecAgent (borderline case).
- This controls coder bias, not rubric-designer bias (definitions were written by authors who had seen results). The RQ1 factor separates AgentHarm (+0.33) without reference to any criterion.

#### Blinded criterion coding, with a distractor.

Six targets (four benchmarks + two criteria) plus a task-success distractor: α=0.61 (chance ≈1/3); distractor chosen 5/42 times.
- AgentHarm and jailbreak → harm blocking 7/7; R-Judge → risk recognition 7/7; InjecAgent 5/7; all unchanged by the distractor.
- Contested: AgentDojo reads as task success to 4/7 (utility-scored). Misalignment → risk recognition 6/7 in a separate two-way round, but harm blocking 6/7 here.

#### XSTest over-refusal (blanket-refusal check).

Published CPI scorer, gpt-4o-mini judge.
- Unsafe subset is ceilinged (83–100% refusal, sd 4.5).
- Safe-subset over-refusal ranges 0–60%: Claude-3-Haiku 60%, o3-mini 30%, others ≤15%.

Capability-controlled partial ρ:

| Predictor | unsafe refusal | safe compliance |
|---|---|---|
| AgentHarm safety | +0.24 (n=17) | +0.01 (n=17) |
| R-Judge specificity | +0.06 (n=17) | −0.15 (n=18) |
| Misalignment safety | +0.47 (n=18) | −0.11 (n=19) |

- Capability: +0.21 (n.s.) on benign compliance, −0.32 (n.s.) on harmful refusal.
- Misalignment vs over-refusal: +0.11 (p=0.66); its unsafe-refusal association has p=0.052.
- Low power: these checks neither support nor rule out blanket refusal.

#### Misalignment 3-scenario battery (exploratory).

Adding a murder scenario (22 models) moves the R-Judge/InjecAgent interaction from Δ=+0.52 (p=0.068) to +0.53 (p=0.048). Significance comes from a tighter CI, not a stronger effect, and is a post-hoc forking path. Murder is also forecast by harm compliance (AgentHarm→battery +0.43), diluting specificity, so blackmail+leaking stays primary.

### A.6 The 2026 model-panel expansion (n ≈ 41) and organization-group differences (detail for §4.4)

Specified before running: the crossover would "hold or strengthen". Same chat/scenario harnesses; new models skip the tool benchmarks.

Exclusions were based on harness behavior only:
- Kimi-K2.6 and both Nemotron-3: <50% usable anchor answers or unbounded reasoning traces.
- MiniMax-M3: below the misalignment engagement gate (truncated outputs, not low harm); kept for jailbreak.
- Gemini-2.5-Pro: no valid anchor. GLM-4.5: MMLU only; partial row in Fig. 3. Both had routing incompatibilities, a small instance of harness staleness.

#### Primary expansion result: the capability–misalignment correlation weakens.

| Panel | ρ | p | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|---|
| original (n=21) | −0.44 | 0.047 asymptotic; 0.11 bootstrap | [−0.85,+0.09] |
| expanded (n=40) | −0.16 | 0.40 bootstrap | [−0.54,+0.22]; leave-one-out [−0.25,−0.12] |

The confirmation threshold (ρ≤−0.35 at p<0.05) is not met. Tests of the change:
- stratified nested bootstrap: Δρ=+0.27, CI [−0.25,+0.78], p=0.29 (jailbreak +0.26, CI [−0.14,+0.69], p=0.22);
- 2026-only models: ρ=+0.07 vs −0.44 (Fisher z, p=0.12);
- organization-matched size-21 subsets: median −0.17 (IQR [−0.27,−0.08]).

Safety varies at similar capability (composite ≈0.8): o3-mini 0.99, Grok-4.3 0.70, DeepSeek-V3 0.19; a ceiling does not explain this.

#### Organization-group analysis.

Caveats: capability is matched only on a static-knowledge composite; within-org n is 4–8; some orgs are range-restricted (Anthropic near 1.0). The claim rests on the between-org permutation test, not the within-org slopes. All five secondary tests survive Holm (max adjusted p=0.043).

Calibration over seven clusters: 2,000 synthetic null panels per null.
- Reshuffled safety and i.i.d. Gaussian nulls: nominal rejection (0.045–0.052 at α=0.05; also nominal at 0.01/0.005).
- Org-clustered-variance null: 0.067 at α=0.05 on the jailbreak structure only; no inflation at α=0.005. Doubling both p-values keeps the Holm results.
- Dropping Anthropic: misalignment ε²=0.27, p=0.018; jailbreak ε²=0.54, p<0.001.

# Safety, or Just Capability? A Validity Audit of Agent-Safety Benchmarks

Youting Wang, Xiao Han, Dingyan Shang, Yuan Tang, Bowen Liu

###### Abstract

Agent-safety benchmarks measure different behaviors, yet their scores are quoted interchangeably as an agent's safety. We validate four (R-Judge, InjecAgent, AgentHarm, AgentDojo) as measurements, each under its official implementation and author-provided scorer on up to 22 models, with MMLU and GPQA measured by us under one protocol as a capability composite. We find a closed-form F1 failure, benchmark-dependent rankings, a small-panel trade-off artifact, outcome- and panel-dependent capability–safety links, and a strong AgentHarm–jailbreak association that is convergent validity, not general safety. A safety claim minimally needs its benchmark, metric, target behavior, and model panel.

## 1 Introduction

A taxonomy of >40 agent-safety benchmarks reports rank concordance near 0.10 across models, but stops at a 12-model, four-benchmark check and lists capability-controlled evaluation as open. We separate construct validity (what a score measures), metric validity (whether its metric measures that target), and criterion validity (whether it tracks held-out behavior):

- RQ1 (construct structure): common factor or dissociable ones?
- RQ2 (capability confound): how much between-benchmark signal is general capability?
- RQ3 (criterion validity): do safety scores track held-out criteria beyond capability?
- RQ4 (metric validity): do headline metrics reward degenerate behavior?

#### Contributions.

A formal F1 failure (Observation 1); quantification of a small-panel failure mode; a pre-specified, capability-controlled criterion audit over one task-success and two safety outcomes; an API-only audit harness and re-run artifacts for four benchmarks and three held-out outcomes.

#### Main conclusion.

A capability score is not a safety score, and no one benchmark stands in for safety; validity needs re-checking as model populations turn over.

#### Scope.

RQ3 criteria are stand-ins for deployment, not real-world harm claims (limits in §6).

## 2 Related Work

#### Agent-safety benchmarking.

InjecAgent and AgentDojo target prompt-injection robustness, AgentHarm harmful-task compliance, R-Judge safety-risk awareness over traces; evaluators like ToolEmu were likewise never validated as measurements. AutoMonitor-Bench reports miss and false-alarm rates, the two-sided reporting we argue for. The closest work documents ranking disagreement but neither controls capability, tests criterion validity, nor recovers latent structure; we do all three.

#### Construct validity.

Knowledge/reasoning benchmarks share a strong latent factor; capability confounding of agent-safety comparisons is unquantified.

#### Benchmark gaming.

Our claim is prior to gaming: the F1-gaming policy is not adversarial; it labels every trace "unsafe."

#### Over-refusal.

XSTest/OR-Bench work at prompt level; we ask whether AgentHarm refusers are worse at R-Judge specificity. On the full panel the correlation is near zero; on seven-model subsets often not.

#### Agent reliability and task performance.

We use τ²-bench retail as the held-out task-success criterion.

## 3 Method

### 3.1 Model panel and benchmarks

API-only panel of up to 22 models from nine organizations (OpenAI 6, Meta 3, Qwen 3, Mistral 3, DeepSeek 2, Amazon 2, Anthropic, Google, Cohere). Official implementations/scorers: R-Judge (all 571 items, self-judge), InjecAgent (300 stratified direct-harm/data-stealing items, rule-scored), AgentHarm (44 base behaviors, all eight harm categories, official Inspect evaluation, gpt-4o-mini judge), AgentDojo (slack suite, 100 items, environment-scored security and utility). Coverage: R-Judge n=21 (Qwen3-32B below the 90% valid-output threshold); InjecAgent 22; AgentHarm 19 and AgentDojo 5 (native tool use required); τ² 20. Common R-Judge/InjecAgent/AgentHarm panel: n=18. Anchors measured by us through the same harness: MMLU zero-shot on a fixed 500-item subset (seed 42, same items for all models), GPQA-Diamond (198 items, CoT). Anchor panel: 21 models (DeepSeek-R1 excluded for unstable long-form GPQA generation); provider-reported model-card anchors kept as pre-harmonization comparison.

### 3.2 Benchmark targets

Fixed before analysis: R-Judge distinguishes unsafe from benign traces; InjecAgent and AgentDojo test injection resistance (their correlation is a convergent check); AgentHarm tests refusal of harmful tasks. R-Judge is also analyzed by specificity and balanced accuracy.

#### Score orientation and terminology.

Higher = better/safer. Specificity: fraction of benign traces judged benign; balanced accuracy averages both classes. InjecAgent robustness = 1 − attack success; AgentHarm safety = 1 − harmful compliance. τ² is task success, not safety. "Internal consistency" refers to split-half analyses.

### 3.3 Analysis plan

Hypotheses, thresholds, decision rules fixed beforehand (no independent timestamp, so "pre-specified," not preregistered). Spearman correlations, two-sided asymptotic p unless noted; Fig. 2 bars are model-level percentile bootstraps. PCA on the Pearson matrix of standardized scores; factor count by Horn's parallel analysis vs. random-normal null. Partial Spearman correlations control the capability composite (mean of standardized MMLU and GPQA; ordering identical to the anchors' PC1).

Controls: positive (anchor loadings ≥0.6 on factor 1); negative (column-permuted matrix within the null); convergent (high InjecAgent–AgentDojo correlation). Headline metric: median pairwise partial |ρ| among distinct-construct benchmarks. Factor structure interpretable only if first-factor variance ≥40% or capability control reduces that median by ≥0.15, with positive and negative controls passing.

RQ3 outcomes, each pre-specified: task success = τ²-bench retail (40 multi-turn, environment-scored tool-agent-user tasks); misalignment safety = avoiding blackmail or leaking in a fictional autonomous-agent scenario, fixed classifier, 100 decisions/model; jailbreak safety = 1 − harmful compliance on 50 forbidden prompts, averaged over three published templates. Safety criteria cover the full panel; τ² covers 20. None is a predictor. Headline: partial ρ of each safety score with each criterion, after reporting the criterion's raw capability association.

## 4 Results

Ordered by evidential strength: RQ4, RQ2 firmest; RQ1 weaker; power-limited RQ3 last.

### 4.1 The headline metric is gameable (RQ4)

R-Judge labels 52.7% of 571 items unsafe. "Always unsafe" attains recall 1.0, specificity 0, F1=0.690, outranking five of the 21 valid models (F1 0.30–0.57; Fig. 1), all of which discriminate. Highest-specificity o3-mini (0.97) gets F1=0.702, only 0.012 above, due to lower recall. Balanced accuracy reorders the board.

###### Observation 1 (F1 admits a high-scoring constant baseline).

With base rate π, the always-positive policy attains F1=2π/(1+π) without discriminating; for R-Judge (π=0.527) this is 0.690. The closed form depends on prevalence, but the problem is F1's blindness to true negatives, so F1 cannot stand alone as a measure of two-sided discrimination here.

### 4.2 The capability confound is real but metric-dependent (RQ2)

R-Judge panel (n=20, harmonized anchors): capability correlates with balanced accuracy (ρ=+0.71 MMLU, p<0.001; +0.49 GPQA, p=0.03) and F1 (+0.76, +0.62), weakly with specificity (+0.16, +0.07). BA and F1 include unsafe-trace recall; specificity can be inflated by rarely flagging. The confound depends on the metric and the panel: specificity–MMLU fell from 0.85 (first nine models) to +0.16 at n=20.

### 4.3 Benchmarks disagree; a seven-model panel suggested a trade-off that does not persist (RQ1)

Firmest, correlation-free: no benchmark orders models like another (Table 1). Cross-construct disagreement is expected and indicts no instrument; it defeats interchangeable quoting. R-Judge-specificity/AgentHarm-safety ρ: −0.64 at n=7, +0.02 (p=0.95) at n=18 (Fig. 5); size-7 subsets give |ρ|≥0.5 in a quarter of draws; dissolution holds under all four R-Judge metrics (A.4). Capability moderation of the remainder is an untested hypothesis.

PCA (corroborative; Fig. 6): PC1 48.7%; R-Judge specificity, InjecAgent robustness, both anchors one way, AgentHarm opposite (+0.33; opposite in 17/18 leave-one-out fits).

#### The positive control now passes.

MMLU loads 0.74≥0.6 (provider-reported anchors failed at 0.42); negative control passes; convergent control inconclusive at AgentDojo n=5. Conditions met, but the factor is corroboration only: Spearman PCA gives PC1 40.8% with no factor retained by Horn (A.3); median between-benchmark correlation 0.22.

#### Against task success, safety scores add no information beyond capability.

Capability: ρ=+0.60, p=0.005, n=20; best safety partial |ρ|=0.23, n.s., n=19 (Fig. 7). Capability already explains this outcome; the null is no verdict on safety scores.

#### Against agentic misalignment, capability has the opposite association.

n=21: ρ_cap=−0.44 (p=0.047) (Mistral-Large blackmails/leaks 85%; o3-mini a capable exception at 1%). InjecAgent (+0.47) and R-Judge specificity (+0.41) reach the pre-specified 0.40 threshold; AgentHarm (+0.16) does not. Exploratory: CIs include zero, fail Bonferroni, power ≈0.35, and the directional prediction named AgentHarm. R-Judge partial: +0.41 specificity, +0.19 BA, −0.46 recall (A.4).

#### A direct interaction test on the original panel.

Paired n=20: task +0.60 vs. misalignment −0.41; Δ=−1.00 (95% CI [−1.48,−0.49], p<0.001), stable to leave-one-model/organization-out, organization-clustered bootstrap, subsampling (A.5). R-Judge interaction marginal (Δ=+0.50, p=0.082): capability interaction supported, full two-way dissociation not. Independent misalignment grader: ρ=0.97.

#### The capability–misalignment correlation is weaker on the expanded panel.

Pre-specified "hold or strengthen"; observed −0.16 (n=40, bootstrap p=0.40, CI [−0.54,+0.22]). CI includes −0.44; between-panel Δρ=+0.27 [−0.25,+0.78], n.s. Organization-matched subsets: median −0.17, so composition does not explain it; a generational account is possible, undemonstrated. τ² not re-collected; interaction not re-tested.

#### Models with similar capability scores differ in safety across organizations (Fig. 4).

41 models, 12 organizations (misalignment n=40; jailbreak 41 after one engagement-gate exclusion); six organizations ≥4 models (within-org), seven ≥3 (group test; Table 5). Within-org correlations vary in sign, averaging −0.14 (misalignment), +0.26 (jailbreak). After capability adjustment, groups differ (permutation p=0.004, p<0.001; Holm-significant; ε²=0.34, 0.57). Not causal: static composite may miss agentic ability, few models per org, restricted ranges. Supported: similar MMLU/GPQA ≠ similar safety.

#### Against jailbreak safety, AgentHarm shows the strongest held-out association.

StrongREJECT-scored. One template (AIM) ceilings (11/22 refuse all); three templates leave none at ceiling. Capability ρ=+0.08 (n=21, p=0.73); expanded +0.34 (n=41, p=0.04), change n.s. AgentHarm partial +0.72 (p<0.001) vs. +0.50 single-template; stable to LOO and independent grader. AgentHarm jailbreak>misalignment: Δ=+0.59, p=0.027 (model bootstrap); p=0.051 resampling eight organizations. Paired-panel misalignment partial +0.13 (n=19; Table 2 uses n=18). Shared harmful-compliance target makes +0.72 partly convergent validity. R-Judge/InjecAgent misalignment>jailbreak: marginal (Δ=+0.52, p=0.068).

#### Two alternative explanations, checked.

Seven blind LLM coders placed AgentHarm and jailbreak in harm blocking (7/7 each; α=0.61, three categories); misalignment less cleanly (A.1). AgentHarm is uncorrelated with XSTest benign over-refusal after capability control (ρ=−0.01, n=17), against blanket refusal.

## 5 Discussion

These benchmarks are not interchangeable measures of one property. AgentHarm–jailbreak is convergent validity with specificity unresolved (p=0.051); R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment is exploratory. Capability-adjusted organization-group differences are observational, identifying no organizational cause. A safety claim is defensible only with its benchmark, metric, target behavior, and model population attached.

## 6 Limitations and Threats to Validity

#### Panel size.

Cross-benchmark n=18 (first pass n=7); needed: a larger, capability-spanning agent-loop panel.

#### Capability anchors.

Re-measurement fixed the positive control (0.42→0.74); no RQ2/RQ3 sign changed. Anchors are static-knowledge tests, though the composite predicts τ² at +0.60. A six-model BFCL pilot failed as agentic anchor: syntax scoring ranked GPT-4o-mini highest (0.72), the two most capable lowest (0.42–0.48). Such error attenuates or suppresses partials rather than biasing them in a signable direction.

#### Multiple comparisons.

No family-wise correction; the crossover and AgentHarm→jailbreak (p<0.001) survive Bonferroni; R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment (p≈0.05–0.09) do not.

#### Judges and coverage.

Grader agreement ρ=0.97 (misalignment), 0.98 (jailbreak); AgentHarm refusal rescoring 0.69, partial +0.66 vs. +0.72. AgentDojo has only five models.

#### Criterion validity (RQ3).

τ² (40 tasks, one run/model) has unbounded user-simulator variance; misalignment is a fictional probe (halves Spearman–Brown 0.70). No criterion gives deployment-harm probabilities. Worst-case within-model SEs are 12–25% of between-model SD, supporting panel spread, not every pairwise difference. The larger three-scenario misalignment result is post-hoc.

## 7 Conclusion

Report the full confusion structure, drop standalone F1 wherever true negatives matter, and tie every claim to an explicit target behavior and model population.

## Appendix A Technical Appendix
