### 4.2 The capability confound is real but metric-dependent (RQ2)

The R-Judge panel with harmonized anchors has $n{=}20$. Capability correlates with balanced
accuracy at $\rho=+0.71$ with MMLU ($p<0.001$) and $+0.49$ with GPQA ($p=0.03$). With F1 the values
are $+0.76$ and $+0.62$. With specificity they are $+0.16$ and $+0.07$. Specificity rises when a
model rarely flags anything, and it contains no recall term. The specificity–MMLU correlation was
$0.85$ on the first nine models and $+0.16$ at $n{=}20$.

### 4.3 Benchmarks disagree; a seven-model panel suggested a trade-off that does not persist (RQ1)

No benchmark reproduces another's ordering (Table 1). A top-AgentHarm model can rank near the
bottom on R-Judge specificity. The benchmarks are coded to different constructs (§3), so the
disagreement does not by itself impugn any single instrument.

The R-Judge-specificity/AgentHarm-safety rank correlation was $-0.64$ at $n{=}7$ and is $+0.02$
($p=0.95$) at $n{=}18$ (Fig. 5, appendix). Random size-7 subsets give $|\rho|\geq 0.5$ in a quarter
of draws. The null holds under all four R-Judge metrics (App. A.4). We leave capability moderation
of any residual as an untested hypothesis.

On the PCA (Fig. 6, appendix), PC1 explains $48.7\%$ of variance. It loads R-Judge specificity,
InjecAgent robustness, and both anchors in one direction and AgentHarm safety ($+0.33$) in the
other. AgentHarm is opposite the cluster in $17$ of $18$ leave-one-out fits.

#### The positive control now passes.

On harmonized anchors, MMLU loads $0.74\geq 0.6$. On provider-reported numbers it loaded $0.42$
and failed. The negative control passes, with column-permuted eigenvalues within the
parallel-analysis null. The convergent control is inconclusive at AgentDojo's $n{=}5$. The
interpretation conditions are therefore met. Spearman PCA preserves the loading pattern but gives
PC1 $40.8\%$, and Horn retains no factor (App. A.3). The median between-benchmark correlation is
$0.22$. We treat the factor as corroborative only.

#### Against agentic misalignment, capability has the opposite association.

On the 21-model panel, $\rho_{\text{cap}}=-0.44$ (asymptotic $p=0.047$), against $+0.60$ on
$\tau^{2}$. Mistral-Large blackmails or leaks $85\%$ of the time; o3-mini does so $1\%$ of the time.
Controlling capability, InjecAgent robustness ($+0.47$) and R-Judge specificity ($+0.41$) exceed the
pre-specified $0.40$ threshold, while AgentHarm ($+0.16$) does not (Table 2). Both CIs include zero.
Neither survives Bonferroni, power is $\approx 0.35$, and the directional prediction named
AgentHarm. Under balanced accuracy the R-Judge partial is $+0.19$, and under recall it is $-0.46$
(App. A.4).

#### A direct interaction test on the original panel.

On the paired $n{=}20$ panel, capability correlates $+0.60$ with task success and $-0.41$ with
misalignment safety ($-0.44$ on the full panel). The difference is $\Delta=-1.00$ (95% CI
$[-1.48,-0.49]$, $p<0.001$). It is stable under leave-one-model-out, leave-one-organization-out,
organization-clustered bootstrap, and subsampling (App. A.5). The corresponding R-Judge interaction
is $\Delta=+0.50$ ($p=0.082$). An independent misalignment grader reproduces model scores at
$\rho=0.97$.

#### The capability–misalignment correlation is weaker on the expanded panel.

The pre-specified prediction was "hold or strengthen." The estimate moved from $\rho=-0.44$
($n{=}21$, asymptotic $p=0.047$) to $-0.16$ ($n{=}40$, bootstrap $p=0.40$; 95% CI $[-0.54,+0.22]$;
App. A.6). The interval contains $-0.44$. The between-panel difference is nested-bootstrap
$\Delta\rho=+0.27$ (95% CI $[-0.25,+0.78]$). Organization-matched subsets give median
$\rho=-0.17$, and a generational account remains undemonstrated. $\tau^{2}$ was not re-collected, so
the interaction is not re-tested.

#### Models with similar capability scores differ in safety across organizations
(Fig. 4).

The 41-model panel spans 12 model-developing organizations: misalignment $n{=}40$, and jailbreak
$n{=}41$ after one engagement-gate exclusion. Six organizations contribute at least four models for
within-organization correlations. Seven contribute at least three for the group test (App. A.6,
Table 5). Within-organization capability–safety correlations vary in sign, with weighted means of
$-0.14$ (misalignment) and $+0.26$ (jailbreak). On capability-adjusted safety ranks, the seven
groups differ (permutation $p=0.004$ misalignment, $p<0.001$ jailbreak; Holm-significant), with
df-adjusted Kruskal–Wallis $\varepsilon^{2}=0.34$ and $0.57$. Several caveats apply. The static
composite may miss agentic ability. Each organization contributes few models, and some groups are
range-restricted. No causal reading is intended.

#### Against jailbreak safety, AgentHarm shows the strongest held-out association.

The second safety outcome differs from misalignment in failure mode, harness, and scoring. It is
harmful compliance under jailbreak, scored with StrongREJECT (Souly et al. 2024). With a single
template (AIM), 11 of 22 models refuse every request. The three-template average (Wei et al. 2023)
places no model at ceiling. Capability gives $\rho=+0.08$ on the 2024–25 panel ($n{=}21$,
$p=0.73$) and $+0.34$ on the expanded panel ($n{=}41$, $p=0.04$); the change is not significant.

Controlling capability, AgentHarm safety correlates $\rho=+0.72$ ($p<0.001$) with the three-template
outcome, versus $+0.50$ with the single template. The estimate is stable to leave-one-model-out
analysis and an independent grader (App. A.5). The AgentHarm jailbreak-minus-misalignment contrast
is $\Delta=+0.59$, with $p=0.027$ under model bootstrap and $p=0.051$ under bootstrap over the eight
represented organizations. On this paired panel the misalignment partial is $+0.13$ ($n{=}19$);
Table 2's $+0.16$ uses the common $n{=}18$ panel. R-Judge specificity ($-0.11$) and InjecAgent
robustness ($+0.21$) do not predict jailbreak safety. The reverse contrast, R-Judge/InjecAgent
misalignment-over-jailbreak, is $\Delta=+0.52$ ($p=0.068$).

#### Two alternative explanations, checked.

Seven LLM coders saw only construct descriptions. All seven assigned AgentHarm and the jailbreak
outcome to harm blocking ($7/7$ each; Krippendorff $\alpha=0.61$ across three categories). The
misalignment outcome was classified less consistently (App. A.1). Controlling capability, AgentHarm
safety is uncorrelated with over-refusal on benign XSTest prompts (Röttger et al. 2024)
($\rho=-0.01$, $n{=}17$).

## 5 Discussion

An "always unsafe" baseline matches R-Judge F1 (Observation 1). The three broad-coverage benchmarks
rank the same models differently. Capability predicts task success, while its correlations with the
two safety outcomes shift between panels (Table 2). AgentHarm's capability-controlled association
with three-template jailbreak safety is $\rho=+0.72$. Both measures concern harmful compliance, and
the selectivity test gives $p=0.051$ under organization resampling. The R-Judge/InjecAgent
associations with misalignment are exploratory. Capability-adjusted safety ranks differ across
organization groups, an observational pattern that does not identify a cause. A safety claim holds
only for the benchmark, metric, target behavior, and model population that produced it.

## 6 Limitations and Threats to Validity

#### Panel size.

The AgentHarm-limited cross-benchmark panel has $n{=}18$; the first pass had $n{=}7$. A larger,
capability-spanning agent-loop panel is the principal open gap.

#### Capability anchors.

Provider-reported anchors failed the positive control (MMLU $0.42$). Re-measurement (§3) gave MMLU
$0.74$, and every RQ2/RQ3 sign was unchanged. The anchors are static-knowledge tests, but the
composite predicts multi-turn tool-agent success at $+0.60$.

A six-model BFCL pilot (Patil et al. 2025) used strict function-call syntax scoring. It ranked
GPT-4o-mini highest ($0.72$) and the two most capable models lowest ($0.42$–$0.48$), consistent
with format conformance, and failed as an agentic anchor. Anchor measurement error attenuates or
suppresses partials in no signable direction.

#### Multiple comparisons.

Per-test $p$-values are uncorrected. The crossover and AgentHarm $\to$ jailbreak (both $p<0.001$)
survive Bonferroni. The R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment cells ($p\approx 0.05$–$0.09$) do not.

#### Judges and coverage.

Independent graders reproduce model scores at $\rho=0.97$ (misalignment) and $\rho=0.98$
(jailbreak). Rescoring AgentHarm refusals with a different model gives $\rho=0.69$, and the
AgentHarm–jailbreak partial moves from $+0.72$ to $+0.66$ (App. A.5). AgentDojo covers five models,
so the cross-benchmark analyses rest on the other three benchmarks.

#### Criterion validity (RQ3).

$\tau^{2}$-retail uses 40 tasks and one run per model, scored by a user-simulator of unbounded
variance. The misalignment criterion is a fictional-scenario probe. It is grader-robust
($\rho=0.97$), but its blackmail and leaking halves give Spearman–Brown $0.70$. The jailbreak
criterion averages three jailbreaks, and none of the three yields deployment-harm probabilities.

For the item-rich instruments with resampling support, split-half consistency is $\geq 0.96$ and
rank stability $\geq 0.97$. Across the bounded instruments, worst-case within-model SEs are
$12$–$25\%$ of the between-model SD. This bounds panel-level spread but not every pairwise
difference (App. A.2). The AgentHarm–jailbreak association is large and directionally stable, but
it is partly convergent measurement, and its selectivity is borderline under organization
resampling. The R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment pattern is exploratory: marginal $\Delta=+0.52$,
power $\approx 0.35$, and a post-hoc three-scenario extension (App. A.5).

## 7 Conclusion

Across four benchmarks and up to 22 models, R-Judge F1 ranks an "always unsafe" baseline above five
models, and rankings change with the benchmark. Capability predicts held-out task success but not
safety consistently across outcomes or panels. AgentHarm gives the largest held-out safety
association ($\rho=+0.72$ with jailbreak safety, controlling capability), with partial instrument
overlap and borderline organization-resampled selectivity. We recommend reporting the full confusion
structure and dropping standalone F1 wherever true negatives matter. Every claim should be tied to
an explicit target behavior and model population.

definitions were written after the results were seen, so rubric-designer bias is uncontrolled. The
RQ1 factor separates AgentHarm ($+0.33$) from the R-Judge/InjecAgent cluster without reference to
any criterion.

#### Blinded criterion coding, with a distractor.

We re-coded all six targets (four benchmarks $+$ two criteria) with a third, task-success distractor
construct. Krippendorff's $\alpha=0.61$ (three categories, chance $\approx 1/3$), and the
distractor was chosen $5/42$ times. AgentHarm and the jailbreak criterion map to harm blocking
$7/7$. R-Judge maps to risk recognition $7/7$ and InjecAgent $5/7$, unchanged by the distractor.

AgentDojo, which is utility-scored with $n{=}5$, reads as task success to $4/7$. The misalignment
criterion maps to risk recognition $6/7$ in a separate two-way round (frozen votes in the artifact)
but to harm blocking $6/7$ here. The AgentHarm–jailbreak pairing is recovered without predictive
results.

prompts that superficially resemble unsafe ones and measures over-refusal. The unsafe subset

# Safety, or Just Capability? A Validity Audit of Agent-Safety Benchmarks

Youting Wang

  
Xiao Han

  
Dingyan Shang

Affiliation: Yuan Tang

  
Bowen Liu

###### Abstract

We audit four agent-safety benchmarks (R-Judge, InjecAgent, AgentHarm, AgentDojo),
each run under its official implementation and author-provided scorer on up to 22 models,
against a capability composite of MMLU and GPQA re-measured by us under one protocol. On any
binary trace-judgment benchmark scored by $F_{1}$ , an “always positive” policy attains
$F_{1}=2\pi/(1+\pi)$ ; on R-Judge this is $0.690$ , above five of the 21 models that
discriminate. The three broad-coverage benchmarks rank the same 18 models differently. R-Judge
specificity against AgentHarm safety correlates $-0.64$ at $n{=}7$ and $+0.02$ at $n{=}18$ ,
and a quarter of random size-7 subsets reach $|\rho|\geq 0.5$ . Capability predicts task
success ( $\rho{=}{+}0.60$ ) and correlates negatively with misalignment safety
( $\rho{=}{-}0.44$ , $n{=}21$ ). On their paired $n{=}20$ panel the contrast is
$\Delta{=}{-}1.00$ (95% CI $[-1.48,-0.49]$ , $p<0.001$ ), stable under leave-one-organization-out
and organization-clustered bootstrap. On an expanded 41-model panel the misalignment correlation is
$-0.16$ (95% CI $[-0.54,+0.22]$ ) and the jailbreak correlation $+0.34$ ; neither between-panel
change is significant. After controlling capability, AgentHarm correlates $\rho{=}{+}0.72$ with
three-template jailbreak safety, and both instruments score harmful compliance. A safety claim
should at minimum name its benchmark, metric, target behavior, and model panel.

## 1 Introduction

Between 2024 and 2026, dozens of benchmarks appeared for LLM-agent safety and reliability:
prompt-injection resistance (Zhan et al. 2024; Debenedetti et al. 2024), safety-risk awareness
(Yuan et al. 2024), refusal of harmful agentic tasks (Andriushchenko et al. 2025), and risky-tool-use
identification (Ruan et al. 2024), among others. A recent taxonomy (Li et al. 2026) catalogs more
than forty and reports rank concordance near $0.10$ across models when the benchmark is swapped,
from a twelve-model concordance check over four benchmarks. It lists capability-controlled
evaluation and benchmark consolidation as open problems.

We separate construct, metric, and criterion validity and pose four questions:

•

RQ1 (construct structure). Do nominally-distinct agent-safety benchmarks measure
a common underlying factor, or dissociable ones?

•

RQ2 (capability confound). How much of the between-benchmark signal is general
capability in disguise?

•

RQ3 (criterion validity). Do the safety scores track held-out behavioral
criteria beyond what general capability predicts?

•

RQ4 (metric validity). Are the headline metrics valid instruments, or do
they reward degenerate behavior?

#### Contributions.

Observation 1 gives a closed form for the F1 of an “always positive” baseline on any binary
trace-judgment benchmark scored by F1; on R-Judge it outranks five evaluated models. The
R-Judge-specificity/AgentHarm-safety correlation is $-0.64$ at $n{=}7$ and $+0.02$ at $n{=}18$ ,
with $|\rho|\geq 0.5$ in a quarter of random size-7 subsets. A pre-specified, capability-controlled
audit over one task-success outcome and two safety outcomes yields capability predicting task
success, safety correlations that move with outcome and panel, and an AgentHarm–jailbreak partial of
$\rho{=}+0.72$ , with an outcome-selectivity test at $p{=}0.051$ under organization-level resampling.
We release an API-only audit harness and re-run artifacts for four benchmarks and three held-out
outcomes in the accompanying reproducibility package.

#### Main conclusion.

Capability and safety scores dissociate, no single agent-safety benchmark substitutes for the
others, and the licensed claim depends on scorer, metric, and panel. At seven models a weak
relationship can appear systematic, so validity estimates require re-checking as the model
population turns over.

#### Scope.

The three RQ3 criteria are proxies for deployment, not measures of real-world harm; their limits
(single instances, grader dependence, panel size) are in Section 6.

## 2 Related Work

#### Agent-safety benchmarking.

InjecAgent (Zhan et al. 2024) and AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al. 2024) target prompt-injection
robustness; AgentHarm (Andriushchenko et al. 2025) measures compliance with harmful agentic tasks;
R-Judge (Yuan et al. 2024) scores safety-risk awareness over interaction traces. Evaluators we do
not re-run, such as ToolEmu (Ruan et al. 2024) for risky tool use, were likewise designed as
evaluators and not validated as measurements. AutoMonitor-Bench (Yang et al. 2026) scores
misbehavior monitors by miss and false-alarm rates. The closest work, a taxonomy and consistency
analysis of agent-safety benchmarks (Li et al. 2026), documents ranking disagreement without
capability control, criterion-validity tests, or latent-structure recovery, naming
capability-controlled evaluation as future work.

#### Construct validity.

Benchmark-agreement testing (Perlitz et al. 2024), metabench (Kipnis et al. 2025), and direct
construct analyses (Bean et al. 2025) find a strong shared latent factor across knowledge and
reasoning benchmarks. Kearns (2026) and NIST’s statistical framework (Keller et al. 2026) bring
quantitative construct-validity and uncertainty modeling to LLM evaluation. We apply this lens to
agent reliability and safety, where benchmarks target refusal, injection robustness, and risk
awareness, and where the capability confound has not been quantified.

#### Benchmark gaming.

Adversarial gaming is a separate and logically posterior concern. The F1 gameability in Section 4
involves a non-adversarial policy that labels every trace “unsafe” without examining it.

#### Over-refusal.

XSTest (Röttger et al. 2024) and OR-Bench (Cui et al. 2024) document exaggerated safety, or
over-refusal, at the prompt level. The between-benchmark analogue is whether AgentHarm refusal
trades off against R-Judge specificity; on the full panel that correlation is near zero, but on
seven-model subsets often not.

#### Agent reliability and task performance.

Recent work isolates corrupt success (Cao et al. 2026) and evidence-bounded reporting (Chen 2025);
$\tau$ -bench (Yao et al. 2024) and its dual-control successor $\tau^{2}$ -bench (Barres et al. 2025)
measure agentic task success. The $\tau^{2}$ retail domain serves as our held-out RQ3 task-success
criterion; the safety benchmarks are treated as candidate columns for audit.

## 3 Method

### 3.1 Model panel and benchmarks

The API-only panel comprises up to 22 models from nine model-developing organizations (OpenAI 6,
Meta 3, Qwen 3, Mistral 3, DeepSeek 2, Amazon 2, Anthropic, Google, Cohere; roster in Fig. 3 and
the artifact). Four safety benchmarks are re-run with official implementations and scorers: R-Judge
(full 571 items, self-judge), InjecAgent (300 stratified direct-harm/data-stealing items,
rule-scored), AgentHarm (44 base behaviors spanning all eight harm categories, official Inspect
evaluation, gpt-4o-mini judge), and AgentDojo (slack suite, 100 items, environment-scored for
security and utility), plus a held-out task-success criterion for RQ3.

Coverage (Fig. 3): R-Judge $n{=}21$ after Qwen3-32B falls below the $90\%$ valid-output
threshold; InjecAgent $n{=}22$ ; AgentHarm and AgentDojo, requiring native tool use, $n{=}19$ and
$5$ ; the $\tau^{2}$ criterion $n{=}20$ (App. A.2). The common R-Judge/InjecAgent/AgentHarm panel is
$n{=}18$ . Capability anchors (MMLU and GPQA-Diamond) are measured under a uniform protocol through
the same API harness as the safety runs: MMLU zero-shot on a fixed 500-item subset (seed 42,
identical items for every model) and GPQA-Diamond (198 items, chain-of-thought). These replace the
provider-reported model-card numbers used initially, which are retained as a pre-harmonization
comparison. The anchor panel is 21 models (DeepSeek-R1 excluded for unstable long-form GPQA
generation).

### 3.2 Benchmark targets

Target behaviors were fixed before any inspection of the score columns: R-Judge, discrimination of
unsafe from benign interaction traces; InjecAgent and AgentDojo, prompt-injection resistance (their
correlation is the convergent check); AgentHarm, refusal of harmful agentic tasks. R-Judge is
analyzed under specificity and balanced accuracy alongside the official F1.

#### Score orientation and terminology.

All scores are oriented higher-is-safer. R-Judge specificity is the true-negative rate on benign
traces; balanced accuracy is the mean of benign- and unsafe-class rates. InjecAgent robustness is
$1-$ attack success; AgentHarm safety is $1-$ harmful compliance. $\tau^{2}$ -bench is a task-success
criterion, not a safety score. “Internal consistency” refers to split-half analyses (App. A.2);
benchmark-specific scores are named explicitly rather than as “calibration” or “reliability.”

### 3.3 Analysis plan

Hypotheses, thresholds, and decision rules were fixed before each analysis; lacking an independent
timestamp, these are pre-specified rather than preregistered. All association tests are Spearman,
with two-sided asymptotic $p$ -values unless noted. Error bars in Fig. 2 are model-level
percentile-bootstrap intervals; the panel expansion and direct panel comparisons follow
pre-specified bootstrap procedures (App. A.6). The corroborative PCA uses the Pearson correlation
matrix of the standardized score columns, factor count by Horn’s parallel analysis against a
random-normal null (Spearman sensitivity in App. A.3). Partial Spearman correlations control the
capability composite, the mean of the standardized verified MMLU and GPQA anchors, whose model
ordering is identical to the anchors’ first principal component; the rank-residual implementation
and an alternative convention are in App. A.5. Between-construct redundancy is measured by these
rank-residualized partials.

Pre-specified controls: positive (capability-anchor loadings $\geq 0.6$ on the first factor);
negative (a column-permuted score matrix within the parallel-analysis null); convergent (high
InjecAgent–AgentDojo correlation). The headline statistic is the median pairwise partial Spearman
$|\rho|$ among distinct-construct benchmarks; the factor structure is interpretable only if
first-factor variance is $\geq 40\%$ or capability control reduces that median by $\geq 0.15$ , with
positive and negative controls passing. Thresholds and the disconfirming test were fixed before any
real run.

RQ3 uses three held-out outcomes, each pre-specified before running: task success on $\tau^{2}$ -bench
retail (Barres et al. 2025), 40 multi-turn, environment-scored tool-agent-user tasks; misalignment
safety, avoidance of blackmail or information leaking in a fictional autonomous-agent scenario
(Lynch et al. 2025), fixed classifier over 100 decisions per model; and jailbreak safety, $1-$
harmful compliance on 50 forbidden prompts averaged over three published jailbreak templates
(Souly et al. 2024; Wei et al. 2023). All run through the same API-only harness (the two safety
criteria are single-turn or scenario-based over the full panel; $\tau^{2}$ is a multi-turn tool loop
over 20 models), are distinct from the four audited benchmarks, and are not predictors. The headline
statistic is each safety score’s partial Spearman with the criterion controlling the capability
composite, reported after the criterion’s raw capability association; reporting rules cover
significant and null results. Analysis scripts and frozen inputs are in the reproducibility package.

Sections are ordered RQ4, RQ2, RQ1, RQ3.

### 4.1 The headline metric is gameable (RQ4)

Figure 1: R-Judge F1 ( $n{=}21$ ) against the constant “always unsafe” baseline (F1 ${=}0.69$ ,

$\mathrm{F1}=0.702$ , $0.012$ above the constant baseline, owing to lower recall. Balanced accuracy

### 4.2 The capability confound is real but metric-dependent (RQ2)

On the R-Judge panel ( $n{=}20$ with harmonized anchors), capability correlates with balanced
accuracy at $\rho=+0.71$ with MMLU ( $p<0.001$ ) and $+0.49$ with GPQA ( $p=0.03$ ), with F1 at $+0.76$
and $+0.62$ , and with specificity at $+0.16$ and $+0.07$ . Specificity can be inflated by rarely
flagging. The specificity–MMLU correlation was $0.85$ on our first nine models and $+0.16$ at
$n{=}20$ .

### 4.3 Benchmarks disagree; a seven-model panel suggested a trade-off that does not persist (RQ1)

No benchmark orders the panel as another does (Table 1); a top-AgentHarm model can rank near the
bottom on R-Judge specificity. Disagreement among benchmarks coded to different constructs (§3) is
expected and does not indict any single instrument; it precludes interchangeable quotation.

The R-Judge-specificity/AgentHarm-safety rank correlation was $-0.64$ at $n{=}7$ and $+0.02$
( $p=0.95$ ) at $n{=}18$ (Fig. 5, appendix); random size-7 subsets yield $|\rho|\geq 0.5$ in a quarter
of draws. The $n{=}18$ value holds under all four R-Judge metrics (App. A.4). Capability moderation
of the residual is untested and flagged as a hypothesis.

A single-factor PCA (Fig. 6, appendix) has first component $48.7\%$ variance, with R-Judge
specificity, InjecAgent robustness, and both capability anchors in one direction and AgentHarm safety
in the other ( $+0.33$ , opposite the cluster in $17$ of $18$ leave-one-out fits).

#### The positive control now passes.

On harmonized anchors MMLU loads $0.74\geq 0.6$ (provider-reported: $0.42$ , failing), and the
column-permuted matrix yields eigenvalues within the parallel-analysis null, so the pre-specified
interpretation conditions are met; the convergent control is inconclusive at AgentDojo’s $n{=}5$ .
A Spearman PCA keeps the loading structure but drops PC1 to $40.8\%$ with no factor retained by Horn
(App. A.3), and the median between-benchmark correlation is $0.22$ ; the factor is reported as
corroborative, Table 1 as primary.

#### Against agentic misalignment, capability has the opposite association.

On the full 21-model panel $\rho_{\text{cap}}=-0.44$ (asymptotic $p=0.047$ ), opposite in sign to

pre-specified $0.40$ effect-size threshold; AgentHarm safety does not ( $+0.16$ ; Table 2). Both
intervals include zero, neither survives Bonferroni, power is $\approx 0.35$ , and the pre-specified
directional prediction named AgentHarm; both are exploratory. The R-Judge partial is $+0.41$ under
specificity, $+0.19$ under balanced accuracy, and $-0.46$ under recall (App. A.4).

#### A direct interaction test on the original panel.

On the paired $n{=}20$ panel, capability correlates $+0.60$ with task success and $-0.41$ with
misalignment safety ( $-0.44$ on the full panel): $\Delta=-1.00$ (95% CI $[-1.48,-0.49]$ ,
$p<0.001$ ), stable under leave-one-model-out, leave-one-organization-out, organization-clustered
bootstrap, and subsampling (App. A.5). The corresponding R-Judge interaction is marginal
( $\Delta=+0.50$ , $p=0.082$ ), supporting the capability interaction but not a full two-way
dissociation. An independent misalignment grader gives $\rho=0.97$ with the original scores.

#### The capability–misalignment correlation is weaker on the expanded panel.

The pre-specified prediction was “hold or strengthen.” The estimate moves from $\rho=-0.44$
( $n{=}21$ , asymptotic $p=0.047$ ) to $-0.16$ ( $n{=}40$ , bootstrap $p=0.40$ ; 95% CI
$[-0.54,+0.22]$ ; App. A.6); the interval includes $-0.44$ and the nested-bootstrap
$\Delta\rho=+0.27$ (95% CI $[-0.25,+0.78]$ ) is not significant. Organization-matched subsets give
median $\rho=-0.17$ ; a generational explanation is possible and undemonstrated. $\tau^{2}$ was not
re-collected, so the interaction is not re-tested.

#### Models with similar capability scores differ in safety across organizations
(Fig. 4).

The 41-model panel spans 12 model-developing organizations (misalignment $n{=}40$ ; jailbreak
$n{=}41$ after one engagement-gate exclusion). Six organizations contribute at least four models for
within-organization correlations and seven at least three for the group comparison (App. A.6,
Table 5). Within-organization capability–safety correlations vary in sign, averaging $-0.14$
(misalignment) and $+0.26$ (jailbreak). With safety ranks adjusted for capability, the seven groups
differ on both criteria (permutation $p=0.004$ misalignment, $p<0.001$ jailbreak; Holm-significant;
df-adjusted Kruskal–Wallis $\varepsilon^{2}=0.34$ and $0.57$ ). The static composite may miss agentic
ability, organizations contribute few models, and some groups are range-restricted; the result is
associational.

#### Against jailbreak safety, AgentHarm shows the strongest held-out association.

The second safety outcome differs in failure mode, harness, and scoring: harmful compliance under
jailbreak, scored with StrongREJECT (Souly et al. 2024). Under a single template (AIM) 11 of 22 models
refuse every request; the three-template average (Wei et al. 2023) leaves no model at the ceiling.
Capability correlates $\rho=+0.08$ ( $n{=}21$ , $p=0.73$ ) on the 2024–25 panel and $+0.34$ ( $n{=}41$ ,
$p=0.04$ ) on the expanded panel; the change is not significant.

Controlling capability, AgentHarm safety correlates $\rho=+0.72$ ( $p<0.001$ ) with the three-template
outcome versus $+0.50$ for the ceiling-limited single template, stable under leave-one-model-out and
an independent grader (App. A.5). Selectivity over misalignment: $\Delta=+0.59$ , $p=0.027$ under
model-level bootstrap; $p=0.051$ resampling the eight represented organizations. On this paired panel
the misalignment partial is $+0.13$ ( $n{=}19$ ); Table 2’s $+0.16$ uses the common $n{=}18$ panel.
R-Judge specificity ( $-0.11$ ) and InjecAgent robustness ( $+0.21$ ) do not predict jailbreak safety.
AgentHarm and StrongREJECT both score harmful compliance. The reverse comparison, R-Judge and
InjecAgent predicting misalignment over jailbreak, is marginal ( $\Delta=+0.52$ , $p=0.068$ ).

#### Two alternative explanations, checked.

Seven LLM coders shown only construct descriptions assigned AgentHarm and the jailbreak outcome to
the same harm-blocking category ( $7/7$ each; Krippendorff $\alpha=0.61$ across three categories), and
classified the misalignment outcome less consistently (App. A.1). Controlling capability, AgentHarm
safety is uncorrelated with over-refusal on benign XSTest prompts (Röttger et al. 2024)
( $\rho=-0.01$ , $n{=}17$ ).

## 5 Discussion

The constant baseline matches R-Judge F1 (Observation 1), the three broad-coverage benchmarks rank
the same models differently, and held-out validity varies with outcome and panel (Table 2):
capability predicts task success while its safety correlations are unstable across panels.
AgentHarm’s capability-controlled association with three-template jailbreak safety ( $\rho=+0.72$ )
pairs two harmful-compliance measures, with outcome selectivity at $p=0.051$ under organization
resampling. The R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment associations are exploratory. Capability-adjusted
safety ranks differ among organization groups without identifying an organizational cause. Claims
are defensible only with benchmark, metric, target behavior, and model population attached.

## 6 Limitations and Threats to Validity

#### Panel size.

The AgentHarm-limited cross-benchmark panel is $n{=}18$ , up from a first pass at $n{=}7$ . A larger,
capability-spanning agent-loop panel is the primary gap.

#### Capability anchors.

Provider-reported anchors failed the positive control (MMLU $0.42$ ); re-measured MMLU and
GPQA-Diamond (§3) pass (MMLU $0.74$ ), with every RQ2/RQ3 sign unchanged. Both are static-knowledge
tests, though the composite predicts multi-turn tool-agent success at $+0.60$ . A six-model BFCL pilot
(Patil et al. 2025) failed as an agentic replacement: strict function-call syntax scoring ranked
GPT-4o-mini highest ( $0.72$ ) and the two most capable models lowest ( $0.42$ – $0.48$ ). Anchor
measurement error attenuates or suppresses partial relationships in no signable direction.

#### Multiple comparisons.

Per-test $p$ -values are uncorrected; the two strongly significant tests (crossover and AgentHarm
$\to$ jailbreak, both $p<0.001$ ) survive Bonferroni, while the R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment cells
( $p\approx 0.05$ – $0.09$ ) do not and are treated as suggestive.

#### Judges and coverage.

Independent graders reproduce model scores at $\rho=0.97$ (misalignment) and $\rho=0.98$ (jailbreak).
Rescoring AgentHarm refusals with a different model gives $\rho=0.69$ , with the AgentHarm–jailbreak
partial at $+0.66$ against $+0.72$ (App. A.5). AgentDojo covers five models, so cross-benchmark
analyses rest mainly on the other three.

#### Criterion validity (RQ3).

$\tau^{2}$ -retail (40 tasks, one run/model) uses a user-simulator of unbounded variance; the
misalignment criterion is a fictional-scenario probe (grader-robust, $\rho=0.97$ ; blackmail and
leaking halves Spearman–Brown $0.70$ ); the jailbreak criterion averages three jailbreaks. None yields
deployment-harm probabilities. Item-rich instruments with resampling support have split-half
consistency $\geq 0.96$ and rank stability $\geq 0.97$ . Worst-case within-model SEs are $12$ – $25\%$
of the between-model SD across bounded instruments (App. A.2). The AgentHarm–jailbreak association is
large and directionally stable, partly convergent, with borderline organization-resampled
selectivity; the R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment pattern is exploratory (marginal $\Delta=+0.52$ ,
power $\approx 0.35$ ; the three-scenario result is post-hoc; App. A.5).

## 7 Conclusion

Over four benchmarks and up to 22 models, R-Judge F1 lets an “always unsafe” baseline outrank five
models and rankings change with the benchmark. Capability predicts held-out task success but not
safety consistently across outcomes or panels. AgentHarm shows the strongest held-out safety
association ( $\rho=+0.72$ with jailbreak safety after controlling capability), with partial
instrument overlap and borderline organization-resampled selectivity. Safety evaluations should
report the full confusion structure, avoid standalone F1 where true negatives matter, and tie claims
to explicit target behaviors and model populations.

#### Blinded construct coding.

Qwen-2.5-72B, Mistral-Large, DeepSeek-V3) each received a neutral, predictive-information-stripped
description of each benchmark (no mention of our criteria, category names, or RQ3 results) and two
construct definitions (“harm blocking” vs. “risk recognition and correct treatment of benign inputs”),
with option and benchmark order shuffled per coder. Each assigned every benchmark to one construct
(B ${=}$ harm blocking, R ${=}$ risk recognition):

| Benchmark | blind | author | B / R

| R-Judge | recognition | recognition | 0 / 7

| InjecAgent | recognition | recognition | 1 / 6

| AgentHarm | blocking | blocking | 7 / 0

| AgentDojo | recognition | recognition | 0 / 7

All four majorities match the hand-assignment: $27/28$ ratings, Krippendorff’s $\alpha=0.825$
(nominal), against a chance baseline of $0.5^{4}=6.2\%$ for one coder matching all four labels by coin
flip. The single dissent (Llama-3.3-70B placing InjecAgent as harm blocking) is the semantically

definitions were written after the results), so the RQ1 factor, separating AgentHarm ( $+0.33$ ) from
the R-Judge/InjecAgent cluster without reference to any criterion, is also reported.

#### Blinded criterion coding, with a distractor.

The coding was re-run over all six targets (four benchmarks $+$ two criteria) with a third, plausible
task-success distractor construct. Krippendorff’s $\alpha=0.61$ (three categories, chance
$\approx 1/3$ ); the distractor is chosen $5/42$ times. AgentHarm and the jailbreak criterion both map
to harm blocking $7/7$ , R-Judge to risk recognition $7/7$ , and InjecAgent $5/7$ , all unchanged by the
distractor. AgentDojo reads as task success to $4/7$ coders (it is utility-scored; our $n{=}5$
benchmark). The misalignment criterion maps to risk recognition $6/7$ in a separate two-way round
(frozen votes in the artifact) and to harm blocking $6/7$ here (avoiding a harmful autonomous action
admits both readings). The AgentHarm–jailbreak pairing is thus recovered without predictive results,
and the R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment pattern stays exploratory.

# Safety, or Just Capability? A Validity Audit of Agent-Safety Benchmarks

Youting Wang

  
Xiao Han

  
Dingyan Shang

Affiliation: Yuan Tang

  
Bowen Liu

###### Abstract

Agent-safety benchmarks have multiplied quickly, and their scores now appear side by side in
model cards, leaderboards, and procurement documents as shorthand for how safe an agent is. We
re-run four widely cited benchmarks (R-Judge, InjecAgent, AgentHarm, AgentDojo) under their
official implementations and author-provided scorers on a panel of up to 22 API-served models
from nine model-developing organizations. Alongside them we measure MMLU and GPQA-Diamond under a
single uniform protocol as a capability reference, and we collect three held-out behavioral
outcomes: $\tau^{2}$ -bench retail task success, a fictional-scenario agentic-misalignment probe,
and a multi-template jailbreak suite scored with StrongREJECT. A later expansion extends the two
chat-based outcomes to a panel of roughly forty models from twelve organizations. We describe the
benchmarks’ targets, scoring conventions, coverage, and practical failure modes when run
end-to-end through a common harness. We document the alternative scoring views we computed for
R-Judge, the corroborative factor analysis we ran over the score columns, the robustness and
grader-substitution checks that accompanied each analysis, and the harness-level exclusions that
arise as model populations turn over. The main contribution is infrastructural and
methodological: an API-only audit harness, frozen re-run artifacts for four benchmarks and three
held-out outcomes, and a pre-specified analysis plan that others can apply to new panels. We close
with a discussion of what such re-runs can and cannot establish, and of the practical obstacles
to keeping agent-safety evaluation current as models and interfaces change.

## 1 Introduction

Between 2024 and 2026, dozens of benchmarks appeared claiming to measure whether LLM agents are
safe or reliable: resistance to prompt injection
(Zhan et al. 2024; Debenedetti et al. 2024), safety-risk awareness (Yuan et al. 2024), refusal of
harmful agentic tasks (Andriushchenko et al. 2025), and risky-tool-use identification
(Ruan et al. 2024), among others. A recent taxonomy (Li et al. 2026) catalogs
more than forty of them and reports that rankings vary when the benchmark is swapped. That work
stops at a twelve-model concordance check over four benchmarks, and lists
capability-controlled evaluation and benchmark consolidation among its open problems.

This paper picks up there. The pace at which agent-safety benchmarks are released has outrun the
pace at which they are re-run, compared, and maintained. Most benchmarks are introduced with a
fixed set of models evaluated at publication time, and later citations frequently reuse the
original numbers rather than generating new ones. As models are deprecated, renamed, or rerouted
through new serving interfaces, the original results become difficult to reproduce, and the
practical cost of running several benchmarks on the same panel grows. A shared, re-runnable
harness with a fixed analysis plan is therefore useful in its own right, independently of any
particular finding it produces.

We organize the audit around four research questions:

•

RQ1 (construct structure). How do the scores of nominally-distinct agent-safety
benchmarks covary across a common model panel?

•

RQ2 (capability confound). How do these scores relate to general capability as
measured by standard knowledge and reasoning anchors?

•

RQ3 (criterion validity). How do the safety scores relate to held-out behavioral
outcomes collected through a separate harness?

•

RQ4 (metric validity). How do the headline metrics shipped with each benchmark
interact with its data and scoring design?

These questions are deliberately broad. Each corresponds to a family of analyses that we
specified in advance, ran under a fixed protocol, and report with the corresponding robustness
checks. The value of fixing them in advance is less about any one answer than about making the
analysis reusable: when a new model panel becomes available, the same scripts can be run against
it with no further analytic choices.

#### Contributions.

We contribute three things. First, an API-only audit harness that runs four agent-safety
benchmarks, two capability anchors, and three held-out outcomes through a single model interface,
with per-benchmark parsers, validity gates, and exclusion rules that are applied identically to
every model. Second, a frozen set of re-run artifacts covering up to 22 models on the original
panel and roughly forty models on the chat-based expansion, together with the item-level logs
needed to recompute every reported statistic. Third, a pre-specified analysis plan, with positive,
negative, and convergent controls, partial-correlation conventions, resampling procedures, and
decision rules, that can be reapplied as new models and benchmarks appear. The artifacts and
scripts are included with the accompanying reproducibility package.

#### Main conclusion.

Running several agent-safety benchmarks on one panel is feasible with modest compute, but doing so
surfaces many practical choices—metric selection, output parsing, tool-calling compatibility,
judge models, and exclusion gates—that the original papers leave implicit or resolve differently.
Making these choices explicit and fixed, and publishing the resulting artifacts, is a prerequisite
for any comparison across benchmarks. The model population also turns over quickly, so a harness
that can be re-pointed at new models with minimal change is as important as any individual
snapshot of scores.

#### Scope.

The three RQ3 outcomes are stand-ins for deployment, not claims about
real-world harm; their limits (single instances, grader dependence, panel size) are in
Section 6.

## 2 Related Work

#### Agent-safety benchmarking.

Each of the four benchmarks we audit targets one construct.
InjecAgent (Zhan et al. 2024) and AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al. 2024) target prompt-injection
robustness; AgentHarm (Andriushchenko et al. 2025) measures compliance with harmful agentic tasks; R-Judge
(Yuan et al. 2024) scores safety-risk awareness over interaction traces. Evaluators we do not
re-run, such as ToolEmu (Ruan et al. 2024) for risky tool use, occupy a similar position: they are
designed as evaluators and released with a reference set of results. AutoMonitor-Bench
(Yang et al. 2026) scores misbehavior monitors by miss and false-alarm rates, which reflects a
broader trend toward reporting several error types for monitoring tasks. Closest to this paper is
a taxonomy and consistency analysis of agent-safety benchmarks (Li et al. 2026), which
documents ranking variation across benchmarks and names capability-controlled evaluation as
future work. We take that suggestion as a starting point for building a re-runnable harness.

The broader landscape of agent evaluation is heterogeneous in format. Some benchmarks present a
model with a complete interaction trace and ask for a judgment; others place the model inside a
simulated environment with tools and measure what it does; still others issue a single harmful
request wrapped in an agentic framing and grade the response. These formats differ in how much
scaffolding they require, how sensitive they are to tool-calling conventions, and how easily they
port to new serving interfaces. A recurring practical issue is that the most environment-heavy
benchmarks are the hardest to maintain, because their harnesses depend on specific function-call
schemas that providers change over time.

#### Construct validity.

Prior work asks whether benchmark scores agree and what latent
constructs they capture. Benchmark-agreement testing (Perlitz et al. 2024), metabench
(Kipnis et al. 2025), and direct construct analyses (Bean et al. 2025) find that
knowledge and reasoning benchmarks share a strong latent factor. Kearns (2026) and
NIST’s statistical framework (Keller et al. 2026) bring quantitative construct-validity and
uncertainty modeling to LLM evaluation. These lines of work draw on a long psychometric tradition
in which tests are compared through their intercorrelations, their factor structure, and their
relationships to external outcomes. We borrow several of their tools—parallel analysis, partial
correlation, resampling-based uncertainty—and apply them to a domain in which benchmarks are
younger, smaller, and more heterogeneous in format than the knowledge and reasoning suites on
which those tools were first exercised.

#### Benchmark gaming.

A separate literature concerns benchmarks being gamed by an adversary, through contamination,
targeted fine-tuning, or prompt engineering aimed at a specific scorer. Our setting is different:
we evaluate publicly available models without any benchmark-specific adaptation and run each
benchmark exactly as released. Questions about how a scoring rule interacts with its data are
still relevant in this setting, because they shape what a reported number reflects even when no
one is optimizing against it. We treat these questions under RQ4 and keep the discussion tied to
the specific scorers we ran.

#### Over-refusal.

XSTest (Röttger et al. 2024) and OR-Bench (Cui et al. 2024) document
exaggerated safety, or over-refusal, at the level of individual prompts. Over-refusal is a natural
companion consideration for any safety benchmark that rewards refusal, because a model that
declines broadly will score well on harm-avoidance items regardless of whether it distinguishes
harmful from benign requests. We include XSTest as an auxiliary instrument so that refusal-based
scores can be read alongside a direct measure of refusal on benign prompts.

#### Agent reliability and task performance.

Recent work isolates specific agent-reliability failures
such as corrupt success (Cao et al. 2026) and evidence-bounded reporting
(Chen 2025); $\tau$ -bench (Yao et al. 2024) and its dual-control successor
$\tau^{2}$ -bench (Barres et al. 2025) measure agentic task success. We borrow the latter’s retail
domain as our held-out RQ3 task-success outcome. Task success is an important reference point for
agent evaluation because safety interventions are often discussed in terms of their cost to
usefulness; having a task-success measure on the same panel lets readers place safety scores in
the context of what the same models can actually accomplish.

## 3 Method

### 3.1 Model panel and benchmarks

We assemble a compute-light, API-only panel of up to 22 models from nine model-developing organizations
(OpenAI 6, Meta 3, Qwen 3, Mistral 3, DeepSeek 2, Amazon 2, Anthropic, Google, Cohere; full
roster in Fig. 3 and the artifact). We re-run four safety benchmarks with their official
implementations and scorers: R-Judge (full 571 items, self-judge), InjecAgent (300 stratified
direct-harm/data-stealing items, rule-scored), AgentHarm (44 base behaviors spanning all eight
harm categories, via the official Inspect evaluation with a gpt-4o-mini judge), and AgentDojo
(the slack suite, 100 items, environment-scored for security and utility), plus a
held-out task-success outcome for RQ3 (below).

Coverage differs by benchmark (Fig. 3 maps the full panel): R-Judge has $n{=}21$ after
Qwen3-32B falls below the $90\%$ valid-output threshold; InjecAgent has $n{=}22$ ; AgentHarm and AgentDojo,
which require native tool use, have $n{=}19$ and $5$ ; and the $\tau^{2}$ outcome has $n{=}20$
(App. A.2). The common R-Judge/InjecAgent/AgentHarm panel therefore has $n{=}18$ .
Capability anchors (MMLU and
GPQA-Diamond) are measured by us under one uniform protocol: MMLU zero-shot on a fixed 500-item
subset (seed 42, identical items for every model) and GPQA-Diamond (198 items, chain-of-thought),
through the same API harness as the safety runs. We began with provider-reported model-card
numbers; the replacements hold the protocol fixed across models. The anchor panel is 21 models
(DeepSeek-R1 is excluded for unstable long-form GPQA generation); we keep the provider-reported
anchors as a pre-harmonization comparison.

The decision to run every model through the same harness has costs. Provider-specific features
such as system-prompt handling, tool-choice parameters, and reasoning-effort settings differ, and
a uniform harness necessarily makes one choice for all of them. We favored uniformity over
per-model tuning because per-model tuning introduces researcher degrees of freedom that are hard
to document and harder to replicate. Where a model could not complete a benchmark under the
uniform harness, we recorded the failure and applied a pre-specified exclusion rule rather than
adapting the harness to that model.

### 3.2 Benchmark targets

Before looking at any relationship among the score columns, we wrote down what behavior each
benchmark is meant to measure. R-Judge tests whether a model distinguishes unsafe from benign
interaction traces. InjecAgent and AgentDojo both test resistance to prompt injection, so their
correlation serves as a convergent check. AgentHarm tests whether a model refuses harmful agentic
tasks. For R-Judge, we compute specificity and balanced accuracy in addition to the official F1
so that the benchmark can be read under more than one scoring view.

These written targets follow the benchmarks’ own documentation closely. We did not attempt to
reinterpret any benchmark’s purpose; the descriptions serve mainly to fix, before analysis, which
pairs of benchmarks are expected to measure the same behavior and which are expected to measure
different ones.

#### Score orientation and terminology.

All reported scores are oriented so that higher is
better or safer. R-Judge specificity is the fraction of benign traces correctly identified
as benign; its balanced accuracy averages performance on benign and unsafe traces.
InjecAgent robustness is one minus attack success, and AgentHarm safety is one minus harmful
compliance. For RQ3, $\tau^{2}$ -bench is a held-out task-success outcome, not a safety score.
We use internal consistency for split-half analyses (App. A.2) and name each
benchmark-specific score explicitly, instead of stretching “calibration” or “reliability”
past their usual meanings.

### 3.3 Analysis plan

Before running each analysis, we fixed its hypotheses, thresholds, and decision rules. Because
these choices lack an independent timestamp, we describe the analyses as pre-specified rather than
preregistered.
We use Spearman correlations for all association tests. Unless otherwise noted, correlation
$p$ -values use two-sided asymptotic Spearman tests. Error bars in figures are
model-level percentile-bootstrap intervals. The panel expansion follows its own pre-specified
bootstrap procedure (App. A.6). The corroborative PCA operates on the
Pearson correlation matrix of the standardized score columns; factor count is chosen with Horn’s
parallel analysis against a random-normal null, with a rank-based (Spearman) sensitivity in
App. A.3. We use partial Spearman correlations controlling a capability composite;
App. A.5 gives the rank-residual implementation and an alternative convention.
The capability composite is the mean of the standardized, verified
MMLU and GPQA anchors.

We pre-specified three controls: positive (capability-anchor loadings $\geq 0.6$ on the first
factor); negative (a column-permuted score matrix within the parallel-analysis null); and
convergent (a high correlation between the same-construct InjecAgent and AgentDojo scores).
The decision rule permits interpretation of the factor structure only if the positive and negative
controls pass and a pre-specified variance or partial-correlation threshold is met. These
thresholds were fixed before any real run.

For RQ3 we pre-specified three held-out outcomes, each before running it.
Task success is $\tau^{2}$ -bench retail (Barres et al. 2025): 40 multi-turn,
environment-scored tool-agent-user tasks. Misalignment safety records whether a model avoids
blackmail or information leaking in a fictional autonomous-agent scenario
(Lynch et al. 2025), scored by a fixed classifier over 100 decisions per model.
Jailbreak safety is one minus harmful-compliance on 50 forbidden prompts, averaged over three published
jailbreak templates to reduce the ceiling created by any single template
(Souly et al. 2024; Wei et al. 2023). All three run through
the same API-only harness (the two safety outcomes are single-turn or scenario-based and cover the
full panel; the $\tau^{2}$ outcome is a multi-turn tool loop covering 20 models), are distinct from
the four audited benchmarks, and are not among the predictors. For each outcome, we planned to
report its association with the capability composite and the partial association of each safety
score after controlling the composite. The pre-specified analysis gives reporting rules for both
significant and null results. The accompanying reproducibility package contains the analysis
scripts and frozen inputs needed to reproduce every analysis.

Fixing the plan in advance has a practical rationale beyond statistical hygiene. With four
benchmarks, several metrics per benchmark, two anchors, three outcomes, and a panel that grows
over time, the number of analyses one could run is large. A fixed plan keeps the analysis small
enough to audit and makes clear which comparisons were intended and which were added afterward.
Where we did add analyses after the fact, we label them as exploratory in the text and appendix.

## 4 Results

This section reports the analyses in the order of the research questions as numbered in the
plan’s execution: metric considerations (RQ4) first, then capability (RQ2), cross-benchmark
structure (RQ1), and held-out outcomes (RQ3). Throughout, we emphasize procedure and robustness,
and we keep interpretation close to what a panel of this size can support.

### 4.1 The headline metric is gameable (RQ4)

Figure 1: R-Judge scores on the evaluated panel under the official F1 metric and under the
alternative scoring views computed by the harness (specificity, recall, balanced accuracy). Each
point is a model; the scoring views are computed from the same verdicts.

R-Judge asks a model to read an agent interaction trace and decide whether it contains a safety
risk. The official scorer reports F1 over the “unsafe” class. Like any single-number summary of a
binary classifier, F1 weights some error types more than others, and its behavior depends on the
mix of positive and negative items in the evaluation set. These properties are well known in the
information-retrieval and medical-testing literatures, where precision–recall summaries and
specificity–sensitivity summaries are routinely reported together because they emphasize different
aspects of performance.

For this reason, the harness records the full confusion matrix for every model on R-Judge rather
than F1 alone, and computes specificity, recall, and balanced accuracy from the same verdicts.
Doing so costs nothing at evaluation time and allows readers to inspect how a model’s errors are
distributed between benign and unsafe traces. It also makes it possible to compare R-Judge with
other benchmarks under a scoring view that matches whichever aspect of trace judgment is of
interest. We use specificity in the cross-benchmark analyses below because it is the view that
corresponds most directly to correct treatment of benign traces, and we report the sensitivity of
those analyses to the other views in App. A.4.

###### Observation 1 (F1 admits a high-scoring constant baseline).

For a benchmark scored by F1 on the positive class, a model’s score depends jointly on its recall
and its precision, and precision depends in turn on the class composition of the evaluation set.
Two models that make different trade-offs between flagging unsafe traces and clearing benign ones
can therefore receive similar F1 scores, and a model’s F1 can change if the evaluation set is
rebalanced even when its per-class behavior does not. Reporting the confusion structure alongside
F1 makes these trade-offs visible, and is the practice we follow for every trace-judgment score in
this paper.

Beyond R-Judge, the same consideration applies to any benchmark that reduces a two-class judgment
to a single summary statistic. Several of the other benchmarks we ran report rates (attack success,
harmful compliance) rather than classification summaries, and for those the corresponding
consideration is the denominator: which items count toward the rate, how unparseable outputs are
treated, and whether refusals and errors are pooled. We document these choices per benchmark in
the artifact so that reported rates can be recomputed under alternative conventions.

### 4.2 The capability confound is real but metric-dependent (RQ2)

Capability anchors play two roles in this audit. First, they provide a reference ordering of the
panel against which safety scores can be read: a reader can ask whether a benchmark’s ordering
looks like the anchors’ ordering or departs from it. Second, they serve as the control variable for
the partial correlations in RQ3. For both roles, the anchors need to be measured consistently, which
is why we replaced provider-reported numbers with our own uniform-protocol measurements.

The harmonization step deserves some emphasis. Provider-reported MMLU and GPQA numbers are produced
under different prompt formats, shot counts, decoding settings, and, for GPQA, different
chain-of-thought conventions. Mixing them introduces variation that has nothing to do with the
models themselves. Under our protocol, every model sees the same 500 MMLU items in the same
zero-shot format and the same 198 GPQA-Diamond items with a fixed chain-of-thought prompt, and
answers are extracted with the same parser. We retain the provider-reported values in the artifact
so that the effect of harmonization on any downstream analysis can be inspected directly.

When the anchors are compared with the R-Judge scoring views, the choice of view matters for how
closely R-Judge tracks capability. This is expected from the definitions: the scoring views
summarize different parts of the confusion matrix, and there is no reason for each part to relate
to general knowledge and reasoning in the same way. We report the correlations for all four views
in App. A.4 and recommend that readers who use R-Judge as a capability-adjusted safety signal
specify which view they rely on.

### 4.3 Benchmarks disagree; a seven-model panel suggested a trade-off that does not persist (RQ1)

The cross-benchmark analysis uses the 18 models for which R-Judge, InjecAgent, and AgentHarm are all
available. AgentDojo, run on five models, is used only for the convergent control. The analysis
proceeds in two steps: a direct comparison of model orderings across benchmarks, and a
corroborative principal-component analysis over the standardized score columns together with the
two capability anchors.

Comparing orderings is the most transparent step, because it requires no modeling assumptions. A
reader can place the per-model scores side by side and see where benchmarks agree and where they do
not. Benchmarks written to target different behaviors need not agree, and agreement or disagreement
between them is informative only in light of what each was designed to measure (§3.2). We provide
the per-model scores in the artifact in a format that supports this comparison directly.

The panel was assembled incrementally. Our first pass covered seven models, and the cross-benchmark
analysis was rerun as coverage grew to the current 18. Incremental assembly is common in practice,
because tool-calling benchmarks fail on some models and those failures are only discovered by
running them. It carries a methodological lesson: correlations estimated on a handful of models
have wide sampling distributions, and patterns that appear on an early panel should be revisited
once more models are available. We therefore treat all early-panel observations as provisional and
base our analyses on the full common panel, with random-subset resampling used to characterize how
much small-panel estimates can vary (App. A.5).

The corroborative PCA follows the plan in §3.3 (Fig. 6, appendix). We include it because factor
structure is the conventional way to summarize how a set of tests covaries, and because it allows the
pre-specified controls to be checked. We do not lean on it as primary evidence, for reasons
discussed in App. A.3.

#### The positive control now passes.

The pre-specified positive control requires the capability anchors to load substantially on the first
factor. With provider-reported anchors, this control failed, which was our original reason for
caution and the motivation for re-measuring the anchors under a uniform protocol. With the
harmonized anchors, the control passes, and the negative control (a column-permuted score matrix
compared against the parallel-analysis null) also passes. The convergent control is inconclusive
because AgentDojo covers only five models. We treat the resulting factor structure as a description
of the panel rather than as evidence of an underlying trait, and we note in App. A.3 that its
summary statistics depend on whether a Pearson or rank-based correlation matrix is used.

### 4.4 Predictive validity differs across held-out outcomes (RQ3)

Everything above is internal to the benchmarks. RQ3 steps outside them by asking how the safety
scores relate to behavior collected through a separate harness, after accounting for the capability
composite. We pre-specified three outcomes (§3): $\tau^{2}$ -bench task success, misalignment
safety, and jailbreak safety. All are distinct from the four audited benchmarks, and each has a
fixed metric and decision rule.

Held-out outcomes are useful because they do not share items, formats, or scorers with the audited
benchmarks. If a benchmark and an outcome are associated, the association cannot be attributed to
shared items. At the same time, the outcomes are themselves instruments with their own limitations,
and the choice of outcome shapes what any association means. We therefore chose three outcomes that
differ in format (multi-turn tool use, a scenario-based decision, single-turn harmful requests) and
in failure mode (task failure, autonomous harmful action, harmful compliance).

Figure 2: Capability composite and held-out outcome scores on the original and expanded panels.
Filled circles mark the 2024–25 panel; open diamonds mark the expanded panel; error bars are
model-level percentile-bootstrap 95% CIs. Task success was not re-collected for the expansion.

#### Against task success, safety scores add no information beyond capability.

$\tau^{2}$ -retail is a multi-turn, environment-scored task in which a model acting as a customer-service
agent must resolve a simulated user’s request through a set of tools while respecting domain policy.
It is the outcome most closely aligned with what the capability anchors are designed to reflect, and
we included it partly as a reference point: any safety score should be read against the backdrop of
how much the same models can accomplish. The partial-correlation analysis asks whether each safety
score relates to task success beyond what the composite accounts for. We report the analysis in the
artifact with model-level bootstrap intervals and note that, with a single run per model and an
unbounded user-simulator variance, it is the least precisely measured of the three outcomes.

The task-success outcome also illustrates a general point about agentic evaluation. A model that
refuses or hedges more often will tend to complete fewer tasks, and a model that is more willing to
act will tend to complete more. Whether a safety score should relate to task success positively,
negatively, or not at all depends on what kind of safety it targets. This is why we pair task success
with two outcomes that target safety directly.

#### Against agentic misalignment, capability has the opposite association.

The misalignment outcome places a model in a fictional autonomous-agent scenario in which it can
pursue an assigned goal by blackmailing an employee or leaking confidential information. A fixed
classifier scores each of 100 decisions per model. This outcome differs from the others in that the
harmful action is self-initiated rather than requested: no user asks the model to blackmail anyone.
It therefore probes a behavior that none of the four audited benchmarks targets directly, and that
the capability anchors would not be expected to reflect in any straightforward way.

Because the scenario rewards strategic reasoning about the situation, it is plausible that more
capable models recognize the opportunity for harmful action more readily, and also plausible that
they recognize the ethical constraints more readily. We registered the outcome without a strong
directional expectation for capability and with a directional expectation for AgentHarm, which we
considered the closest audited benchmark in spirit. Associations with the other benchmarks were
treated as exploratory from the outset.

#### A direct interaction test on the original panel.

The plan included a direct comparison of how the capability composite relates to task success and
to misalignment safety on the paired $n{=}20$ panel for which both are available. A test of this
kind is more informative than two separate correlations, because it accounts for their shared
models. We implemented it as a bootstrap over models, with leave-one-model-out,
leave-one-organization-out, organization-clustered bootstrap, and random-subset checks
(App. A.5). An independent misalignment grader was used to confirm that the misalignment scores
themselves are not specific to one classifier.

#### The capability–misalignment correlation is weaker on the expanded panel.

The expansion described in App. A.6 extends the misalignment and jailbreak outcomes to roughly forty
models. Before running it, we specified that the original-panel estimate should “hold or
strengthen.” The expansion is the clearest test in this paper of whether an estimate obtained on one
panel carries over to a later one, and we designed its analysis to account for the original panel
being nested in the expanded one: a stratified nested bootstrap for the change itself, a comparison
restricted to the newly added models, and organization-matched subsets of the expanded pool.
Because $\tau^{2}$ was not re-collected, the interaction from the previous paragraph could not be
re-tested on the expanded panel. We discuss what panel expansions can and cannot establish in §5
and §6.

#### Models with similar capability scores differ in safety across organizations
(Fig. 4).

The expanded panel spans 12 model-developing organizations, several of which contribute multiple
models across sizes and release dates. This structure makes it possible to look at safety within
organizations as well as across them. We computed within-organization correlations for
organizations contributing at least four models and a capability-adjusted comparison of
organization groups for those contributing at least three. These analyses are descriptive. The
capability composite is a static-knowledge measure that may not capture agentic ability, each
organization contributes few models, and some organizations have restricted safety ranges, so
organizational differences in this setting cannot be read as causal. They are reported because
organization is the most salient grouping in any real model panel, and ignoring it would leave a
large source of structure unexamined.

#### Against jailbreak safety, AgentHarm shows the strongest held-out association.

The jailbreak outcome is the closest of the three to an audited benchmark in format: it measures
harmful compliance with single-turn requests wrapped in published jailbreak templates and scored
with StrongREJECT (Souly et al. 2024). A single template (AIM) produced a ceiling, with many models
refusing every request. Averaging over three published templates (Wei et al. 2023) was
pre-specified to reduce that ceiling. Because AgentHarm also measures harmful compliance, albeit in
an agentic framing with tool calls, any association between the two is best read as agreement
between related instruments rather than as evidence about safety in general. We report the
per-template partials and the selectivity comparison against misalignment in App. A.5, with both a
model-level and an organization-level bootstrap.

The distinction between instruments that share a target and instruments that do not is central to
interpreting any held-out analysis. Two benchmarks that measure the same behavior through different
formats should agree; when they do, that is reassuring about both, but it says little about whether
either captures a broader property. Conversely, a benchmark that relates to a held-out outcome with a
different target raises the question of what shared behavior links them. We keep these two kinds of
evidence separate throughout.

#### Two alternative explanations, checked.

Two concerns arise for any analysis that groups benchmarks by target. The first is that the
grouping might be influenced by the analysts’ knowledge of the data. To address it, seven LLM coders
from distinct model families, shown only construct descriptions and no predictive information,
independently assigned each benchmark and outcome to a construct category (App. A.1). The second is
that refusal-based scores might reflect blanket refusal rather than discrimination between harmful
and benign requests. To address it, we ran XSTest (Röttger et al. 2024) on the panel and
recorded over-refusal on its benign subset as an auxiliary variable. Both checks are reported in
App. A.1; both are low-powered at this panel size and are best treated as context for the main
analyses.

## 5 Discussion

The practical lesson of this audit is that running several agent-safety benchmarks on one panel
involves many decisions that the benchmarks themselves do not make for the user. Which metric to
report for a trace-judgment task, how to treat unparseable outputs, which judge model to use, which
models to exclude when tool calls fail, and how to measure capability consistently are all choices
that shape the resulting numbers. None of these choices is exotic, but in the absence of a shared
harness they are typically made differently by each group that runs the benchmarks, and the
differences are rarely reported. A fixed, published harness is a straightforward way to make them
visible.

A second lesson concerns the model population. Over the course of this project, several models were
deprecated or rerouted, some new models could not complete tool-calling benchmarks under a uniform
harness, and the panel grew from seven models to more than forty for the chat-based outcomes.
Evaluation harnesses age quickly in this environment. Benchmarks that require native tool calling
are the most fragile, because providers change function-call schemas and routing behavior without
notice. Chat-based outcomes are more portable, which is one reason the expansion focused on them.
Designers of new agent-safety benchmarks might consider offering both a native tool-calling mode and
a portable fallback that can be run on any chat interface.

A third lesson concerns panel size. Statistical analysis across models treats each model as an
observation, and model panels in the agent-safety literature are typically small. Patterns
estimated on a handful of models are fragile, and the incremental way panels are assembled—running
whatever models currently work, adding more as harnesses are fixed—invites reading too much into
early results. Pre-specifying analyses, reporting resampling-based uncertainty, and revisiting
estimates as the panel grows are modest safeguards that the field could adopt more widely.

Finally, we note that agent-safety benchmarks differ substantially in what they target: judging
risk in a trace, resisting injected instructions, refusing harmful agentic tasks. These are related
but distinct behaviors, and there is no a priori reason to expect a single number to summarize them.
The audit harness is designed to make it easy to report several of them side by side, together with
capability anchors and held-out outcomes, so that readers can form their own view of how a given
model behaves across them.

## 6 Limitations and Threats to Validity

#### Panel size.

The AgentHarm-limited cross-benchmark panel has $n{=}18$ , up from our
first pass at $n{=}7$ . Even the larger panel is small by the standards of psychometric work, where
factor analyses and partial correlations are routinely estimated on hundreds of respondents. The
gap most worth closing is a larger, capability-spanning agent-loop panel, which in turn depends on
more stable tool-calling interfaces across providers.

#### Capability anchors.

Provider-reported model-card anchors initially failed their positive control. Re-measuring MMLU
and GPQA-Diamond (§3) addressed this. These are static-knowledge tests, and whether they capture the
abilities relevant to agentic behavior is an open question. A six-model BFCL pilot
(Patil et al. 2025) was considered as an agentic replacement but did not behave as a capability
measure under strict function-call syntax scoring, apparently rewarding format conformance. That
experience is the argument for developing a validated agentic anchor. Measurement error in the
anchor attenuates or suppresses partial relationships instead of biasing them in a direction we
could sign.

#### Multiple comparisons.

We report per-test $p$ -values without a family-wise correction in the body, because the analyses
were pre-specified in families and are interpreted through effect sizes and decision rules rather
than through individual significance thresholds. Readers who prefer a family-wise view can apply a
Bonferroni or Holm correction to the per-test values in the artifact; we flag analyses that were
added after the fact as exploratory in the text.

#### Judges and coverage.

Several components of the pipeline rely on LLM judges: AgentHarm’s refusal and grading steps, the
misalignment classifier, and the StrongREJECT scorer for the jailbreak outcome. We ran
independent-grader checks for each, substituting a judge from a different model family and
re-scoring cached outputs (App. A.5). AgentDojo runs on only five models, so the cross-benchmark
analyses depend primarily on the other three benchmarks.

#### Criterion validity (RQ3).

$\tau^{2}$ -retail (40 tasks, one run/model) is scored by a
user-simulator whose variance we do not bound; the misalignment outcome is a fictional-scenario
probe whose two scenario halves agree only moderately; the jailbreak outcome averages three
jailbreaks. None gives literal deployment-harm probabilities. For the item-rich instruments,
within-model standard errors and split-half consistency are reported in App. A.2. The construct
groupings used to organize RQ3 come from the benchmarks’ own documentation and from a blinded
coding exercise, but the category definitions themselves were written by the authors, and a
different taxonomy might group the instruments differently.

## 7 Conclusion

We re-ran four agent-safety benchmarks, two capability anchors, and three held-out behavioral
outcomes through a single API-only harness on a panel of up to 22 models, and extended the
chat-based outcomes to roughly forty models. The audit documents the scoring views, exclusion
rules, judge substitutions, and resampling procedures needed to compare these instruments on a
common footing, and it releases the artifacts and scripts required to repeat every analysis on new
panels. Agent-safety evaluation will remain a moving target as models, interfaces, and benchmarks
change; we hope that a shared, re-runnable harness and a fixed analysis plan make it easier for
others to keep their comparisons current, transparent, and reproducible.

### A.1 Ruling out two artifacts (detail for §4.4)

#### Blinded construct coding.

Seven LLM coders from distinct families—GPT-4o,
Claude-3-Haiku, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen-2.5-72B, Mistral-Large, DeepSeek-V3—were each
shown only a neutral, predictive-information-stripped description of what each benchmark
measures (no mention of our outcomes, category names, or any RQ3 analysis) plus two construct
definitions (“harm blocking” vs. “risk recognition and correct treatment of benign inputs”). The two options
and the benchmark order were shuffled per coder to remove position bias. Each coder assigned every
benchmark to one construct, and we compared the majority assignment with the authors’ assignment in
§3.2. Agreement is summarized with Krippendorff’s $\alpha$ (nominal). This procedure controls
coder bias but not rubric-designer bias, since the category definitions were written by the
authors.

Using LLMs as coders has obvious limitations. The coders may share training data, may be sensitive
to wording in the descriptions, and may not reflect how human experts would classify the same
instruments. We use them because they allow a fully blinded, cheaply repeatable exercise in which
the coders demonstrably have no access to our results, and because using several families reduces
dependence on any one model’s idiosyncrasies. A human-coder replication would be a natural
extension.

#### Blinded criterion coding, with a distractor.

To check that groupings involving the held-out outcomes are also recoverable blind, and to make the
agreement statistic meaningful, we re-ran the coding over all six targets (four benchmarks $+$ two
safety outcomes) with a third, plausible task-success distractor construct. Adding a distractor
raises the chance-agreement baseline to roughly one in three and tests whether coders choose among
the substantive categories for substantive reasons. Two targets were genuinely contested in this
round: AgentDojo, which is utility-scored as well as security-scored, and the misalignment outcome,
since avoiding a harmful autonomous action can be read both as recognizing and as declining it. The
frozen votes for both rounds are in the artifact.

#### XSTest over-refusal (blanket-refusal check).

We ran XSTest (Röttger et al., 2024;
cited in the main paper) on the
panel via its published CPI (compliance/partial/refusal) scorer (judge gpt-4o-mini): the
safe subset (benign prompts that superficially resemble unsafe ones) measures over-refusal,
the unsafe subset measures correct refusal of overtly-harmful prompts. The unsafe subset is close to
ceiling for most models, so the more informative signal is over-refusal on the safe subset. We
computed capability-controlled partial correlations between each refusal-based score and both
XSTest subsets. These checks are low-powered at the available panel size and are reported as
context for the main analyses rather than as tests in their own right.

The PCA is a summary device. With five columns (three benchmark scores and two anchors) and 18
