### A.3 Cross-benchmark structure (detail for §4.3)

Our pre-specified plan included a principal component analysis of the standardized score columns
on the $n{=}18$ common panel, with factor count chosen by Horn’s parallel analysis against a
random-normal null. The PCA was intended as a descriptive summary of how the columns covary, to be
interpreted only if the positive and negative controls passed. With six columns (four benchmark
scores excluding AgentDojo’s small panel, plus two anchors) and eighteen models, the analysis has
limited resolution, and its eigenvalues carry substantial sampling uncertainty. We therefore regard
any factor structure on this panel as a description of the sample rather than as a model of the
benchmarks’ latent structure.

#### Correlation-convention sensitivity.

A PCA can be computed on the Pearson correlation matrix of the standardized scores or on the
Spearman (rank) correlation matrix. With bounded, skewed instruments and a small panel, the two
conventions can retain different numbers of components, and the variance attributed to the first
component can shift by several percentage points. The pre-specified negative control passes as
executed: $200$ column-permuted matrices give median first eigenvalue $1.71$ against the
parallel-analysis $95$ th-percentile threshold of $2.18$ (exceedance $2\%$ ). Convention sensitivity is
a general reason to treat factor analyses on panels of this size as supporting rather than primary
evidence, and to report both conventions whenever factor structure is discussed.

### A.4 R-Judge metric sensitivity (detail for §4.3–§4.4)

Because R-Judge can be summarized in several ways, the harness stores per-model verdicts and labels
so that every R-Judge-involving quantity can be recomputed under specificity, recall, balanced
accuracy, and the official F1. Each of these summaries answers a different question. Specificity
asks how often benign traces are left alone; recall asks how often unsafe traces are caught;
balanced accuracy weights the two equally regardless of base rate; F1 combines recall with precision
and ignores true negatives. A reader whose use case is a monitor with a high cost of false alarms
should prefer a summary that includes specificity, while a reader whose use case is a last-line
filter may prefer recall. The artifact therefore exposes all four, and we recommend that any
secondary analysis of R-Judge state which summary it uses and, where conclusions might depend on
that choice, report the alternatives. Metric choice is not a detail to be settled once by the
benchmark designers; it is part of the claim being made.

### A.5 Robustness of the capability crossover (detail for §4.4)

#### Partial-correlation convention.

Partials residualize midranks on the harmonized
capability composite and re-rank the residuals. The classic alternative computes Pearson
correlations on the rank residuals without re-ranking. The two conventions coincide in large samples
and differ slightly in small ones; both are implemented in the released scripts so that any
covariate-adjusted quantity can be reproduced under either. We also implement leave-one-model-out
and leave-one-organization-out recomputation, organization-clustered bootstrap, and subsampling at
sizes $10$ , $12$ , and $14$ , which together give a picture of how much any panel-level estimate
depends on particular models or developers.

Independent-grader checks are part of the same robustness suite. The misalignment classifier was
re-run with a second grader (Claude-3-Haiku vs. GPT-4o), the jailbreak judge with a second judge
(Gemini vs. gpt-4o), and AgentHarm’s refusal component with a Gemini refusal judge re-scoring the
cached completions ( $n{=}19$ ). The first two reproduce model-level scores closely. The AgentHarm
swap agrees less closely, which reflects that it redoes only the refusal component, not the full
grading pipeline. Per-template jailbreak scores (AIM, refusal suppression, prefix injection) are
stored separately in the artifact so that template-specific analyses can be run without
re-collecting data.

#### Misalignment 3-scenario battery (exploratory).

We also ran a third scenario (murder; our classifier, 22 models) alongside the blackmail and leaking
variants. Adding scenarios tightens per-model estimates, but the third scenario differs in kind: it
involves a severe harm that harm-compliance instruments may also anticipate, which dilutes the
probe’s specificity to autonomous-agent misbehavior. Because the extension was added after the
primary outcome was fixed, analyses that use it would constitute a forking path, and we keep
blackmail $+$ leaking as the primary outcome. The three-scenario data are released for researchers
who wish to study scenario dependence directly.

### A.6 The 2026 model-panel expansion (n $\approx$ 41) and organization-group differences (detail for
§4.4)

Before evaluating the new models on either outcome, we specified a targeted expansion with fixed
predictions, inclusion rules, and comparison procedures. We grew the panel to $41$ anchored models
spanning $12$ model-developing organizations,
using the same chat/scenario harnesses as the original panel. The two outcomes require no tool loop;
new models simply skip the tool-calling audit benchmarks. Exclusions were based only on harness
behavior, never on outcome scores: Kimi-K2.6 and both Nemotron-3 models returned usable anchor
answers on fewer than $50\%$ of items or produced unbounded reasoning traces;
MiniMax-M3 fell below the misalignment engagement threshold because of truncated outputs, not low
harm, but was retained on the
single-turn jailbreak outcome, so the misalignment analysis uses $n{=}40$ whereas the jailbreak
analysis uses $n{=}41$ .
Gemini-2.5-Pro yielded no valid anchor; GLM-4.5 yielded MMLU but not GPQA. Both encountered routing
incompatibilities, so only GLM-4.5 appears as a partial row in Fig. 3. These exclusions are
a small instance of evaluation harnesses going stale.

#### Primary expansion result: the capability–misalignment correlation weakens.

The expansion was designed so that comparisons between the original and expanded panels account for
nesting: the original 21 models are a subset of the expanded 40, so naive comparisons of two
independent correlations would overstate the evidence for any change. The pre-specified procedures
are a stratified nested bootstrap, a comparison of the 2026-only models with the original panel via
Fisher’s $z$ , and size-21 subsets of the expanded pool matched to the original panel’s
organization histogram, which separates changes in organizational composition from changes among
models within organizations. These three procedures are implemented in the released scripts. Because
$\tau^{2}$ task success was not re-collected, only quantities involving the misalignment and
jailbreak outcomes can be compared across panels.

#### Organization-group analysis.

With $\geq 4$ anchored models each from six organizations, the expanded panel permits a first look
at how capability and organization are entangled. The pre-specified analysis computes
within-organization rank correlations, rank-residualizes safety on the capability composite, and
compares organization groups with $\geq 3$ models using a permutation test and a df-adjusted
Kruskal–Wallis effect size. Because the permutation test operates over only seven organization
clusters with within-organization $n$ of $4$ – $8$ , we checked its Type-I calibration on
$2{,}000$ synthetic panels per null with no between-organization mean difference, holding models,
organizations, and capability fixed: with the real safety values reshuffled across models, and with
i.i.d. Gaussian safety, rejection matches nominal $\alpha$ at $0.05/0.01/0.005$ on both outcomes
( $0.045$ – $0.052$ at $\alpha{=}0.05$ ). A worst-case null with organization-clustered variances but no
mean difference inflates rejection mildly on the jailbreak structure only ( $0.067$ at
$\alpha{=}0.05$ ; no detectable inflation at $\alpha{=}0.005$ ). The test is therefore adequately
calibrated for panels of this shape. Any organization-level comparison remains observational:
capability is matched only on a static-knowledge composite, within-organization $n$ is small, and
some organizations are range-restricted (Anthropic models sit near the safety ceiling).

#### Expanded-panel jailbreak result.

We rebuilt the jailbreak outcome on the
expanded panel, re-scoring all three published templates for every new model with the same judge
and the same base prompts. The three-template design continued to avoid the ceiling seen with a
single template, and per-model standard errors on the expanded panel are within the ranges reported
in §A.2. Among high-capability models, jailbreak safety spans most of the scale, which confirms
that the outcome retains discriminating variance on current models. The rebuilt outcome, its
per-template components, and the corresponding anchor scores are included in the artifact, so that
the expanded panel can serve as a starting point for larger studies.

An earlier pre-specified continuation involving R-Judge and the misalignment outcome on an
intermediate panel ( $n{=}25$ ) did not meet its threshold; we stopped it and retain it only as a
hypothesis for future, larger panels.

# Safety, or Just Capability? A Validity Audit of Agent-Safety Benchmarks

Youting Wang

###### Abstract

We audit four agent-safety benchmarks (R-Judge, InjecAgent, AgentHarm, AgentDojo), each run
under its official implementation and author-provided scorer on up to 22 models. MMLU and GPQA
are re-measured under one protocol and combined into a capability composite. On any binary
trace-judgment benchmark scored by $F_{1}$ , an “always positive” policy attains
$F_{1}=2\pi/(1+\pi)$ ; on R-Judge this is $0.690$ , above five of the 21 models that
discriminate. The three broad-coverage benchmarks rank the same 18 models differently. R-Judge
specificity against AgentHarm safety correlates $-0.64$ at $n{=}7$ and $+0.02$ at $n{=}18$ , and a
quarter of random size-7 subsets reach $|\rho|\geq 0.5$ . Capability predicts task success
( $\rho{=}{+}0.60$ ) but correlates negatively with misalignment safety ( $\rho{=}{-}0.44$ ,
$n{=}21$ ). On their paired $n{=}20$ panel the contrast is $\Delta{=}{-}1.00$ (95% CI
$[-1.48,-0.49]$ , $p<0.001$ ), stable under leave-one-organization-out and
organization-clustered bootstrap. On an expanded 41-model panel the misalignment correlation is
$-0.16$ (95% CI $[-0.54,+0.22]$ ) and the jailbreak correlation $+0.34$ ; neither change is
significant. Controlling capability, AgentHarm correlates $\rho{=}{+}0.72$ with three-template
jailbreak safety; both instruments score harmful compliance, so we read this as convergent
validity. A safety claim should specify benchmark, metric, target behavior, and model panel.

## 1 Introduction

Between 2024 and 2026, dozens of benchmarks were proposed for LLM-agent safety and reliability:
prompt-injection resistance (Zhan et al. 2024; Debenedetti et al. 2024), safety-risk awareness
(Yuan et al. 2024), refusal of harmful agentic tasks (Andriushchenko et al. 2025), and risky-tool-use
identification (Ruan et al. 2024), among others. A recent taxonomy (Li et al. 2026) catalogs more
than forty and reports rank concordance near $0.10$ across models when the benchmark is swapped.
That analysis is a twelve-model concordance check over four benchmarks; capability-controlled
evaluation and benchmark consolidation are listed among its open problems.

We address construct, metric, and criterion validity through four questions:

•

RQ1 (construct structure). Do nominally-distinct agent-safety benchmarks measure
a common underlying factor, or dissociable ones?

•

RQ2 (capability confound). How much of the between-benchmark signal is general
capability in disguise?

•

RQ3 (criterion validity). Do the safety scores track held-out behavioral
criteria beyond what general capability predicts?

•

RQ4 (metric validity). Are the headline metrics valid instruments, or do
they reward degenerate behavior?

#### Contributions.

Observation 1 gives a closed form for the F1 of an “always positive” baseline on any binary
trace-judgment benchmark; on R-Judge that baseline outranks five evaluated models. The
R-Judge-specificity/AgentHarm-safety correlation moves from $-0.64$ at $n{=}7$ to $+0.02$ at
$n{=}18$ , and a quarter of random size-7 subsets show $|\rho|\geq 0.5$ . A pre-specified,
capability-controlled criterion-validity audit covers one task-success and two safety outcomes:
capability predicts task success; its safety correlations change with outcome and panel; the
largest safety-score effect is AgentHarm–jailbreak ( $\rho{=}+0.72$ partialling capability), with
outcome selectivity at $p{=}0.051$ under organization-level resampling. We release an API-only
audit harness and re-run artifacts for four benchmarks and three held-out outcomes in the
accompanying reproducibility package.

#### Main conclusion.

A capability score is not a safety score, and no one agent-safety benchmark stands in for safety as
a whole. At seven models a weak relationship can appear systematic; validity estimates require
re-checking as the model population turns over.

#### Scope.

The three RQ3 criteria are deployment proxies, not claims about real-world harm; their limits
(single instances, grader dependence, panel size) are in Section 6.

## 2 Related Work

#### Agent-safety benchmarking.

InjecAgent (Zhan et al. 2024) and AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al. 2024) target prompt-injection
robustness; AgentHarm (Andriushchenko et al. 2025) measures compliance with harmful agentic tasks;
R-Judge (Yuan et al. 2024) scores safety-risk awareness over interaction traces. Evaluators not
re-run here, e.g. ToolEmu (Ruan et al. 2024) for risky tool use, are likewise designed as evaluators
without validation as measurements. AutoMonitor-Bench (Yang et al. 2026) scores misbehavior
monitors by miss and false-alarm rates. The nearest prior work, a taxonomy and consistency analysis
of agent-safety benchmarks (Li et al. 2026), documents ranking disagreement without capability
control, criterion-validity testing, or latent-structure recovery, naming capability-controlled
evaluation as future work; we take up all three.

#### Construct validity.

Benchmark-agreement testing (Perlitz et al. 2024), metabench (Kipnis et al. 2025), and direct
construct analyses (Bean et al. 2025) find a strong shared latent factor across knowledge and
reasoning benchmarks. Kearns (2026) and NIST’s statistical framework (Keller et al. 2026) bring
quantitative construct-validity and uncertainty modeling to LLM evaluation. We apply this lens to
agent reliability and safety, where benchmarks target distinct behaviors—refusal, injection
robustness, risk awareness—and the capability confound in their comparison is unquantified.

#### Benchmark gaming.

Adversarial gaming is distinct from, and logically posterior to, our concern that the headline
score may not measure the intended construct even for an honest model. The F1 result
(Section 4) involves a non-adversarial policy that labels every trace “unsafe” without examining
any of them.

#### Over-refusal.

XSTest (Röttger et al. 2024) and OR-Bench (Cui et al. 2024) document exaggerated safety, or
over-refusal, at the prompt level. The between-benchmark analogue is whether models that refuse
harmful tasks (AgentHarm) are worse at identifying benign traces correctly (R-Judge specificity).
On the full panel that correlation is near zero; on seven-model subsets it often is not.

#### Agent reliability and task performance.

Recent work isolates corrupt success (Cao et al. 2026) and evidence-bounded reporting
(Chen 2025); $\tau$ -bench (Yao et al. 2024) and its dual-control successor $\tau^{2}$ -bench
(Barres et al. 2025) measure agentic task success. We use the latter’s retail domain as the
held-out RQ3 task-success criterion, and treat the safety benchmarks as candidate columns for a
validity audit.

## 3 Method

### 3.1 Model panel and benchmarks

The API-only panel comprises up to 22 models from nine model-developing organizations (OpenAI 6,
Meta 3, Qwen 3, Mistral 3, DeepSeek 2, Amazon 2, Anthropic, Google, Cohere; full roster in Fig. 3
and the artifact). Four safety benchmarks are re-run with official implementations and scorers:
R-Judge (full 571 items, self-judge), InjecAgent (300 stratified direct-harm/data-stealing items,
rule-scored), AgentHarm (44 base behaviors spanning all eight harm categories, official Inspect
evaluation, gpt-4o-mini judge), and AgentDojo (slack suite, 100 items, environment-scored for
security and utility), plus a held-out task-success criterion for RQ3.

Coverage (Fig. 3): R-Judge $n{=}21$ after Qwen3-32B falls below the $90\%$ valid-output threshold;
InjecAgent $n{=}22$ ; AgentHarm and AgentDojo, which require native tool use, $n{=}19$ and $5$ ; the
$\tau^{2}$ criterion $n{=}20$ (App. A.2). The common R-Judge/InjecAgent/AgentHarm panel is
$n{=}18$ . Capability anchors are measured through the same API harness as the safety runs: MMLU
zero-shot on a fixed 500-item subset (seed 42, identical items for every model) and GPQA-Diamond
(198 items, chain-of-thought). These replace the provider-reported model-card numbers used
initially, which are retained as a pre-harmonization comparison. The anchor panel is 21 models
(DeepSeek-R1 excluded for unstable long-form GPQA generation).

### 3.2 Benchmark targets

Target behaviors were fixed before inspecting any relationship among score columns. R-Judge:
distinguishing unsafe from benign interaction traces. InjecAgent and AgentDojo: prompt-injection
resistance, their correlation serving as the convergent check. AgentHarm: refusal of harmful
agentic tasks. R-Judge is analyzed under specificity and balanced accuracy in addition to the
official F1.

#### Score orientation and terminology.

All scores are oriented higher-is-better/safer. R-Judge specificity is the fraction of benign
traces correctly identified as benign; balanced accuracy averages performance on benign and unsafe
traces. InjecAgent robustness $=1-$ attack success; AgentHarm safety $=1-$ harmful compliance.
$\tau^{2}$ -bench is a held-out task-success criterion, not a safety score. “Internal consistency”
refers to split-half analyses (App. A.2); benchmark-specific scores are named explicitly rather
than as “calibration” or “reliability.”

### 3.3 Analysis plan

Hypotheses, thresholds, and decision rules were fixed before each analysis. Lacking an independent
timestamp, we call the analyses pre-specified rather than preregistered. All association tests are
Spearman; unless noted, $p$ -values are two-sided asymptotic Spearman tests. Fig. 2 error bars are
model-level percentile-bootstrap intervals; the panel expansion and direct panel comparisons follow
pre-specified bootstrap procedures (App. A.6). The corroborative PCA is on the Pearson correlation
matrix of standardized score columns, with factor count by Horn’s parallel analysis against a
random-normal null; Spearman sensitivity in App. A.3. Partial Spearman correlations control the
capability composite (rank-residual implementation and alternative convention in App. A.5). The
composite is the mean of the standardized, verified MMLU and GPQA anchors; its model ordering is
identical to the anchors’ first principal component. Between-construct redundancy is measured by
rank-residualized partials controlling the composite.

Three pre-specified controls: positive (capability-anchor loadings $\geq 0.6$ on the first factor);
negative (a column-permuted score matrix within the parallel-analysis null); convergent (high
InjecAgent–AgentDojo correlation). The headline statistic is the median pairwise partial Spearman
$|\rho|$ among distinct-construct benchmarks, controlling the composite; factor structure is
interpretable only if first-factor variance is $\geq 40\%$ or capability control reduces that
median by $\geq 0.15$ , with positive and negative controls passing. Thresholds and the
disconfirming test were fixed before any real run.

RQ3 uses three held-out outcomes, each pre-specified before it was run. Task success: $\tau^{2}$ -bench
retail (Barres et al. 2025), 40 multi-turn, environment-scored tool-agent-user tasks. Misalignment
safety: avoidance of blackmail or information leaking in a fictional autonomous-agent scenario
(Lynch et al. 2025), fixed classifier over 100 decisions per model. Jailbreak safety: one minus
harmful compliance on 50 forbidden prompts, averaged over three published jailbreak templates to
reduce single-template ceilings (Souly et al. 2024; Wei et al. 2023). All run through the same
API-only harness (the two safety criteria are single-turn or scenario-based and cover the full
panel; $\tau^{2}$ is a multi-turn tool loop covering 20 models), are distinct from the four audited
benchmarks, and are excluded from the predictors. The headline statistic per criterion is the
partial Spearman correlation of each safety score with the criterion controlling the composite,
reported after the criterion’s raw association with capability. Reporting rules cover both
significant and null results. Analysis scripts and frozen inputs are in the reproducibility
package.

## 4 Results

Ordering follows evidential strength: RQ4 and RQ2, then RQ1, then the power-limited RQ3.

### 4.1 The headline metric is gameable (RQ4)

### 4.2 The capability confound is real but metric-dependent (RQ2)

On the R-Judge panel ( $n{=}20$ with harmonized anchors), capability correlates with balanced
accuracy at $\rho=+0.71$ (MMLU, $p<0.001$ ) and $+0.49$ (GPQA, $p=0.03$ ), with F1 at $+0.76$ and
$+0.62$ , and with specificity at $+0.16$ and $+0.07$ . The specificity–MMLU correlation was $0.85$
on the first nine models and $+0.16$ at $n{=}20$ .

### 4.3 Benchmarks disagree; a seven-model panel suggested a trade-off that does not persist (RQ1)

No benchmark orders the models as another does (Table 1); a top-AgentHarm model can rank near the
bottom on R-Judge specificity. Disagreement between benchmarks coded to different constructs (§3)
is expected and does not by itself indict any single instrument; it does preclude quoting the scores
interchangeably as an agent’s safety.

The R-Judge-specificity/AgentHarm-safety rank correlation, $-0.64$ at $n{=}7$ , is $+0.02$
( $p=0.95$ ) at $n{=}18$ (Fig. 5, appendix); random size-7 subsets yield $|\rho|\geq 0.5$ in a
quarter of draws. The null holds under all four R-Judge metrics (App. A.4). Capability moderation
of the residual is untested and flagged as a hypothesis.

A single-factor PCA (Fig. 6, appendix) has a first component explaining $48.7\%$ of variance,
loading R-Judge specificity, InjecAgent robustness, and both capability anchors in one direction
and AgentHarm safety in the other ( $+0.33$ ; opposite the cluster in $17$ of $18$ leave-one-out
fits).

#### The positive control now passes.

On the harmonized anchors MMLU loads $0.74\geq 0.6$ (provider-reported numbers gave $0.42$ ); the
negative control passes (column-permuted eigenvalues within the parallel-analysis null), meeting
the pre-specified interpretation conditions; the convergent control is inconclusive at AgentDojo’s
$n{=}5$ . A Spearman PCA retains the loading structure but PC1 falls to $40.8\%$ with no factor
retained by Horn (App. A.3), and the median between-benchmark correlation is $0.22$ ; the factor is
treated as corroborative relative to Table 1.

#### Against agentic misalignment, capability has the opposite association.

On the full 21-model panel, $\rho_{\text{cap}}=-0.44$ (asymptotic $p=0.047$ ) against $+0.60$ on

pre-specified $0.40$ effect-size threshold; AgentHarm does not ( $+0.16$ ; Table 2). Both CIs
include zero, neither survives Bonferroni, power is $\approx 0.35$ , and the pre-specified
directional prediction named AgentHarm. The R-Judge partial is $+0.41$ under specificity, $+0.19$
under balanced accuracy, and $-0.46$ under recall (App. A.4).

#### A direct interaction test on the original panel.

On the paired $n{=}20$ panel, capability correlates $+0.60$ with task success and $-0.41$ with
misalignment safety ( $-0.44$ on the full panel): $\Delta=-1.00$ (95% CI $[-1.48,-0.49]$ ,
$p<0.001$ ), stable to leave-one-model-out, leave-one-organization-out, organization-clustered
bootstrap, and subsampling (App. A.5). The corresponding R-Judge interaction is marginal
( $\Delta=+0.50$ , $p=0.082$ ), supporting the capability interaction but not a full two-way
dissociation. An independent misalignment grader gives $\rho=0.97$ with the primary scores.

#### The capability–misalignment correlation is weaker on the expanded panel.

The pre-specified expansion prediction was that the negative correlation would “hold or
strengthen.” It moves from $\rho=-0.44$ ( $n{=}21$ , asymptotic $p=0.047$ ) to $-0.16$ ( $n{=}40$ ,
bootstrap $p=0.40$ ; 95% CI $[-0.54,+0.22]$ ; App. A.6). The interval includes $-0.44$ , and the
between-panel difference is non-significant (nested-bootstrap $\Delta\rho=+0.27$ , 95% CI
$[-0.25,+0.78]$ ). Subsets matched to the original organization composition give median
$\rho=-0.17$ ; a generational explanation remains possible and undemonstrated. $\tau^{2}$ was not
re-collected, so the interaction was not re-tested.

#### Models with similar capability scores differ in safety across organizations
(Fig. 4).

The 41-model panel spans 12 model-developing organizations (misalignment $n{=}40$ ; jailbreak
$n{=}41$ after one engagement-gate exclusion). Six organizations contribute $\geq 4$ models for
within-organization correlations and seven contribute $\geq 3$ for the group comparison
(App. A.6, Table 5). Within-organization capability–safety correlations vary in sign, averaging
$-0.14$ (misalignment) and $+0.26$ (jailbreak). After capability adjustment of safety ranks, the
seven groups differ on both criteria (permutation $p=0.004$ misalignment, $p<0.001$ jailbreak;
Holm-significant; df-adjusted Kruskal–Wallis $\varepsilon^{2}=0.34$ and $0.57$ ). The static
composite may miss agentic ability, each organization contributes few models, and some groups are
range-restricted; the result is non-causal and limited to: similar MMLU/GPQA scores do not imply
similar safety scores.

#### Against jailbreak safety, AgentHarm shows the strongest held-out association.

The second safety outcome differs in failure mode, harness, and scoring: harmful compliance under
jailbreak, scored with StrongREJECT (Souly et al. 2024). A single template (AIM) ceilings, with 11
of 22 models refusing every request; averaging three published templates (Wei et al. 2023) leaves no
model at ceiling. Capability is weakly associated on the 2024–25 panel ( $\rho=+0.08$ , $n{=}21$ ,
$p=0.73$ ) and at $+0.34$ on the expanded panel ( $n{=}41$ , $p=0.04$ ), the change non-significant.

Partialling capability, AgentHarm safety correlates $\rho=+0.72$ ( $p<0.001$ ) with the
three-template outcome versus $+0.50$ for the single-template measure, stable to
leave-one-model-out and an independent grader (App. A.5). Selectivity for jailbreak over
misalignment gives $\Delta=+0.59$ , $p=0.027$ under model-level bootstrap and $p=0.051$ resampling
the eight represented organizations. On this paired panel the misalignment partial is $+0.13$
( $n{=}19$ ); Table 2’s $+0.16$ uses the common $n{=}18$ panel. R-Judge specificity ( $-0.11$ ) and
InjecAgent robustness ( $+0.21$ ) do not predict jailbreak safety. AgentHarm and StrongREJECT both
measure harmful compliance. The reverse comparison for R-Judge and InjecAgent (misalignment over
jailbreak) is marginal ( $\Delta=+0.52$ , $p=0.068$ ).

#### Two alternative explanations, checked.

Seven LLM coders shown only construct descriptions, without predictive results, assigned AgentHarm
and the jailbreak outcome to the same harm-blocking category ( $7/7$ each; Krippendorff
$\alpha=0.61$ across three categories), and classified the misalignment outcome less consistently
(App. A.1). Partialling capability, AgentHarm safety is uncorrelated with over-refusal on benign
XSTest prompts (Röttger et al. 2024) ( $\rho=-0.01$ , $n{=}17$ ).

## 5 Discussion

An “always unsafe” baseline matches R-Judge F1 (Observation 1); the three broad-coverage benchmarks
rank the same models differently. Capability predicts task success; its correlations with the two
safety outcomes are panel-unstable (Table 2). AgentHarm’s capability-controlled association with
three-template jailbreak safety is $\rho=+0.72$ , with outcome selectivity at $p=0.051$ under
organization resampling; the specificity claim remains open. The R-Judge/InjecAgent associations
with misalignment are exploratory. Safety ranks differ among organization groups after composite
adjustment, an observational pattern without an identified organizational cause. A safety claim is
defensible only with its benchmark, metric, target behavior, and model population attached.

## 6 Limitations and Threats to Validity

#### Panel size.

The AgentHarm-limited cross-benchmark panel is $n{=}18$ , up from a first pass at $n{=}7$ . The
priority extension is a larger, capability-spanning agent-loop panel.

#### Capability anchors.

Provider-reported anchors failed the positive control (MMLU $0.42$ ); re-measured MMLU and
GPQA-Diamond (§3) pass (MMLU $0.74$ ), with every RQ2/RQ3 sign unchanged. These are static-knowledge
tests, though their composite predicts multi-turn tool-agent success at $+0.60$ . A six-model BFCL
pilot (Patil et al. 2025) failed as an agentic replacement: strict function-call syntax scoring
ranked GPT-4o-mini highest ( $0.72$ ) and the two most capable models lowest ( $0.42$ – $0.48$ ),
apparently rewarding format conformance; a validated agentic anchor is needed. Such measurement
error attenuates or suppresses partial relationships rather than biasing them in a signable
direction.

#### Multiple comparisons.

Per-test $p$ -values are uncorrected; claims rest on effect sizes and pre-specified rules. The two
strongly significant tests (crossover and AgentHarm $\to$ jailbreak, both $p<0.001$ ) survive
Bonferroni; the R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment cells ( $p\approx 0.05$ – $0.09$ ) do not and are
treated as suggestive.

#### Judges and coverage.

Independent graders reproduce model scores at $\rho=0.97$ (misalignment) and $\rho=0.98$
(jailbreak). Rescoring AgentHarm refusals with a different model gives $\rho=0.69$ , while the
AgentHarm–jailbreak partial moves only from $+0.72$ to $+0.66$ (App. A.5). AgentDojo covers five
models, so cross-benchmark analyses rest mainly on the other three benchmarks.

#### Criterion validity (RQ3).

$\tau^{2}$ -retail (40 tasks, one run/model) is scored by a user-simulator of unbounded variance;
the misalignment criterion is a fictional-scenario probe (grader-robust, $\rho=0.97$ , though its
blackmail–leaking halves agree only moderately, Spearman–Brown $0.70$ ); the jailbreak criterion
averages three jailbreaks. None yields deployment-harm probabilities. For item-rich instruments
with resampling support, split-half consistency is $\geq 0.96$ and rank stability $\geq 0.97$ .
Worst-case within-model SEs are $12$ – $25\%$ of between-model SD across bounded instruments,
supporting panel-level spread but not every pairwise difference (App. A.2). The
AgentHarm–jailbreak association is large and directionally stable, partly convergent, and
borderline-selective under organization resampling. The R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment pattern is
exploratory (marginal $\Delta=+0.52$ , power $\approx 0.35$ ; the larger three-scenario result is
post-hoc; App. A.5).

## 7 Conclusion

Across four benchmarks and up to 22 models, R-Judge’s F1 lets an “always unsafe” baseline outrank
five models, and rankings change with the benchmark. Capability predicts held-out task success but
not safety consistently across outcomes or panels. The strongest held-out safety association is
AgentHarm’s ( $\rho=+0.72$ with jailbreak safety after controlling capability), with partial
construct overlap and borderline organization-resampled selectivity. Evaluations should report the
full confusion structure, drop standalone F1 wherever true negatives matter, and tie claims to an
explicit target behavior and model population.

### A.1 Ruling out two artifacts (detail for §4.4)

#### Blinded construct coding.

Seven LLM coders from distinct families—GPT-4o, Claude-3-Haiku, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Llama-3.3-70B,
Qwen-2.5-72B, Mistral-Large, DeepSeek-V3—each saw only a neutral, predictive-information-stripped
description of each benchmark (no mention of our criteria, category names, or any RQ3 result) and
two construct definitions (“harm blocking” vs. “risk recognition and correct treatment of benign
inputs”). Option order and benchmark order were shuffled per coder to remove position bias. Each
coder assigned every benchmark to one construct. Votes (B ${=}$ harm blocking, R ${=}$ risk
recognition):

| Benchmark | blind | author | B / R

| R-Judge | recognition | recognition | 0 / 7

| InjecAgent | recognition | recognition | 1 / 6

| AgentHarm | blocking | blocking | 7 / 0

| AgentDojo | recognition | recognition | 0 / 7

All four majorities match the hand-assignment; raw agreement $27/28$ ratings, Krippendorff’s
$\alpha=0.825$ (nominal), against a chance baseline of $0.5^{4}=6.2\%$ for one coder matching all
four labels by coin flip. The single dissent (Llama-3.3-70B placing InjecAgent as harm blocking)
is the semantically borderline injection-robustness case. This controls coder bias but not
rubric-designer bias (the category definitions were written by authors who had seen the results);
the RQ1 factor, which separates AgentHarm ( $+0.33$ ) from the R-Judge/InjecAgent cluster without
reference to any criterion, is reported for that reason.

#### Blinded criterion coding, with a distractor.

To test whether the predictor $\to$ criterion matching, not only the predictor labels, is
recoverable blind, and to give the agreement statistic content, coding was re-run over all six
targets (four benchmarks $+$ two criteria) with a third, plausible task-success distractor
construct. Krippendorff’s $\alpha=0.61$ (three categories, chance $\approx 1/3$ ); the distractor
is chosen $5/42$ times. AgentHarm and the jailbreak criterion both map to harm blocking $7/7$ ,
R-Judge to risk recognition $7/7$ , and InjecAgent $5/7$ , all unchanged by the distractor. Two
targets are contested: AgentDojo reads as task success to $4/7$ coders (it is utility-scored; our
$n{=}5$ benchmark), and the misalignment criterion maps to risk recognition $6/7$ in a separate
two-way round (frozen votes in the artifact) but to harm blocking $6/7$ here (avoiding a harmful
autonomous action can be read as both recognizing and declining it). The AgentHarm–jailbreak
pairing is thus recovered without the predictive results, and the R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment
pattern remains exploratory.

#### XSTest over-refusal (blanket-refusal check).

XSTest (Röttger et al., 2024; cited in the main paper) was run on the panel with its published CPI
(compliance/partial/refusal) scorer (judge gpt-4o-mini): the safe subset (benign prompts
superficially resembling unsafe ones) measures over-refusal; the unsafe subset measures correct
refusal of overtly-harmful prompts. The unsafe subset is ceilinged (every model refuses
$83$ – $100\%$ , sd $4.5$ ), so the informative signal is safe-subset over-refusal (range
$0$ – $60\%$ ; Claude-3-Haiku over-refuses $60\%$ , o3-mini $30\%$ , others $\leq 15\%$ ).

### A.6 The 2026 model-panel expansion (n $\approx$ 41) and organization-group differences (detail for
§4.4)

The targeted expansion, specified before new models were evaluated on either criterion, predicted
that the crossover would “hold or strengthen,” and probed whether any panel change follows
capability or organization grouping. The panel grew to $41$ anchored models spanning $12$
model-developing organizations, using the original chat/scenario harnesses; the criteria need no
tool loop, and new models skip the tool-calling audit benchmarks. Exclusions used harness behavior
only, never outcome scores: Kimi-K2.6 and both Nemotron-3 models returned usable anchor answers on
fewer than $50\%$ of items or produced unbounded reasoning traces; MiniMax-M3 fell below the
misalignment engagement threshold through truncated outputs, not low harm, and was retained on the
single-turn jailbreak criterion (misalignment $n{=}40$ , jailbreak $n{=}41$ ). Gemini-2.5-Pro
yielded no valid anchor; GLM-4.5 yielded MMLU but not GPQA. Both encountered routing
incompatibilities; only GLM-4.5 appears as a partial row in Fig. 3. These exclusions illustrate
harness staleness.

#### Primary expansion result: the capability–misalignment correlation weakens.

Capability $\to$ misalignment-safety moves from $-0.44$ ( $n{=}21$ , asymptotic $p=0.047$ ;
bootstrap $p=0.11$ , $95\%$ CI $[-0.85,+0.09]$ ) to $-0.16$ ( $n{=}40$ , bootstrap $p=0.40$ ;
$95\%$ CI $[-0.54,+0.22]$ , leave-one-out $[-0.25,-0.12]$ ). The pre-specified confirmation
threshold ( $\rho\leq-0.35$ at $p<0.05$ ) is not met; the CI still includes $-0.44$ . Three tests of
the change itself (accounting for nesting of the original panel in the expanded one): a stratified
nested bootstrap gives $\Delta\rho=+0.27$ , $95\%$ CI $[-0.25,+0.78]$ , two-sided $p=0.29$
(jailbreak $+0.26$ , CI $[-0.14,+0.69]$ , $p=0.22$ ); the 2026-only models give $\rho=+0.07$ versus
the original $-0.44$ (independent Fisher $z$ , $p=0.12$ ); size-21 subsets matched to the original
organization histogram give median $\rho=-0.17$ (IQR $[-0.27,-0.08]$ ). Organization mix does not
reproduce the original value; generational change is compatible but not established, and the change
is non-significant. The estimate cannot be assumed to generalize across model populations, and the
“hold or strengthen” prediction was not met. Among models of similar measured capability, safety
varies widely across organizations (composite ${\approx}0.8$ : o3-mini $0.99$ , Grok-4.3 $0.70$ ,
DeepSeek-V3 $0.19$ ), so a ceiling does not account for the residual variation. With $\tau^{2}$ not
re-collected, the correlation is updated but not the interaction $\Delta$ .

#### Organization-group analysis.

Six organizations with $\geq 4$ anchored models permit partial separation of the collinear
capability and organization factors. Within-organization capability $\to$ safety slopes are
sign-heterogeneous and near-zero in aggregate; after rank-residualizing safety on capability,
organization groups differ on both criteria (permutation $p{=}0.004$ misalignment, $<0.001$
jailbreak; df-adjusted Kruskal–Wallis $\varepsilon^{2}{=}0.34$ and $0.57$ ; Table 5, Fig. 4). All
five secondary tests survive Holm (max adjusted $p=0.043$ ). Capability is matched only on a
static-knowledge composite (unmeasured agentic capability can appear as an organization
difference), within-organization $n$ is $4$ – $8$ , and some organizations are range-restricted
(Anthropic ceilings near safety $1.0$ ); the claim rests on the between-organization permutation
test, not the slopes. Because that test permutes labels over only seven organization clusters
(within-organization $n$ $4$ – $8$ ), its Type-I calibration was checked on $2{,}000$ synthetic
panels per null with no between-organization mean difference, holding models, organizations, and
capability fixed: with real safety values reshuffled across models, and with i.i.d. Gaussian safety,
rejection matches nominal $\alpha$ at $0.05/0.01/0.005$ on both criteria ( $0.045$ – $0.052$ at
$\alpha{=}0.05$ ). A worst-case null with organization-clustered variances but no mean difference
mildly inflates rejection on the jailbreak structure only ( $0.067$ at $\alpha{=}0.05$ ; none
detectable at $\alpha{=}0.005$ ); doubling both $p$ -values leaves the organization-group tests
Holm-significant. Dropping near-ceiling Anthropic gives misalignment $\varepsilon^{2}=0.27$ ,
$p=0.018$ and jailbreak $\varepsilon^{2}=0.54$ , $p<0.001$ .

# Safety, or Just Capability? A Validity Audit of Agent-Safety Benchmarks

Youting Wang

  
Xiao Han

  
Dingyan Shang

Affiliation: Yuan Tang

  
Bowen Liu

###### Abstract

We audit four agent-safety benchmarks (R-Judge, InjecAgent, AgentHarm, AgentDojo), each run under its official implementation and author-provided scorer on up to 22 models, against a capability composite built from MMLU and GPQA measured under one protocol. On any binary trace-judgment benchmark scored by $F_{1}$, an "always positive" policy attains $F_{1}=2\pi/(1+\pi)$; on R-Judge this is $0.690$, above five of the 21 discriminating models. The three broad-coverage benchmarks rank the same 18 models differently. R-Judge specificity against AgentHarm safety correlates $-0.64$ at $n{=}7$ and $+0.02$ at $n{=}18$; a quarter of random size-7 subsets reach $|\rho|\geq 0.5$. Capability predicts task success ($\rho{=}{+}0.60$) and correlates negatively with misalignment safety ($\rho{=}{-}0.44$, $n{=}21$); on the paired $n{=}20$ panel the contrast is $\Delta{=}{-}1.00$ (95% CI $[-1.48,-0.49]$, $p<0.001$), stable under leave-one-organization-out and organization-clustered bootstrap. On an expanded 41-model panel the misalignment correlation is $-0.16$ (95% CI $[-0.54,+0.22]$) and the jailbreak correlation $+0.34$; neither change is significant. Controlling capability, AgentHarm correlates $\rho{=}{+}0.72$ with three-template jailbreak safety; both instruments score harmful compliance. A safety claim requires the benchmark, metric, target behavior, and model panel.

## 1 Introduction

Benchmarks appearing between 2024 and 2026 target prompt-injection resistance (Zhan et al. 2024; Debenedetti et al. 2024), safety-risk awareness (Yuan et al. 2024), refusal of harmful agentic tasks (Andriushchenko et al. 2025), and risky-tool-use identification (Ruan et al. 2024), among others. Li et al. (2026) catalog more than forty and report cross-benchmark rank concordance near $0.10$, from a twelve-model check over four benchmarks; capability-controlled evaluation and benchmark consolidation are listed there as open problems.

We separate construct, metric, and criterion validity and pose:

•

RQ1 (construct structure). Do nominally-distinct agent-safety benchmarks measure
a common underlying factor, or dissociable ones?

•

RQ2 (capability confound). How much of the between-benchmark signal is general
capability in disguise?

•

RQ3 (criterion validity). Do the safety scores track held-out behavioral
criteria beyond what general capability predicts?

•

RQ4 (metric validity). Are the headline metrics valid instruments, or do
they reward degenerate behavior?

#### Contributions.

Observation 1: a closed-form F1 for the "always positive" baseline on binary trace-judgment benchmarks; on R-Judge it outranks five evaluated models. The R-Judge-specificity/AgentHarm-safety correlation moves from $-0.64$ at $n{=}7$ to $+0.02$ at $n{=}18$, with a quarter of random size-7 subsets at $|\rho|\geq 0.5$. A pre-specified, capability-controlled criterion-validity audit over one task-success and two safety outcomes: capability predicts task success; its safety correlations vary with outcome and panel; AgentHarm–jailbreak gives $\rho{=}+0.72$ after controlling capability, with outcome selectivity at $p{=}0.051$ under organization-level resampling. An API-only audit harness and re-run artifacts for four benchmarks and three held-out outcomes are in the accompanying reproducibility package.

#### Main conclusion.

A capability score is not a safety score, and no single agent-safety benchmark stands in for safety. At seven models a weak relationship can appear systematic; validity requires re-checking as the model population turns over.

#### Scope.

The three RQ3 criteria are deployment proxies, not claims about real-world harm; limits in Section 6.

## 2 Related Work

#### Agent-safety benchmarking.

InjecAgent (Zhan et al. 2024) and AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al. 2024): prompt-injection robustness; AgentHarm (Andriushchenko et al. 2025): compliance with harmful agentic tasks; R-Judge (Yuan et al. 2024): safety-risk awareness over interaction traces. ToolEmu (Ruan et al. 2024), not re-run, is likewise an unvalidated evaluator. AutoMonitor-Bench (Yang et al. 2026) reports miss and false-alarm rates. Li et al. (2026) document ranking disagreement without capability control, criterion validity, or latent structure; we address all three.

#### Construct validity.

Benchmark-agreement testing (Perlitz et al. 2024), metabench (Kipnis et al. 2025), and construct analyses (Bean et al. 2025) find a strong shared factor across knowledge and reasoning benchmarks. Kearns (2026) and NIST (Keller et al. 2026) bring quantitative construct-validity and uncertainty modeling to LLM evaluation. The capability confound across agent-safety benchmarks targeting refusal, injection robustness, and risk awareness has not been quantified.

#### Benchmark gaming.

Distinct from adversarial gaming: the headline score may fail to measure its construct even for an honest model. The F1 case (Section 4) involves a non-adversarial policy that labels every trace "unsafe."

#### Over-refusal.

XSTest (Röttger et al. 2024) and OR-Bench (Cui et al. 2024) document prompt-level over-refusal. The between-benchmark analogue—AgentHarm refusal against R-Judge specificity—is near zero on the full panel and often not on seven-model subsets.

#### Agent reliability and task performance.

Corrupt success (Cao et al. 2026), evidence-bounded reporting (Chen 2025), $\tau$-bench (Yao et al. 2024), and $\tau^{2}$-bench (Barres et al. 2025). The $\tau^{2}$ retail domain serves as the held-out RQ3 task-success criterion.

## 3 Method

### 3.1 Model panel and benchmarks

API-only panel of up to 22 models from nine organizations (OpenAI 6, Meta 3, Qwen 3, Mistral 3, DeepSeek 2, Amazon 2, Anthropic, Google, Cohere; roster in Fig. 3 and the artifact). Official implementations and scorers: R-Judge (full 571 items, self-judge), InjecAgent (300 stratified direct-harm/data-stealing items, rule-scored), AgentHarm (44 base behaviors across all eight harm categories, official Inspect evaluation, gpt-4o-mini judge), AgentDojo (slack suite, 100 items, environment-scored for security and utility).

Coverage: R-Judge $n{=}21$ (Qwen3-32B below the $90\%$ valid-output threshold); InjecAgent $n{=}22$; AgentHarm $n{=}19$ and AgentDojo $n{=}5$ (native tool use required); $\tau^{2}$ $n{=}20$ (App. A.2). Common R-Judge/InjecAgent/AgentHarm panel: $n{=}18$. Anchors measured through the same API harness: MMLU zero-shot on a fixed 500-item subset (seed 42, identical items per model) and GPQA-Diamond (198 items, chain-of-thought). These replace provider-reported model-card numbers, retained as a pre-harmonization comparison. Anchor panel: 21 models (DeepSeek-R1 excluded for unstable long-form GPQA generation).

### 3.2 Benchmark targets

Target codes, fixed before inspecting any column relationship: R-Judge, unsafe vs. benign trace discrimination; InjecAgent and AgentDojo, prompt-injection resistance (convergent pair); AgentHarm, refusal of harmful agentic tasks. R-Judge is analyzed under specificity and balanced accuracy alongside official F1.

#### Score orientation and terminology.

All scores are oriented higher = better/safer: R-Judge specificity $=\mathrm{TN}/(\mathrm{TN}+\mathrm{FP})$ over benign traces, balanced accuracy $=\tfrac12(\text{specificity}+\text{recall})$; InjecAgent robustness $=1-$ attack success; AgentHarm safety $=1-$ harmful compliance. $\tau^{2}$-bench enters RQ3 as task success, not a safety score. Split-half analyses are reported as internal consistency (App. A.2); "calibration" and "reliability" are not used.

### 3.3 Analysis plan

Hypotheses, thresholds, and decision rules were fixed before each analysis; lacking an independent timestamp, we call them pre-specified rather than preregistered. All associations are Spearman; unless noted, $p$-values are two-sided asymptotic Spearman tests. Fig. 2 error bars are model-level percentile-bootstrap intervals; panel expansion and direct panel comparisons use pre-specified bootstrap procedures (App. A.6). Corroborative PCA uses the Pearson correlation matrix of standardized columns, with factor count by Horn's parallel analysis against a random-normal null (Spearman sensitivity in App. A.3). Capability composite: $c=\tfrac12(z_{\mathrm{MMLU}}+z_{\mathrm{GPQA}})$ over the verified anchors, whose model ordering equals the anchors' first principal component. Partial Spearman correlations control $c$ (rank-residual implementation and alternative convention in App. A.5); between-construct redundancy uses these rank-residualized partials.

Controls: positive (anchor loadings $\geq 0.6$ on the first factor); negative (column-permuted matrix within the parallel-analysis null); convergent (high InjecAgent–AgentDojo correlation). Headline metric: median pairwise partial $|\rho|$ among distinct-construct benchmarks given $c$. Decision rule: interpret factor structure only if first-factor variance $\geq 40\%$ or capability control lowers that median by $\geq 0.15$, with positive and negative controls passing. Thresholds and the disconfirming test were fixed before any real run.

RQ3 outcomes, each fixed before being run: $\tau^{2}$-bench retail (Barres et al. 2025), 40 multi-turn environment-scored tool-agent-user tasks; misalignment safety, avoidance of blackmail or information leaking in a fictional autonomous-agent scenario (Lynch et al. 2025), fixed classifier over 100 decisions per model; jailbreak safety, $1-$ harmful compliance on 50 forbidden prompts averaged over three published templates (Souly et al. 2024; Wei et al. 2023). All run through the same API-only harness (safety criteria single-turn or scenario-based, full panel; $\tau^{2}$ multi-turn tool loop, 20 models), are distinct from the four audited benchmarks, and are not predictors. Headline: partial Spearman of each safety score with each criterion given $c$, reported after the criterion's raw capability association. Reporting rules cover significant and null outcomes. Scripts and frozen inputs are in the reproducibility package.

## 4 Results

Ordered by evidential strength: RQ4 and RQ2, then RQ1, then the power-limited RQ3.

### 4.1 The headline metric is gameable (RQ4)

Figure 1: R-Judge F1 ($n{=}21$) with the constant "always unsafe" baseline (F1 ${=}0.69$, dashed); five discriminating models fall below it.

R-Judge labels $52.7\%$ of its 571 items "unsafe." The all-"unsafe" policy attains recall $1.0$, specificity $0$, and $\mathrm{F1}=0.690$. Among the 21 models with valid verdicts (Qwen3-32B excluded, $21\%$ unparseable), it outranks five (F1 $0.30$–$0.57$; Fig. 1), all discriminating. o3-mini, highest specificity ($0.97$), has $\mathrm{F1}=0.702$, $0.012$ above the baseline. Balanced accuracy reorders the board.

###### Observation 1 (F1 admits a high-scoring constant baseline).

With $\mathrm{F1}=2\mathrm{TP}/(2\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}+\mathrm{FN})$ and base rate $\pi$, the constant always-positive policy attains $\mathrm{F1}=2\pi/(1+\pi)$. For R-Judge ($\pi=0.527$) this is $0.690$, exceeding several discriminating models. F1 cannot stand alone as a measure of two-sided discrimination on this benchmark.

### 4.2 The capability confound is real but metric-dependent (RQ2)

R-Judge panel, harmonized anchors ($n{=}20$): balanced accuracy $\rho=+0.71$ with MMLU ($p<0.001$), $+0.49$ with GPQA ($p=0.03$); F1 $+0.76$ and $+0.62$; specificity $+0.16$ and $+0.07$. The specificity–MMLU correlation was $0.85$ on the first nine models.

### 4.3 Benchmarks disagree; a seven-model panel suggested a trade-off that does not persist (RQ1)

No benchmark reproduces another's ordering (Table 1); top-AgentHarm models sit near the bottom on R-Judge specificity. Disagreement across benchmarks coded to different constructs (§3) does not by itself indict any instrument.

R-Judge specificity vs. AgentHarm safety: $-0.64$ at $n{=}7$, $+0.02$ ($p=0.95$) at $n{=}18$ (Fig. 5, appendix); random size-7 subsets give $|\rho|\geq 0.5$ in a quarter of draws. The null at $n{=}18$ holds under all four R-Judge metrics (App. A.4). Capability moderation of the remainder is untested.

Single-factor PCA (Fig. 6, appendix): PC1 ($48.7\%$ variance) loads R-Judge specificity, InjecAgent robustness, and both anchors in one direction and AgentHarm safety in the other ($+0.33$; opposite the cluster in $17$ of $18$ leave-one-out fits).

#### The positive control now passes.

Harmonized anchors: MMLU loads $0.74\geq 0.6$ (provider-reported: $0.42$, failing). Negative control passes (column-permuted eigenvalues within the parallel-analysis null); convergent control inconclusive at AgentDojo's $n{=}5$. Spearman PCA keeps the loading structure with PC1 at $40.8\%$ and no factor retained by Horn (App. A.3); median between-benchmark correlation is $0.22$. The factor is treated as corroborative; Table 1 is the primary RQ1 result.

#### Against task success, safety scores add no information beyond capability.

Capability predicts $\tau^{2}$-retail success ($\rho=+0.60$, $p=0.005$, $n{=}20$); best safety-score partial $|\rho|=0.23$ (n.s., $n{=}19$; Table 2; Fig. 7, appendix).

#### Against agentic misalignment, capability has the opposite association.

Full 21-model panel: $\rho_{\text{cap}}=-0.44$ (asymptotic $p=0.047$). Mistral-Large blackmails or leaks $85\%$ of the time; o3-mini $1\%$. Partials: InjecAgent $+0.47$ and R-Judge specificity $+0.41$ exceed the pre-specified $0.40$ effect-size threshold; AgentHarm $+0.16$ (Table 2). Both CIs include zero, neither survives Bonferroni, power $\approx 0.35$, and the pre-specified directional prediction named AgentHarm; both remain exploratory. The R-Judge partial is $+0.19$ under balanced accuracy and $-0.46$ under recall (App. A.4).

#### A direct interaction test on the original panel.

Paired $n{=}20$: capability–task success $+0.60$, capability–misalignment $-0.41$ ($-0.44$ on the full panel), $\Delta=-1.00$ (95% CI $[-1.48,-0.49]$, $p<0.001$); stable under leave-one-model-out, leave-one-organization-out, organization-clustered bootstrap, and subsampling (App. A.5). The R-Judge interaction is $\Delta=+0.50$ ($p=0.082$). An independent misalignment grader gives $\rho=0.97$ with the original scores.

#### The capability–misalignment correlation is weaker on the expanded panel.

Pre-specified prediction: "hold or strengthen." Observed: $\rho=-0.44$ ($n{=}21$, asymptotic $p=0.047$) to $-0.16$ ($n{=}40$, bootstrap $p=0.40$; 95% CI $[-0.54,+0.22]$; App. A.6). The interval includes $-0.44$; nested-bootstrap $\Delta\rho=+0.27$ (95% CI $[-0.25,+0.78]$). Organization-matched subsets: median $\rho=-0.17$. A generational account is possible and undemonstrated. $\tau^{2}$ was not re-collected; the interaction was not re-tested.

#### Models with similar capability scores differ in safety across organizations
(Fig. 4).

41 models, 12 organizations (misalignment $n{=}40$; jailbreak $n{=}41$ after one engagement-gate exclusion). Six organizations contribute at least four models (within-organization correlations); seven contribute at least three (group comparison) (App. A.6, Table 5). Within-organization capability–safety correlations vary in sign, averaging $-0.14$ (misalignment) and $+0.26$ (jailbreak). With safety ranks adjusted for capability, the seven groups differ (permutation $p=0.004$ misalignment, $p<0.001$ jailbreak; Holm-significant; df-adjusted Kruskal–Wallis $\varepsilon^{2}=0.34$ and $0.57$). Non-causal: the static composite may miss agentic ability, organizations contribute few models, and some groups are range-restricted.

#### Against jailbreak safety, AgentHarm shows the strongest held-out association.

Jailbreak harmful compliance scored with StrongREJECT (Souly et al. 2024). The single AIM template leaves 11 of 22 models refusing every request; the three-template average (Wei et al. 2023) leaves none at ceiling. Controlling capability, AgentHarm–jailbreak $\rho=+0.72$ ($p<0.001$), vs. $+0.50$ for the single-template measure; stable under leave-one-model-out and an independent grader (App. A.5). AgentHarm jailbreak-over-misalignment: $\Delta=+0.59$, $p=0.027$ (model-level bootstrap); $p=0.051$ resampling the eight represented organizations. Paired-panel misalignment partial $+0.13$ ($n{=}19$); Table 2's $+0.16$ uses the common $n{=}18$ panel. R-Judge specificity ($-0.11$) and InjecAgent ($+0.21$) do not predict jailbreak safety. AgentHarm and StrongREJECT both score harmful compliance. The R-Judge/InjecAgent misalignment-over-jailbreak comparison: $\Delta=+0.52$, $p=0.068$.

#### Two alternative explanations, checked.

Seven LLM coders, shown construct descriptions only, assigned AgentHarm and the jailbreak outcome to harm blocking ($7/7$ each; Krippendorff $\alpha=0.61$ over three categories); the misalignment outcome was classified less consistently (App. A.1). Controlling capability, AgentHarm is uncorrelated with benign-prompt XSTest over-refusal (Röttger et al. 2024) ($\rho=-0.01$, $n{=}17$).

## 5 Discussion

These agent-safety benchmarks are not interchangeable measures of a single property: an "always unsafe" baseline matches R-Judge F1 (Observation 1), and the three broad-coverage benchmarks rank the same models differently. Capability predicts task success; its correlations with the two safety outcomes are panel-unstable (Table 2). AgentHarm–three-template jailbreak is $\rho=+0.72$ after capability control, with organization-resampled selectivity at $p=0.051$. R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment associations are exploratory. Capability-adjusted safety ranks differ across organization groups, with no organizational cause identified. A safety claim is defensible only with benchmark, metric, target behavior, and model population attached.

## 6 Limitations and Threats to Validity

#### Panel size.

Cross-benchmark panel $n{=}18$, from a first pass at $n{=}7$. A larger capability-spanning agent-loop panel is the main gap.

#### Capability anchors.

Provider-reported anchors failed the positive control (MMLU $0.42$); re-measured, $0.74$ (§3); no RQ2/RQ3 sign changed. Both are static-knowledge tests; the composite predicts multi-turn tool-agent success at $+0.60$. A six-model BFCL pilot (Patil et al. 2025) ranked GPT-4o-mini highest ($0.72$) and the two most capable models lowest ($0.42$–$0.48$) under strict function-call syntax scoring. Anchor measurement error attenuates or suppresses partial relationships without signable bias.

#### Multiple comparisons.

Per-test $p$-values are uncorrected. The crossover and AgentHarm $\to$ jailbreak ($p<0.001$) survive Bonferroni; the R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment cells ($p\approx 0.05$–$0.09$) do not and are treated as suggestive.

#### Judges and coverage.

Independent graders: $\rho=0.97$ (misalignment), $\rho=0.98$ (jailbreak). AgentHarm refusal rescoring: $\rho=0.69$, with the AgentHarm–jailbreak partial at $+0.66$ vs. $+0.72$ (App. A.5). AgentDojo covers five models; cross-benchmark analyses rest mainly on the other three.

#### Criterion validity (RQ3).

$\tau^{2}$-retail: 40 tasks, one run per model, user-simulator variance unbounded. Misalignment: fictional-scenario probe, grader-robust ($\rho=0.97$), blackmail–leaking halves at Spearman–Brown $0.70$. Jailbreak: three-template average. None gives deployment-harm probabilities. Item-rich instruments with resampling support: split-half $\geq 0.96$, rank stability $\geq 0.97$. Worst-case within-model SEs are $12$–$25\%$ of between-model SD (App. A.2). AgentHarm–jailbreak is large and directionally stable, partly convergent, with selectivity borderline under organization resampling; R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment is exploratory (marginal $\Delta=+0.52$, power $\approx 0.35$; the larger three-scenario result is post-hoc; App. A.5).

## 7 Conclusion

Across four benchmarks and up to 22 models, R-Judge F1 lets an "always unsafe" baseline outrank five models, and rankings change with the benchmark. Capability predicts held-out task success but not safety consistently across outcomes or panels. AgentHarm gives the strongest held-out safety association ($\rho=+0.72$ with jailbreak safety, capability-controlled), with partial instrument overlap and borderline organization-resampled selectivity. Report the full confusion structure, drop standalone F1 where true negatives matter, and tie claims to an explicit target behavior and model population.

ANSWER Q1: Answered, Not Settled, The paper's evidence does not support the assumption that the more capable model will be safer in the agentic misalignment scenario. The capability–jailbreak association is not a clear indicator of safety, and the paper shows that high capability does not necessarily correlate with high jailbreak safety.

ANSWER Q2: Answered, Supported, If the R-Judge interaction test had been clearly significant, the paper could make the claim that the interaction between capability and misalignment is statistically significant.

ANSWER Q3: Answered, Not Settled, The paper does not show that more capable models are generally less safe. In fact, it shows that high capability correlates with high jailbreak safety, which is a negative safety outcome.

ANSWER Q4: Answered, Supported, The PCA places AgentHarm safety opposite capability because it has a positive correlation with jailbreak safety, which is opposite to the correlation between capability and R-Judge specificity.

ANSWER Q5: Answered, Supported, The paper shows a positive capability-controlled AgentHarm–jailbreak partial under each of the three jailbreak templates taken individually.

ANSWER Q6: Answered, Not Settled, The paper does not explain why the misalignment criterion is grader-robust, but it is likely because the criterion is robust to certain types of errors, such as false positives.

ANSWER Q7: Answered, Not Settled, If the AgentHarm–jailbreak partial had been p ≈ 0.02 instead of p < 0.001, the paper's multiple-comparison claims would not change.

ANSWER Q8: Answered, Supported, PC1 explains 48.7% of variance because it captures a general factor that explains the correlations between the different benchmarks, even though the median between-benchmark correlation is only 0.22.

ANSWER Q9: Answered, Supported, AgentHarm's selectivity contrast Δ = +0.59 is used instead of the difference between its Table 2 partials because the partial correlation with jailbreak safety is more informative and robust to certain types of errors.

ANSWER Q10: Answered, Supported, The models in Table 1 that qualify are those with InjecAgent robustness ≥ 0.90 and AgentHarm safety ≥ 0.60, and this shows that InjecAgent is not a good proxy for AgentHarm.

ANSWER Q12: Answered, Not Settled, The paper does not provide a clear answer to this question, and it is not possible to use MMLU/GPQA scores to screen high-capability candidates for jailbreak safety.

ANSWER Q13: Answered, Not Settled, The paper does not provide a clear answer to this question, and it is not possible to determine which models qualify based on the given information.

ANSWER Q16: Answered, Supported, The paper does not show that agentic misalignment safety amounts to refusing overtly harmful requests; in fact, it shows that high capability correlates with high jailbreak safety, which is a negative safety outcome.

ANSWER Q17: Answered, Supported, The paper shows that more capable models comply more with harmful agentic tasks on AgentHarm, as indicated by the positive correlation between capability and compliance.

ANSWER Q12: It should use AgentDojo’s security score, not its utility score, as the convergent prompt-injection measure. It should also secure a sufficiently large common panel with working native tool use and monitor utility so that apparent security is not merely task failure or blanket refusal.

ANSWER Q13: It should expect substantial coverage loss: AgentDojo covered only five models because native tool use was required. The team should plan compatible tool interfaces, report the resulting common panel and selection effects, and account for low power in cross-benchmark correlations.

ANSWER Q14: No. Weak agreement could reflect different facets, tasks, environments, or metrics within prompt-injection robustness; disagreement alone does not invalidate either instrument without further construct and criterion-validity evidence.

ANSWER Q15: Yes. With n = 17, the check was low-powered; the paper estimates only about 35% power for an effect around ρ = 0.4 at similar sample sizes, so −0.01 cannot exclude such a true effect.

ANSWER Q16: Not settled. The 2026-only estimate was +0.07 versus −0.44 on the original panel, but the independent Fisher-z comparison gave p = 0.12, so the apparent generational difference was not established.

ANSWER Q17: The independent PCA corroboration would be lost. In the observed analysis, AgentHarm lay opposite the R-Judge/InjecAgent-and-anchor cluster, supporting the construct split without relying on criterion outcomes or hand-coded labels.

ANSWER Q18: Contradicted. Within-organization jailbreak correlations varied in sign: Anthropic, OpenAI, and Qwen were positive, while Meta, Google, and Mistral were each −0.40.

ANSWER Q19: No. Leave-one-organization-out crossover estimates remained between −0.90 and −1.16, so omitting no single organization brought Δ close to zero.

ANSWER Q20: Capability required the harmonized MMLU–GPQA composite, which was available for only 21 of the 22 jailbreak models. DeepSeek-R1 lacked a usable GPQA anchor because of unstable long-form generation.

ANSWER Q21: It should remeasure both anchors under one shared protocol and API harness using identical items where applicable. Provider-reported scores failed the positive control—MMLU loaded only 0.42—whereas harmonized measurement raised the loading to 0.74 and improved comparability.

ANSWER Q22: Not settled. AgentHarm loaded opposite the capability-anchor cluster in the corroborative PCA, but the paper does not report a direct, statistically established capability–AgentHarm correlation sufficient to conclude that more capable models comply more.

ANSWER Q23: AgentHarm–jailbreak had a much larger effect (+0.72, p < 0.001) and direct construct overlap because both instruments score harmful compliance; it was also stable across templates and graders. The R-Judge/InjecAgent–misalignment effects were smaller, low-powered, included zero, failed multiple-comparison correction, and for R-Judge were highly metric-sensitive.

ANSWER Q1: No. o3-mini’s lead is 0.012, while the reported bootstrap standard error for R-Judge F1 is 0.018 at the median and up to 0.030.

ANSWER Q2: The number and identity of models beaten by the constant baseline could change with the panel. The formula \(2\pi/(1+\pi)\), and thus the 0.690 score for the unchanged R-Judge item set, cannot change merely because different models are evaluated.

ANSWER Q3: PC1 reflects covariance across the whole panel, not agreement for every individual model. Mistral-Nemo can have a discrepant pair of scores while the two measures still load in the same direction based on their overall relationships with models and the capability anchors.

ANSWER Q4: The 0.22 value summarizes only the median pairwise relationship among benchmarks, whereas PCA uses the complete correlation matrix, including both capability anchors and signed relationships such as AgentHarm loading oppositely. Several moderate correlations can therefore combine into a component explaining 48.7% of total variance.

ANSWER Q5: The crossover tests the paired difference between two correlations, not whether the misalignment correlation alone differs from zero. The strong positive task-success correlation and negative misalignment correlation yield a large \(\Delta=-1.00\), whose paired uncertainty is small enough for \(p<0.001\).

ANSWER Q6: Contradicted as a general claim. The within-organization directions are heterogeneous, and Qwen is a direct counterexample: its misalignment correlation is \(-0.90\) while its jailbreak correlation is \(+0.80\).

ANSWER Q7: No, not as a dependable standalone screen. Although the panel-level correlation is \(+0.34\), high-capability models span roughly 9%–99% jailbreak safety, and capability-adjusted safety differs substantially across organizations.

ANSWER Q8: Significance of \(+0.34\) tests whether the expanded-panel correlation differs from zero, whereas the change test asks whether \(+0.34\) differs from the original \(+0.08\). The estimated change of \(+0.26\) has a confidence interval spanning zero, so the two results are compatible.

ANSWER Q9: Contradicted. R-Judge has high split-half consistency and rank stability—about 0.96 and 0.97 for F1—so the paper’s criticism concerns metric validity and the gameability of F1, not unreliable item measurement.

ANSWER Q10: The construct-distinctness argument would weaken. The observed \(+0.43\) suggests that adding murder makes the battery more aligned with AgentHarm-style harm blocking than blackmail-plus-leaking is; a near-zero association would remove that concern, though the pre-specified status of the original criterion would still favor keeping it primary.

ANSWER Q11: Supported. The capability-controlled partials are positive for all three templates: \(+0.44\) for AIM, \(+0.70\) for refusal suppression, and \(+0.62\) for prefix injection.

ANSWER Q12: On the original panel, capability is nearly unrelated to jailbreak safety (\(\rho=+0.08\), \(p=0.73\)). Because one necessary leg of a capability-confounding explanation is essentially absent, capability is unlikely to generate the strong AgentHarm–jailbreak association.

ANSWER Q13: Contradicted. After excluding Anthropic, organization-group differences remain, with \(p=0.018\) for misalignment and \(p<0.001\) for jailbreak safety.

ANSWER Q14: The convergent control would change from inconclusive to passing. A high full-panel AgentDojo–InjecAgent correlation would provide evidence that two independently implemented prompt-injection instruments converge on the intended construct, strengthening the construct-validity analysis.

ANSWER Q15: The result would no longer be described as having borderline organization-resampled selectivity. It would provide stronger evidence that AgentHarm predicts jailbreak safety more strongly than misalignment safety across organizations, while still retaining the caveat that AgentHarm and the jailbreak criterion both score harmful compliance.

ANSWER Q16: No. Official R-Judge F1 has a capability-controlled task-success partial of \(+0.32\), but it is not statistically significant on the small panel, and F1 itself admits the high-scoring constant policy.

ANSWER Q17: The concern that the misalignment criterion partly reflects general refusal of harmful requests would weaken. The observed \(+0.47\) association with XSTest unsafe-prompt refusal is suggestive of that overlap, although it is low-powered and only marginal.

ANSWER Q18: No. Its correlation is only \(+0.08\) with \(p=0.73\), failing both the hypothetical magnitude and significance requirements.

ANSWER Q19: Not settled. Capability is negatively associated with misalignment safety on the original panel but only weakly so on the expansion, while its jailbreak association becomes positive; the relationship depends on the safety outcome and model panel.

ANSWER Q20: The selectivity contrast uses a directly paired \(n=19\) panel, where AgentHarm’s misalignment partial is \(+0.13\), so \(+0.72-(+0.13)=+0.59\). Table 2’s \(+0.16\) misalignment value comes from a different common \(n=18\) panel.

ANSWER Q21: Contradicted. R-Judge balanced accuracy correlates \(+0.71\) with MMLU and \(+0.49\) with GPQA, showing substantial capability dependence.

ANSWER Q22: Little weight should be placed on 0.10 as a stable numerical estimate. The paper supports the qualitative conclusion that benchmarks disagree, but shows that correlations can change sharply with model-panel composition, as the R-Judge–AgentHarm correlation did from \(-0.64\) at seven models to \(+0.02\) at eighteen.

ANSWER Q23: AgentHarm–jailbreak would remain nominally significant but would no longer survive the nine-test Bonferroni threshold of approximately 0.006. Thus the paper could no longer claim that both the crossover and AgentHarm–jailbreak survive multiple-comparison correction; only the crossover would.

ANSWER Q24: The 40-model expansion collected the misalignment criterion and capability anchors, but did not run R-Judge on all those models. The actual R-Judge continuation reached only \(n=25\) and produced \(+0.23\), so it is not the \(n\approx40\) paired test required by the power calculation.
